themes.title: Oneness of Allah
themes.hook: The first truth every prophet taught: God is One, without partner, son or equal.
overview: Tawhid, the oneness of God, is the centre of the Qur'an. Every other teaching, from prayer to justice, rests on it. The shortest statement is Surah al-Ikhlas: God is One, the Eternal Refuge, who neither begets nor is born, with nothing equal to Him.

The Qur'an does not only declare tawhid; it argues for it. If there were other gods, the heavens and earth would have fallen into disorder (21:22). False gods cannot create even a fly (22:73), cannot answer prayers, and cannot help themselves. The order of creation points to one Creator.

Its opposite is shirk, giving any share of God's divinity to another. The Qur'an calls it the greatest injustice and the one sin God does not forgive if a person dies upon it, while every other sin remains open to His forgiveness. Shirk is not only idol worship: it includes claiming that God has a son or partner, and devoting worship sincerely meant for God to anyone else.

Tawhid is also described as natural: every soul bore witness to its Lord before birth (7:172), and the human being is created on an inborn disposition (fitrah) that recognises Him (30:30). Every messenger, from Nuh to Muhammad ﷺ, came with the same call: worship God alone.
lessons: Tawhid is the foundation; every act of worship and every moral rule rests on it.
The order of the universe is itself an argument for one Creator.
Shirk includes devotion given to anyone besides God, not only idols.
Sincerity, devoting worship to God alone, is tawhid lived in practice.

p.l: The whole of tawhid in four verses: One, Eternal, unbegotten, without equal
Your God is one God; none is worthy of worship but Him
The Verse of the Throne: the Ever-Living, Self-Sustaining, owner of all
God, the angels and those of knowledge bear witness that He is One
God speaks to Musa: I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me
An oath that your God is One, Lord of the heavens and the earth
If there were other gods besides God, heaven and earth would be ruined
Each god would have taken away what it created and sought to overcome the others
Had there been other gods, they would have sought a way to the Owner of the Throne
Who created, who answers the desperate, who guides in darkness? Is there a god with God?
Creation, night and day, ships, rain and winds as signs for those who reason

subs.t: He has no son or partner

p.l: How could He have a son when He has no companion and created all things?
The claim that the Most Merciful took a son nearly splits the heavens
Praise to God who has no son, no partner in dominion, and no protector out of weakness
He has not taken a son nor had a partner in dominion
Even the jinn declare He has taken neither wife nor son
God does not forgive association with Him but forgives what is less for whom He wills
Association with God is a far-reaching error
Luqman's first counsel: association with God is a great injustice
Even a prophet's deeds would be void if he associated others with God
Whoever associates with God is like one who falls from the sky
Isa himself said: whoever associates others with God, Paradise is forbidden to him
Those you call upon could never create a fly, even if they all joined together
They do not own even the skin of a date seed, nor hear your call
Idols that create nothing, are themselves created, and cannot help themselves
Who is more astray than one who calls on what will not answer him till the Day?
Taking protectors other than God is like the spider's flimsy house

subs.t: The witness within and sincere devotion

p.l: Before birth every soul testified: Are You not our Lord? Yes
The fitrah of God upon which He created mankind
They were commanded only to worship God, sincere in religion to Him
Pure devotion belongs to God alone, not to intermediaries
You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help
Every messenger was told: there is no god but Me, so worship Me
To every nation a messenger: worship God and avoid false gods
Nuh's call: worship God; you have no god other than Him
Hud's call to 'Ad, in the same words

themes.title: Names and Attributes of Allah
themes.hook: God introduces Himself through His most beautiful names, and invites us to call on Him by them.
overview: The Qur'an speaks of God not in abstractions but through names: the Most Merciful, the Forgiving, the All-Knowing, the Subtle, the Just. "To God belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them" (7:180). Knowing these names is how the believer comes to know whom he worships, and how he speaks to Him in prayer.

Some passages gather many names together. The end of Surah al-Hashr (59:22-24) lists sixteen in three verses; the Verse of the Throne (2:255) describes His life, sustaining power, knowledge and dominion; the opening of Surah al-Hadid (57:1-6) calls Him the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden.

Two principles run through every name. First, nothing is like Him (42:11): His hearing and seeing are real, but unlike any creature's. Second, mercy leads: "My mercy encompasses all things" (7:156), and He has written mercy upon Himself (6:12).

The Qur'an also closes many verses with pairs of names, such as Forgiving and Merciful, or Mighty and Wise. Each pair suits what the verse has just described, so reading the closing names is a key to the verse's message.
lessons: Call on God by the name that fits your need: the Forgiving when you have sinned, the Provider when you are in need.
God's attributes are real but unlike anything in creation.
Mercy is written into God's own description of Himself.
Notice the names that close a verse; they explain it.

subs.t: The command to call on Him by His names

p.l: To God belong the most beautiful names, so call on Him by them
Call Him Allah or call Him the Most Merciful; to Him belong the best names
God, there is no god but Him; to Him belong the best names
Sixteen names in three verses: the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Creator, the Fashioner
The Ever-Living, the Sustainer, who neither sleeps nor tires, whose Throne holds the heavens and earth
The First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, who is with you wherever you are
The Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful, Lord of the worlds, Master of the Day
Owner of sovereignty who gives and takes it, honours and humbles, brings life from death
The Mighty, the Knowing, Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, severe in penalty
He has decreed mercy upon Himself
Whoever does wrong in ignorance then repents, He is Forgiving and Merciful
My mercy encompasses all things
Do not despair of God's mercy; He forgives all sins
I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and My punishment is the painful one
The Forgiving, the Affectionate, Owner of the Throne, doer of what He wills
With Him are the keys of the unseen; not a leaf falls but He knows it
We are closer to him than his jugular vein
I am near; I answer the call of the caller
Does He not know, He who created, when He is the Subtle, the Acquainted?
A mustard seed hidden in a rock: God is Subtle and Acquainted
His command when He wills a thing is only to say Be, and it is
Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, who created death and life to test you
To God belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth
Nothing in the heavens or the earth can escape Him
There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing
Vision does not perceive Him, but He perceives all vision
There is none comparable to Him
The angels: You are the Knowing, the Wise
Isa: if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise
Whoever does wrong then seeks forgiveness will find God Forgiving, Merciful

themes.title: Favours of Allah
themes.hook: If you tried to count God's favours you could never number them; the Qur'an asks us to notice them.
overview: Much of the Qur'an is a reminder of blessings. It names them one by one: the human form, hearing and sight, speech, the pen, the earth spread out, rain, crops, fruit, livestock, milk and honey, the sea and its ships, homes, spouses and children, security and food. Then it adds that they can never be fully counted (14:34; 16:18).

Surah ar-Rahman turns the list into a refrain, asking thirty-one times: "Which of your Lord's favours will you deny?" The question is not rhetorical decoration. Every favour carries a claim on the one who receives it: to recognise its Giver.

The greatest favour named is guidance: sending a messenger who recites God's verses and purifies people (3:164), and completing the religion (5:3). Material blessings are a means; guidance is the end.

Favours are also a test. Sulayman, shown a miracle, said "This is from my Lord's favour, to test whether I will be grateful" (27:40). Gratitude brings increase (14:7); ingratitude brings loss, as the people of Saba' learned when their gardens were swept away (34:15-17). Every person will be asked about the pleasures they were given (102:8).
lessons: Make a habit of naming God's favours; the Qur'an models it.
Guidance is the greatest blessing, above health and wealth.
Gratitude increases blessing; ingratitude erodes it.
Every blessing is also a test, and will be asked about.

p.l: Sky, water, ships, rivers, sun, moon, night and day: if you count them you cannot number them
If you counted God's favours you could not number them; He is Forgiving, Merciful
He has lavished His favours on you, apparent and hidden
The earth, its fruit and grain: which of your Lord's favours will you deny?
Created in the best of forms
He created you, proportioned you and balanced you
Brought out of the womb knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight and hearts
Two eyes, a tongue, two lips, and the two paths shown
The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an, created man and taught him speech
He taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know

subs.t: Earth, sky and the rhythm of life

p.l: The earth a resting place, mountains as pegs, sleep for rest, rain and gardens
The earth a bed, the sky a structure, rain and fruit as provision
If night or day were made endless, who could bring the other?
Rain, crops, sun and moon, colours of the earth, the sea, and stars for guidance
The crops you sow, the water you drink, the fire you kindle: who made them?
Let man look at his food: rain, grain, grapes, olives, dates, gardens
The dead earth revived, grain, palms and grapes
If your water sank away, who could bring you flowing water?
Livestock for warmth, food, beauty and carrying loads; horses, mules and donkeys
We made livestock for them to ride and eat, with other benefits and drinks
Pure milk from between dung and blood
The bee, and the drink of various colours that is healing for people
The sea for fresh meat, ornaments, and ships that seek His bounty
Two seas, sweet and salt, both giving food and ornaments
Two seas meeting with a barrier, pearls and coral, ships like mountains
Spouses from among yourselves, and from them children and grandchildren
Homes as rest, tents of hide, shade, mountains as shelter, garments
Spouses for tranquillity, with affection and mercy between you
Quraysh fed against hunger and made safe from fear
God conferred a great favour in sending a messenger who recites and purifies
Today I have perfected your religion and completed My favour upon you
You were enemies and He joined your hearts; by His favour you became brothers
He found you an orphan and sheltered you; proclaim your Lord's favour
If you are grateful, I will surely increase you
Remember Me and I will remember you; be grateful and do not deny Me
Sulayman: this is from my Lord's favour, to test whether I am grateful
Few of My servants are grateful
Saba': two gardens, then ingratitude, and the flood of the dam
A town secure and provided for, which denied God's favours
Then you will be asked that Day about the pleasures

themes.title: Whom Allah loves, and whom He does not
themes.hook: The Qur'an names the qualities God loves and the ones He does not, so we know what to become.
overview: Rather than only listing commands, the Qur'an describes people God loves and people He does not love. The lists are short, concrete and repeated, so they work as a mirror.

God loves those who do good (muhsinun), those who repent and purify themselves, the God-conscious, the patient, those who rely on Him, the just, and those who stand together in His cause like a solid structure. The way to His love is to follow the Messenger (3:31).

He does not love aggressors, those who spread corruption, the wrongdoers, the arrogant and boastful, the treacherous, the wasteful, and those who gloat over their wealth. Most of these are not ritual failings but failings of character and of how people treat others.
The pattern is a reminder that God's love is not inherited or claimed; it follows qualities that anyone can choose to build, and it is lost through qualities anyone can choose to abandon.
lessons: Use the two lists as a self-check: which qualities do I carry?
God's love follows character and conduct, not lineage or claims.
Repentance itself is beloved to God; falling is not the end.
Arrogance, waste and treachery cut a person off from His love.

p.l: Spend in God's way and do good; God loves the doers of good
God loves those who repent and those who purify themselves
Whoever fulfils his commitment and fears God, God loves the righteous
Those who spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger and pardon people
God loves the steadfast
Consult them, then rely on God; He loves those who rely on Him
Judge with justice; God loves those who act justly
Make peace between them justly; God loves the just
God loves those who fight in His cause in a row, like a solid structure
A mosque founded on righteousness, with men who love to purify themselves
A people He will love and who will love Him, humble with believers
Fight those who fight you but do not transgress; God does not love transgressors
One who spreads corruption on earth; God does not like corruption
God does not like the wrongdoers
God does not like the self-deluding and boastful
God does not love the habitually sinful deceiver
Do not be excessive; He does not like those who commit excess
Eat and drink but do not waste; He does not like the wasteful
God does not like traitors
He does not like the arrogant
Qarun's people: do not exult; God does not like the exultant
So that you do not despair or exult; God does not like the proud and boastful
If you love God, follow me; God will love you and forgive your sins
The Most Merciful will place affection for those who believe and do good

themes.title: Divine decree and why suffering exists
themes.hook: Everything happens by God's measure, yet people choose and are responsible; hardship is a test with hidden wisdom.
overview: The Qur'an holds two truths together. Everything is created in measure (54:49); nothing happens outside God's knowledge and will. And human beings choose: "whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). People are judged for what they choose, not for what was hidden from them.

Why then is there suffering? The Qur'an's first answer is that life is a test: God created death and life "to test which of you is best in deed" (67:2). Fear, hunger and loss are named as part of that test, with good news for the patient (2:155-157).

Its second answer is hidden wisdom. In the story of Musa and Khidr (18:65-82), a ship is damaged, a boy dies and a wall is rebuilt for no visible reason, and each act turns out to serve a mercy that only God could see. "Perhaps you dislike something and it is good for you" (2:216).

Its third answer is accountability: much harm comes from what people's own hands have earned (30:41; 42:30). Finally, no soul is burdened beyond its capacity (2:286), and with hardship comes ease, twice promised (94:5-6). The believer's response is patience, trust and continued effort.
lessons: Belief in decree is not passivity: we act, and leave results to God.
Hardship is a test, not a sign of being abandoned.
What looks like loss may hide a mercy we cannot see yet.
No burden is beyond what a soul can bear, and ease follows hardship.

p.l: We created everything with a measure
He created all things and determined them precisely
No disaster strikes except it is in a register before it happens, so you do not grieve or exult
Not a leaf falls but He knows it
God has set for everything a measure
The truth is from your Lord; whoever wills, let him believe
We guided him to the way, whether he be grateful or ungrateful
The soul was inspired with its wickedness and righteousness; he succeeds who purifies it
God does not change a people until they change what is in themselves
For whoever wills to take a straight way, though you do not will except as God wills
He created death and life to test which of you is best in deed
Fear, hunger, loss of wealth and lives: give good news to the patient
Do people think they will be left to say we believe and not be tested?
We test you with evil and good as a trial
You will surely be tested in your wealth and yourselves
We will test you until We make evident the strivers and the patient
Musa and Khidr: a damaged boat, a boy, a wall, and the mercy behind each
Perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you
You may dislike a thing while God makes in it much good

subs.t: Calamity, permission and our own deeds

p.l: No disaster strikes except by God's permission; He guides the heart of whoever believes
Whatever strikes you is for what your hands have earned, and He pardons much
Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned
With hardship comes ease; truly with hardship comes ease
God will bring ease after hardship
God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity
Nothing will happen to us except what God has decreed; He is our protector
No soul dies except by God's permission at a decreed time
Even had you stayed in your homes, those decreed to be killed would have gone out

themes.title: The human–God relationship
themes.hook: God is near, answers, loves and protects; the human worships, trusts, remembers and returns.
overview: The Qur'an describes a relationship, not only a law. On God's side: He is near, closer than the jugular vein (50:16); He answers the caller (2:186); He remembers those who remember Him (2:152); He loves and is loved (5:54); He is the protector who brings believers out of darkness into light (2:257).

On the human side: the purpose of creation is worship (51:56), which in the Qur'an's wide sense means living for God in every act. It includes trust (tawakkul), remembrance, gratitude, repentance and hope.

The relationship survives failure. The most hopeful verse addresses those who have wronged themselves: "Do not despair of God's mercy; He forgives all sins" (39:53). The door of return stays open as long as life lasts.

Its end is described as mutual pleasure: "God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him" (98:8), and the tranquil soul is invited: "Return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing" (89:27-30).
lessons: God's nearness is the starting point of prayer: you do not need an intermediary to call Him.
Worship is a whole life lived for God, not only rituals.
Failure does not end the relationship; returning to God does.
The goal is mutual pleasure: being content with God and He with you.

p.l: When My servants ask about Me, I am near; I answer the caller
We are nearer to him than his jugular vein
He is with you wherever you are
No three converse privately but He is the fourth
At death We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see
Call upon Me; I will respond to you
Who responds to the desperate one when he calls?
Remember Me and I will remember you

subs.t: Love between God and His servants

p.l: A people He will love and who will love Him
If you love God, follow me and God will love you
Those who believe are stronger in love for God
Whoever fears God, He makes a way out; whoever relies on Him, He is sufficient
God is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs
God is the ally of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light
God is the protector of those who believe
O My servants who have wronged themselves, do not despair of God's mercy
Whoever does wrong then seeks God's forgiveness will find Him Forgiving
I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me
Worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty
O tranquil soul, return to your Lord, well-pleased and pleasing
God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him

themes.title: Angels
themes.hook: Honoured servants of God who never disobey: bearers of revelation, recorders of deeds and helpers of believers.
overview: Belief in angels is part of faith (2:285). The Qur'an describes them as created beings with wings, "two, three or four" (35:1), who glorify God night and day without tiring (21:19-20) and do whatever they are commanded (66:6). They are servants, not daughters or partners of God, a claim the Qur'an firmly rejects.

Their roles are named. Jibril, the Trustworthy Spirit, brought the Qur'an to the Prophet's heart (26:193-195). Angels record every word and deed (50:17-18; 82:10-12). The angel of death takes souls at their appointed time (32:11). Angels guard Hell (66:6; 74:30) and greet the people of Paradise (39:73).

Angels also accompany human history. They bowed to Adam at God's command (2:34). They brought news of sons to Ibrahim and Zakariya, and of Isa to Maryam. They were sent to the people of Lut. At Badr they were sent to strengthen the believers (8:9-12), and on the Night of Decree they descend with every matter (97:4).

For the believer, angels are a source of company and encouragement: they pray for forgiveness for those on earth (42:5; 40:7-9) and descend on those who stand firm, saying "Do not fear and do not grieve" (41:30).
lessons: Every word and act is recorded; live as one who is witnessed.
The angels pray for the believers; you are not alone in your effort.
Angels are honoured servants, never objects of worship.

p.l: God made angels messengers with wings, two, three and four
They exalt Him night and day and do not weaken
Not daughters of God but honoured servants who act by His command
They prostrate to God, are not arrogant, and do what they are commanded
Stern and severe angels who never disobey God
Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, it is he who brought it down to your heart
The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart in clear Arabic
Taught by one intense in strength, who came near and revealed
The word of a noble messenger, with power, obeyed and trustworthy
The Pure Spirit brought it down from your Lord in truth
The angels' question, Adam taught the names, and the command to prostrate
The angels prostrated, all of them together, except Iblis
Two receivers, on the right and the left; not a word is uttered but an observer is ready
Noble recorders who know whatever you do
Our messengers are with them, recording
The angel of death will take you, who has been entrusted with you
Our messengers take him at death and do not fail in their duty
Angels striking the faces and backs of those who disbelieved
The angels take the good, saying: peace be upon you, enter Paradise
At Badr: three thousand, then five thousand angels
A thousand angels following one another, and steadfastness given to hearts
Angels descend on those who stand firm: do not fear and do not grieve
Those who carry the Throne ask forgiveness for the believers
The angels ask forgiveness for those on earth
Over it are nineteen; We have not made the keepers of the Fire except angels
They will call: O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us
The keepers of Paradise: peace be upon you, you have become pure

subs.t: Angels sent to prophets and people

p.l: Messengers come to Ibrahim with good news of Ishaq
Ibrahim's guests, then the messengers to the family of Lut
The angels called Zakariya while he stood praying
The angels said: O Maryam, God has chosen you
On the Night of Decree the angels and the Spirit descend
Two angels at Babylon who warned they were only a trial
Those who do not believe in the Hereafter name the angels female names
They made the angels, servants of the Most Merciful, females
Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?

themes.title: Jinn
themes.hook: A creation of smokeless fire, accountable like humans, some believing and some not.
overview: The jinn are a hidden creation made from smokeless fire (55:15), before humans were made from clay. Like humans, they were created to worship God (51:56), they have free choice, and they will be judged. The Qur'an often addresses the two together: "O company of jinn and men" (55:33).

A whole surah, al-Jinn, tells how a group of jinn heard the Qur'an and said "We have heard an amazing recitation; it guides to the right way, and we have believed in it" (72:1-2). They describe that among them are the righteous and others, and that they used to sit near heaven to eavesdrop until the sky was guarded.

The jinn served Sulayman by God's command, building and diving (34:12-13), yet they did not even know when he had died (34:14), proof that they do not know the unseen. Iblis himself was one of the jinn (18:50).
The Qur'an warns against seeking refuge with jinn, which only increased people in burden (72:6), and against fear of them: protection belongs to God alone.
lessons: The jinn do not know the unseen; fortune-telling built on them is false.
Seek refuge in God, not in any hidden creature.
Even unseen beings who heard the Qur'an were moved to believe.

p.l: Man from clay, and the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire
The jinn We created before from scorching fire
I created jinn and mankind only to worship Me
O company of jinn, did there not come to you messengers from among you?
Many of the jinn and mankind have hearts with which they do not understand
O company of jinn and men, if you can pass beyond the heavens, then pass

subs.t: The jinn who heard the Qur'an

p.l: A group of jinn heard the Qur'an and believed; among them righteous and otherwise
A company of jinn listened, then returned to their people as warners
Jinn worked for Sulayman; they did not know of his death until the termite
His soldiers of jinn, men and birds were gathered
A powerful one of the jinn offered to bring the throne
We found heaven filled with guards and flames
The stars as protection against every rebellious devil
Except one who steals a hearing; a clear flame pursues him
Men used to seek refuge with jinn, and it increased them in burden
They made the jinn partners with God, though He created them
Iblis was of the jinn and departed from his Lord's command
Even if mankind and jinn gathered, they could not produce the like of this Qur'an

themes.title: Iblis and Satan's tactics
themes.hook: The enemy who refused to bow: how he deceives, how far his power goes, and how to be protected.
overview: The story begins with pride. When God commanded the angels to bow to Adam, Iblis refused: "I am better than him; You created me from fire and him from clay" (7:12). He was expelled, asked for respite until the Day of Resurrection, and swore to sit on the straight path and come at people from front, behind, right and left (7:16-17).

The Qur'an then exposes his methods. He promises and creates false hopes (4:120). He threatens people with poverty and commands immorality (2:268). He works by small steps, "footsteps" (24:21). He makes evil look attractive (6:43), stirs enmity through wine and gambling (5:91), and sows discord between people through harsh words (17:53).

His power, however, is limited. He has no authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord (16:99), only over those who take him as an ally. On the Day of Judgment he will disown his followers: "I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me" (14:22).
The defence is named too: seeking refuge in God (7:200; surah 114), remembering God when a suggestion comes (7:201), and repentance after a fall, as Adam and Hawwa showed.
lessons: Pride, "I am better than him", was the first sin.
Satan works by small steps; resist the first step.
He has no real power over the sincere; his weapon is invitation.
When a suggestion comes, remember God and seek refuge in Him.

p.l: All prostrated except Iblis; he refused and was arrogant
I am better than him: You created me from fire and him from clay
He would not be among those who prostrate to a human made of clay
Shall I prostrate to one You created from clay?
Pride made him one of the disbelievers
He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord
Reprieved until the Day; I will come at them from before and behind, right and left
I will make evil attractive to them, except Your sincere servants
By Your might, I will mislead them all, except the sincere
Satan whispered to them and swore he was a sincere adviser
Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that never decays?
He promises them and arouses false desires
Satan threatens you with poverty and orders you to immorality
Do not follow the footsteps of Satan
Satan made attractive to them what they were doing
Satan wants to cause enmity and hatred through intoxicants and gambling
Tell My servants to say what is best; Satan induces dissension
Incite with your voice, assault with your cavalry, share in wealth and children
Private conversation is from Satan, to grieve the believers
Satan is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy
Did I not enjoin you not to worship Satan? He is a clear enemy
Do not follow his footsteps; he orders evil and lies about God
Over My servants you have no authority
He has no authority over those who believe and rely on their Lord
Over My servants you have no authority; sufficient is your Lord as guardian
When an evil suggestion comes, seek refuge in God; the righteous remember and see clearly
My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils
When you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in God from Satan the expelled
Refuge in the Lord of mankind from the retreating whisperer
I had no authority over you except that I invited you, so do not blame me
Like Satan who says to man: disbelieve; then says: I am free of you
Satan is ever, to man, a deserter

themes.title: The soul
themes.hook: The spirit is from God's command; the self can command evil, reproach itself, or reach tranquillity.
overview: The Qur'an uses two words for the inner life. The ruh, spirit, is from God's command and beyond human knowledge: "They ask you about the spirit; say, the spirit is of the affair of my Lord, and you have been given little knowledge" (17:85). God breathed of His spirit into Adam (15:29), which is the source of human dignity.

The nafs, self, is the arena of moral struggle. God swears by it and says it was inspired with both its wickedness and its righteousness: "He has succeeded who purifies it, and failed who corrupts it" (91:7-10). Three states are named: the self that commands evil (12:53), the self that reproaches itself (75:2), and the tranquil self invited to return to its Lord pleased and pleasing (89:27-30).

Every soul will taste death (3:185), each night in a smaller way, as God takes souls in sleep and returns those whose time has not come (39:42). Each soul carries its own account: no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another (6:164), and no soul is burdened beyond its capacity (2:286).
lessons: Human dignity comes from the spirit God breathed into Adam.
The self can be trained: from commanding evil to reproaching itself to tranquillity.
Sleep is a daily reminder of death and return.
Each soul answers for itself alone.

p.l: The spirit is of the affair of my Lord; you have been given little knowledge
When I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit
He began the creation of man from clay, then breathed into him of His spirit
The soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except whom my Lord has mercy on
An oath by the self-reproaching soul
O tranquil soul, return to your Lord well-pleased and pleasing
The soul inspired with its wickedness and righteousness; he succeeds who purifies it
Whoever restrained the soul from desire, Paradise will be his refuge
God takes the souls at death, and those that do not die in their sleep
It is He who takes your souls by night
Every soul will taste death; you will be paid in full on the Day
Every soul will taste death; We test you with evil and good
Every soul will taste death, then to Us you will be returned
Every soul, for what it has earned, will be retained
No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another
God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity

subs.t: The soul at the moment of death

p.l: When the soul reaches the throat
When it reaches the collarbones, and it is said: who will cure him?
The angels extend their hands: discharge your souls

themes.title: Magic and dreams
themes.hook: Sorcery is real but powerless without God's permission; dreams can carry true meaning.
overview: The Qur'an treats magic as real but limited and forbidden. At Babylon people learned from the devils what could separate a man from his wife, "but they do not harm anyone through it except by God's permission" (2:102). Learning it brings harm, not benefit. Pharaoh's magicians cast ropes and staffs that seemed to move, but Musa's staff swallowed their illusions, and the magicians themselves fell in prostration and believed (7:109-126; 20:65-73).

Every prophet was accused of being a magician (51:52), and so was the Prophet ﷺ; the accusation was a way of avoiding the message. Protection from the harm of sorcery is sought in God alone: "from the evil of those who blow on knots" (113:4).

Dreams play a central role in the story of Yusuf: his dream of eleven stars, the sun and moon bowing to him; the dreams of his two prison companions; and the king's dream of seven fat and seven lean cows, whose interpretation saved Egypt from famine. Ibrahim's dream to sacrifice his son was a command and a test. The Prophet's dream of entering Makkah came true (48:27). The Qur'an also recognises "confused dreams" (12:44) that carry no meaning.
lessons: Sorcery cannot harm except by God's permission; seek protection in Him.
Truth outshines illusion, as the staff of Musa showed.
Some dreams carry meaning, but interpreting them needs knowledge.

subs.t: Magic: real but powerless without God's permission

p.l: What the devils taught at Babylon, and Harut and Marut's warning
What you have brought is magic; God will expose its worthlessness
Refuge from the evil of those who blow on knots
The magicians' ropes, the staff that swallowed them, and their belief
It seemed to him their ropes were moving; the magicians fell in prostration
The magicians gathered, defeated, and declared faith despite threats
No messenger came to those before them but they said: a magician or a madman
The disbelievers said: this is a magician and a liar
Is it a wonder that We revealed to a man from among them? They said: a clear magician
He thought and deliberated, then said: this is nothing but magic

subs.t: Dreams in the story of Yusuf

p.l: I saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to me
The prisoners' dreams of wine and bread, and their interpretation
The king's dream of seven fat cows and seven lean
This is the interpretation of my dream of before
O my son, I have seen in a dream that I sacrifice you
God has fulfilled His Messenger's vision in truth
God showed them to you in your dream as few
The vision We showed you was only a trial for the people
A mixture of false dreams, and we are not learned in interpreting them
They said: these are mixed false dreams

themes.title: Revelation and earlier scriptures
themes.hook: How God speaks to prophets, how the Qur'an came down, and its place among the books before it.
overview: The Qur'an explains how revelation (wahy) works: God speaks to a human only by inspiration, from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger angel (42:51). The Qur'an came through Jibril to the Prophet's heart (26:193-194), beginning with the command "Read" (96:1-5) on a blessed night in Ramadan, the Night of Decree (97:1; 2:185). It was then revealed in stages over about twenty-three years, so that hearts could be made firm (25:32).

The Prophet ﷺ did not compose it. He was unlettered and had not read any scripture before (29:48); he was told not to rush his tongue to memorise it, since its collection and recitation were God's responsibility (75:16-19).

The Qur'an places itself in a line of revelation: the Torah given to Musa, the Psalms (Zabur) to Dawud, the Gospel (Injil) to Isa, and the scrolls of Ibrahim and Musa. Believers are required to believe in all of them (2:285). The Qur'an confirms what came before and stands as a guardian over it (5:48), while noting that some earlier people altered words from their places (5:13).
Finally, God Himself promises to preserve it: "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian" (15:9).
lessons: Revelation is God's initiative; the Prophet ﷺ conveyed, he did not compose.
Believing in all earlier books is part of faith.
The Qur'an is the final, preserved reference that confirms and guards the earlier messages.

p.l: By inspiration, from behind a veil, or through a messenger
He does not speak from desire; it is only revelation revealed
The Trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart
Do not move your tongue to hasten it; its collection and recitation are on Us
Do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed
Read in the name of your Lord who created
O you who covers himself, arise and warn
O you who wraps himself, stand in the night

subs.t: The night and month of revelation

p.l: We sent it down on the Night of Decree, better than a thousand months
The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed
We sent it down on a blessed night
A Qur'an We separated, to recite to people over time
Why was it not revealed all at once? To strengthen your heart
He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance
We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light
We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light
And to David We gave the Psalms
To David We gave the book
This is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa
Has he not been informed of what was in the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim?
The Messenger and the believers believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers
We believe in what was revealed to us and to Ibrahim, Musa and Isa
Believe in God, His Messenger, and the Book He sent before
Confirming what preceded it and a criterion over it
A confirmation of what was before it and a detailed explanation
Some heard the word of God then distorted it; woe to those who write with their hands
They distort words from their places and forgot a portion of what they were reminded of
You did not recite any scripture before it, nor write one with your right hand
The unlettered Prophet, whom they find written in the Torah and the Gospel
We sent down the Reminder and We will be its guardian
Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it
A glorious Qur'an in a Preserved Tablet

themes.title: Names of the Qur'an
themes.hook: The Book, the Criterion, the Reminder, the Light, the Healing: each name shows another side of what the Qur'an is.
overview: The Qur'an names itself many times, and each name teaches something. It is al-Qur'an, the recitation, meant to be read aloud and lived. It is al-Kitab, the Book, written and preserved, "in which there is no doubt" (2:2). It is al-Furqan, the Criterion that separates truth from falsehood (25:1).

It is adh-Dhikr, the Reminder (15:9), because it recalls what the human heart already knows. It is Nur, a light that shows the way (4:174; 5:15), and Shifa', a healing for what is in the hearts (10:57; 17:82). It is guidance (huda) and mercy for those who believe.

Its descriptions add more: noble (56:77), glorious (85:21), wise (36:2), blessed (38:29), the best of statements, consistent and oft-repeated (39:23). Each title is also an instruction: a reminder must be remembered, a criterion must be used to judge, a light must be followed, and a healing must be taken.
lessons: Each name of the Qur'an is a way to use it: read it, judge by it, remember with it, be healed by it.
The Qur'an heals hearts first: doubt, hardness and sorrow.

p.l: This is the Book about which there is no doubt, guidance for the righteous
It is a noble Qur'an in a protected register, touched only by the purified
By the clear Book; in the Mother of the Book with Us
Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant
Guidance for people and clear proofs of guidance and criterion
This Qur'an guides to what is most upright
We sent down the Reminder
A blessed Book, that they might reflect and the people of understanding remember
We have made the Qur'an easy to remember
We have sent down to you a clear light
There has come to you a light and a clear Book
Instruction from your Lord, healing for what is in the breasts, guidance and mercy
We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers
We revealed to you a spirit of Our command; We made it a light
A glorious Qur'an
By the honoured Qur'an
By the wise Qur'an
The best statement: a consistent Book, oft-repeated, that makes skins shiver
Seven of the often repeated and the great Qur'an

themes.title: Literary features and divine oaths
themes.hook: Mysterious opening letters, oaths by the sun and the fig, refrains, and a challenge no one has met.
overview: The Qur'an is meant to be heard, and its form is part of its message. Twenty-nine surahs open with separated letters such as Alif Lam Mim, whose meaning God knows best; scholars note they often precede a mention of the Book, as if to say: the Qur'an is made of the same letters you speak, yet you cannot produce its like.

That challenge is explicit. The Qur'an invites its deniers to bring ten surahs like it, then a single surah, calling on any helpers they wish (2:23-24; 10:38; 11:13), and declares that even humans and jinn together could not do it (17:88).

God swears oaths by His creation: the sun and its brightness, the night, the dawn, time itself, the fig and the olive, the pen. An oath draws attention to the thing sworn by and to the truth that follows.

Refrains carry the message home: "Which of your Lord's favours will you deny?" in ar-Rahman, "We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; is there anyone who will remember?" in al-Qamar, "Woe that Day to the deniers" in al-Mursalat. The Qur'an also describes its own verses as precise and others as allegorical (3:7), and invites readers to see that it contains no contradiction (4:82).
lessons: The Qur'an's beauty is part of its proof; listen to it, not only read it.
Oaths point to the signs God wants us to notice: time, light, the pen.
Refrains are invitations to pause and respond.

p.l: Alif Lam Mim. This is the Book
Kaf Ha Ya Ayn Sad
Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to make you suffer
Ya Sin. By the wise Qur'an
Sad. By the Qur'an containing reminder
Qaf. By the honoured Qur'an
Nun. By the pen and what they inscribe
By the sun and its brightness, the moon, the day and the night, the soul
By the fig and the olive, Mount Sinai and this secure city
By the dawn and ten nights, the even and the odd
By time, mankind is in loss, except those who believe and do good
By the morning brightness and the night when it covers
By the racers, panting, striking sparks
By the sky and the night comer, the piercing star
I swear by the positions of the stars, and it is a great oath
So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?
We have made the Qur'an easy to remember; is there any who will remember?
Woe, that Day, to the deniers
In that is a sign, but most of them were not believers
If you are in doubt, produce a surah like it
Bring a surah like it and call upon whoever you can
Bring ten surahs like it, invented
If mankind and jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an they could not
Let them produce a statement like it, if they are truthful
We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an that you might understand
This is a clear Arabic language
Had We made it a foreign Qur'an they would have said: why are its verses not explained?
Some verses are precise, the foundation of the Book; others are unspecific
Had it been from other than God, they would have found much contradiction in it
A consistent Book, oft-repeated

themes.title: Modes of address
themes.hook: "O mankind", "O you who believe", "O children of Adam": who the Qur'an is speaking to shapes what it says.
overview: The Qur'an changes its form of address depending on whom it speaks to, and this is one of the simplest keys to reading it.

"O mankind" (ya ayyuha an-nas) speaks to every human being: about creation from one soul, worship of the Creator, and equality before God (4:1; 49:13). "O children of Adam" reminds people of their origin and of Satan's enmity (7:26-35). "O you who believe" (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu) addresses those who have accepted faith and gives them duties: fasting, justice, honest speech, guarding the family from the Fire. It appears mostly in Madinan surahs, when a believing community existed to receive laws.

There are also addresses to the People of the Book, to the Children of Israel, to the Prophet ﷺ himself ("O Prophet", "O Messenger"), to jinn and humans together, and to the disbelievers. The most tender is God's own "O My servants", used even for those who have wronged themselves: "do not despair of God's mercy" (39:53).
lessons: Notice who a verse is addressing before applying it.
Calls to all mankind carry the universal message; calls to believers carry its duties.
God calls even sinners "My servants".

p.l: O mankind, worship your Lord who created you
O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul
O mankind, We created you from male and female, nations and tribes to know one another
O mankind, you are those in need of God
O mankind, fear your Lord; the quake of the Hour is a great thing
O mankind, there has come to you instruction and healing
O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer
O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you
O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared
O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice
O you who believe, fulfil all contracts
O you who believe, remember God with much remembrance
O you who believe, if a wicked person brings news, verify it
O you who believe, let not a people ridicule another; avoid suspicion and backbiting
O you who believe, fear God and let every soul look to what it sends ahead
O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?
O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire
O children of Adam, We have given you clothing; let not Satan tempt you
O children of Adam, take your adornment at every mosque
O children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among you
Did I not enjoin you, O children of Adam, not to worship Satan?
O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us
O People of the Scripture, do not exceed limits in your religion
O People of the Scripture, Our Messenger has come to you
O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you
O Children of Israel, I preferred you over the worlds
O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, bringer of good tidings and warner
O Prophet, sufficient for you is God and whoever follows you
O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you
O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair
O My servants who have believed, My earth is spacious
O My servants who have believed, fear your Lord

subs.t: O man, and O jinn and men

p.l: O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?
O mankind, you are labouring toward your Lord, and you will meet Him
O company of jinn and mankind
O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship

themes.title: Questions the Qur'an asks
themes.hook: The Qur'an teaches by asking: "Do they not reflect?", "Which favour will you deny?", "Did you think We created you in vain?"
overview: Many verses are questions, and they are not asking for information. They ask the listener to look, think and answer honestly for themselves.

Some questions point to creation: "Do they not look at the camel, how it was created, and at the sky, how it was raised?" (88:17-20). "Were they created by nothing, or were they the creators?" (52:35). Some point to purpose: "Did you think We created you in vain?" (23:115). "Does man think he will be left neglected?" (75:36).

Others challenge ingratitude and forgetfulness: "O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?" (82:6). "Which of your Lord's favours will you deny?" (55). Others ask about the heart: "Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should be humbled?" (57:16). And the Qur'an asks about itself: "Do they not reflect on the Qur'an, or are there locks on their hearts?" (47:24).
Reading these verses as personal questions, and pausing to answer them, is one of the most direct ways to engage with the Qur'an.
lessons: Treat each Qur'anic question as addressed to you, and answer it.
The questions lead from creation to purpose to accountability.

p.l: Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?
Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?
Is there anyone who will remember?
Do they not look at the camels, the sky, the mountains and the earth?
Were they created by nothing, or were they the creators?
Have you seen what you emit, what you sow, the water you drink, the fire you kindle?
Do you see any inconsistency? Return your vision twice
Have the disbelievers not considered that the heavens and earth were joined?
Does man not consider that We created him from a sperm-drop?
Did you think that We created you uselessly?
Does man think that he will be left neglected?
Has there come upon man a period of time when he was nothing?
How can you disbelieve in God when you were lifeless and He gave you life?
O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?
Which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?
Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should become humbly submissive?
Are those who know equal to those who do not know?
Is one whose breast God has expanded to Islam like one who is hard-hearted?

themes.title: Parables
themes.hook: Light and darkness, gardens, spiders, donkeys and dogs: the Qur'an's parables make the unseen easy to see.
overview: God strikes parables "for people, that they may reflect" (59:21), and He is not shy to use even a gnat (2:26). A parable (mathal) takes something unseen, such as faith, hypocrisy or reward, and shows it through something familiar.

Faith is a good tree with firm roots and branches in the sky, giving fruit every season, while a corrupt word is a tree uprooted (14:24-26). God's guidance is light in a niche, from a lamp lit by a blessed olive tree (24:35); the deeds of disbelievers are a mirage, or layers of darkness in a deep sea (24:39-40).

Charity grows like a grain that produces seven ears with a hundred grains each (2:261), but charity spoiled by reminders and hurt is like soil on a smooth rock washed away by rain (2:264). Those who rely on other than God are like the spider and its frail house (29:41); scholars who carry scripture without acting on it are like a donkey carrying books (62:5); the man who abandons God's signs is like a panting dog (7:176).

Parables of people complete the set: the owner of two gardens who forgot God (18:32-44), the town to which three messengers came (36:13-29), and the wives of Nuh, Lut and Pharaoh as examples for all time (66:10-12).
lessons: Parables are to be thought through, not just admired.
Sincerity is the root; without it deeds blow away like ashes.
Knowledge without action is a burden, not an honour.

p.l: God is the light of the heavens and earth: a niche, a lamp, a blessed olive tree
Deeds like a mirage, or darkness upon darkness in a deep sea
One who kindled a fire, then lost the light; a rainstorm with darkness and lightning
A good word like a good tree; a bad word like a tree uprooted
A grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains
Soil on a smooth stone washed away; a garden on high ground
Two men, one with two gardens who said his wealth would never perish
Worldly life is like rain that makes plants grow, then they become dry and scattered
Worldly life like rain whose plants please the farmers, then turn yellow and broken
Believers like a plant that sends out shoots and grows strong
God is not shy to strike a parable, a mosquito or what is smaller
Like a dog: if you chase him he pants, if you leave him he pants
Like the spider who takes a home; the weakest of homes is the spider's
Like a donkey carrying volumes of books
They could not create a fly; if a fly took something from them they could not recover it
Water and foam: the foam passes away; what benefits people remains
The deeds of disbelievers are like ashes blown by wind on a stormy day
Spending like a wind with frost that strikes a harvest
A slave who owns nothing and a man provided with good provision; are they equal?
A man owned by quarrelling partners and a man belonging to one master
The people of the town to whom three messengers came
A town secure and content that denied God's favours
The wives of Nuh and Lut, the wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam
Had We sent this Qur'an on a mountain, you would have seen it humbled

themes.title: Prophecies
themes.hook: Predictions made in the Qur'an, many fulfilled within the Prophet's lifetime and some still awaited.
overview: The Qur'an makes specific statements about the future, and many were fulfilled while people who heard them were alive. When the Byzantines were defeated by the Persians, it said they would be victorious "within a few years" (30:2-5), and they were. It promised the Prophet ﷺ would return to Makkah (28:85) and enter the Sacred Mosque in safety (48:27), and that the united enemy forces would be routed (54:45). It said Abu Lahab would die opposing the message (surah 111), and he did, though he could have proven it wrong simply by professing faith.

Some promises are long-term: no one will produce a surah like it (2:23-24), the Qur'an will be preserved (15:9), and God will show people His signs in the horizons and in themselves until it is clear that it is the truth (41:53).
Others concern the end of time: the release of Gog and Magog, the Beast of the Earth, the descent of Isa as a sign of the Hour, the smoke, and the blowing of the Horn.

The Qur'an also records prophecies made by earlier prophets: Ibrahim's prayer for a messenger from his descendants (2:129), Isa's good news of a messenger named Ahmad (61:6), and the description of the Prophet in the Torah and Gospel (7:157).
lessons: Fulfilled prophecies are part of the Qur'an's evidence for itself.
Promises still awaited should be believed in, not speculated about.

p.l: The Byzantines have been defeated, and within a few years they will overcome

You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in safety
Victory near at hand and many spoils you will take
When the victory of God has come and people enter His religion in multitudes
God will protect you from the people

They will never wish for death, because of what their hands have done
The hypocrites' promises to help will not be kept
And you will never be able to
We will be its guardian
To manifest it over all religion
God has promised those who believe to grant them succession on earth
Today We will save you in body, that you may be a sign
We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves
When Gog and Magog are released, descending from every elevation
When the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level
We will bring forth a creature from the earth speaking to them
And indeed, he (Isa) will be a sign for the Hour
There is none of the People of the Book but will believe in him before his death
Watch for the Day when the sky brings a visible smoke
The day some of the signs come, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before
The Horn will be blown
Ibrahim: our Lord, send among them a messenger from themselves
Isa: bringing good tidings of a messenger to come after me, whose name is Ahmad
Whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel
Yusuf foretells the fates of his two companions in prison
Yusuf foretells seven years of plenty, seven of famine, then a year of relief

themes.title: Numbers stated in the Qur'an
themes.hook: Six days, seven heavens, nineteen keepers, 950 years, 309 years: the numbers the Qur'an itself states.
overview: This theme collects the numbers stated plainly in the Qur'an, grouped by subject. Unlike the contested "numerical miracle" claims (QR-09), these are simply what the text says.

Numbers of time: creation in six days (7:54); a day with God like a thousand years (22:47) or fifty thousand (70:4); Nuh among his people a thousand years less fifty (29:14); the sleepers of the Cave three hundred years and nine more (18:25); Musa's appointment of thirty nights completed by ten (7:142); forty years of wandering (5:26); full maturity at forty (46:15); twelve months, four of them sacred (9:36).
Numbers of the cosmos: seven heavens (67:3), eight bearing the Throne (69:17), nineteen over the Fire (74:30), and seven seas of ink that would not exhaust God's words (31:27).

Numbers in stories and law: eleven stars, seven cows, twelve springs, seventy men; four witnesses, a hundred lashes, two years of nursing, the fractions of inheritance, ten or sixty poor people fed as expiation. And numbers of reward: a good deed multiplied tenfold (6:160), and a grain yielding seven hundred (2:261).
lessons: Numbers in law are precise and must be applied as stated.
Numbers of reward show God's generosity: tenfold and more.

A day whose extent is fifty thousand years
In a day whose extent is a thousand years
Nuh remained among them a thousand years minus fifty
They remained in their cave three hundred years, and exceeded by nine
Thirty nights, completed with ten, so the term was forty nights
Forbidden to them for forty years, wandering the land
When he reaches maturity and reaches forty years
The number of months with God is twelve, of which four are sacred
The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months
He created seven heavens in layers
Eight will bear the Throne of your Lord above them
Over it are nineteen
If the sea were ink, with seven more seas, the words of God would not be exhausted
Eleven stars, the sun and the moon
Seven fat cows eaten by seven lean, seven green spikes and others dry
Twelve springs gushed forth
We sent among them twelve leaders
Musa chose seventy men of his people
Three thousand angels, then five thousand
God caused him to die for a hundred years
How many a small company has overcome a large one
Twenty steadfast will overcome two hundred
Those who accuse and do not bring four witnesses
Lash each of them a hundred lashes
Feeding ten needy people, or freeing a slave, or fasting three days
Fasting two consecutive months or feeding sixty poor
Three days during Hajj and seven when you return: ten complete
Mothers nurse for two complete years
Widows wait four months and ten days
The shares of inheritance: half, a quarter, an eighth, a third, a sixth, two thirds
Even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times
Whoever comes with a good deed will have ten times the like of it
Seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains; God multiplies for whom He wills

themes.title: Numerical-miracle claims (contested)
themes.hook: Popular claims about hidden number patterns, and why most scholars treat them with caution.
overview: Since the twentieth century, books and videos have claimed that the Qur'an contains hidden numerical patterns. The best known is the "Code 19", based on the verse "Over it are nineteen" (74:30) and the nineteen letters of the Basmala; it was popularised by Rashad Khalifa, whose claims led him to reject verses of the Qur'an and are rejected by mainstream scholars. Other claims count words: that "this world" and "the Hereafter" occur equally often, that "day" appears 365 times and "month" twelve, or that the ratio of "land" to "sea" matches the Earth's surface.

These claims are contested for three reasons. The counts depend on choices about which word forms to include, and different counters get different results. The Qur'an never invites its readers to count words; its stated challenge is to produce a surah like it. And the verse about the nineteen itself says the number was given "as a trial" for those who disbelieve and to strengthen those who believe (74:31), not as a code.
This theme is included because users will meet these claims. The app presents the verses involved and the scholarly caution, and does not endorse any count.
lessons: The Qur'an's challenge is its message and language, not word counts.
Check any numerical claim against the actual text and its counting rules.
The nineteen of 74:30 is described as a test, not a code.

p.l: Over it are nineteen; We made their number only a trial
He has enumerated all things in number
He has enumerated them and counted them a full counting
All things We have enumerated in a clear register
Produce a surah like it
Mankind and jinn could not produce its like

subs.t: Verses often cited in count claims

p.l: We sent down iron (the surah's number is cited in claims about iron)
They will say there were three, the fourth their dog; say: my Lord knows their number

themes.title: Makki and Madani, occasions of revelation, abrogation
themes.hook: When and why verses were revealed, how rulings came in stages, and how context shapes meaning.
overview: The Qur'an was revealed over about twenty-three years: thirteen in Makkah and ten in Madinah. Makkan surahs mostly build belief, tell the stories of earlier prophets and speak of the Hereafter, often in short, powerful verses. Madinan surahs, revealed when a community existed, give laws on worship, family, trade, war and peace.

Many verses came in response to events or questions. Some begin "They ask you about...": the new moons, spending, wine and gambling, orphans, menstruation, the spirit, Dhul-Qarnayn, the Hour. Others answer specific situations, such as the woman who pleaded about her husband (58:1), the slander against Aisha (24:11-20), or the blind man who came to the Prophet (80:1-10). Knowing the occasion helps understand the verse, though its lesson is general.

Rulings were often introduced gradually. Wine is the clearest example: first a hint (16:67), then a statement that its harm outweighs its benefit (2:219), then a ban on praying while intoxicated (4:43), and finally full prohibition (5:90-91). The Qur'an itself mentions that God replaces one ruling with another (2:106; 16:101), which scholars call naskh, abrogation. The details of which verses are abrogated are a technical field the app leaves to the tafsir.
lessons: Read a verse with its context: Makkan or Madinan, and its occasion if known.
God taught gradually; change in people is built in stages.
The lesson of a verse is general even when its occasion is specific.

p.l: We do not abrogate a verse or cause it to be forgotten except We bring better or similar
When We substitute a verse in place of another
God eliminates what He wills or confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book

subs.t: Gradual change: the stages of the wine prohibition

p.l: From dates and grapes you take intoxicant and good provision
In wine and gambling is great sin and some benefit, but the sin is greater
Do not approach prayer while intoxicated
Intoxicants and gambling are defilement from Satan's work, so avoid them
Permission is given to those who are fought because they were wronged
Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress
Turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque

subs.t: They ask you: revelation in answer to questions

p.l: They ask you about the new moons
They ask you what they should spend
They ask you about wine and gambling, and about orphans
They ask you about menstruation
They ask you about the spoils of war
They ask you about the soul
They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn
They ask you about the mountains
They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?
God has heard the speech of the one who argues with you concerning her husband
Those who came with falsehood are a group among you
He frowned and turned away because the blind man came to him
The three who were left behind, and their repentance accepted
O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful to you?
A Qur'an We have separated, to recite at intervals
Thus, that We may strengthen your heart with it

themes.title: Knowledge, reason and reflection
themes.hook: The first word revealed was "Read": the Qur'an commands thinking, verifying and seeking knowledge.
overview: The first revelation was a command to read, in the name of the Lord who taught by the pen (96:1-5). From there, knowledge runs through the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ is told to pray "My Lord, increase me in knowledge" (20:114). Those who know and those who do not are not equal (39:9), and God raises in rank those given knowledge (58:11).

The Qur'an repeatedly appeals to reason. Many verses end "for a people who reason", "who reflect", "who understand". It criticises those who follow their fathers' ways without thought (2:170), and those who follow conjecture, which "avails nothing against the truth" (53:28). It commands verification: do not pursue what you have no knowledge of (17:36), and check news brought by an unreliable person before acting on it (49:6).

It invites travel and observation: "Travel through the earth and see how He began creation" (29:20). It also teaches humility: humans have been given only a little knowledge (17:85), and above every knower is one more knowing (12:76). And it sets the method of calling others: with wisdom and good instruction, and arguing in the best way (16:125).
lessons: Seeking knowledge is an act of worship that began with the first revelation.
Verify before you believe or share.
Faith and reason work together; blind imitation is criticised.
Knowledge should bring humility, not pride.

p.l: Read in the name of your Lord, who taught by the pen
Say: my Lord, increase me in knowledge
By the pen and what they inscribe
Are those who know equal to those who do not know?
God will raise those who believe and those given knowledge by degrees
Only those who have knowledge among His servants fear God
Whoever has been given wisdom has been given much good
Signs for a people who use reason
Signs for those of understanding, who remember God and reflect on creation
Signs for a people who give thought, who know, who listen, who reason
Signs for a people who give thought, and for a people who reason
Do you order righteousness and forget yourselves? Will you not reason?
A blessed Book, that they might reflect upon its verses
Do they not reflect upon the Qur'an?
We will follow what we found our fathers doing, even if their fathers understood nothing?
Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon
We found our fathers upon a religion and we are in their footsteps
Do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge
If a disobedient one brings you news, investigate
Most of them follow only assumption; assumption avails nothing against the truth
They follow only assumption
If you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you; they follow assumption
Travel through the land and observe how He began creation
Have they not travelled, so that they have hearts to reason with?
Travel through the land and see the end of those who denied
You have not been given of knowledge except a little
Over every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing
If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted
God alone has knowledge of the Hour
Ask the people of the message if you do not know
Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction

themes.title: Prophethood
themes.hook: Why God sends messengers, what they share, and what makes the last of them the seal.
overview: The Qur'an teaches that God never left humanity without guidance: "We sent to every nation a messenger, saying: worship God and avoid false gods" (16:36). Messengers were sent so that people would have no argument against God after their coming (4:165), and each spoke the language of his people so the message was clear (14:4).

Prophets are human. They ate food, walked in markets, married and had children (25:20; 13:38). Their task was to convey, recite God's verses, purify people and teach the Book and wisdom (62:2). They did not ask for payment (26:109). The Qur'an names twenty-five of them and says there were others whose stories were not told (40:78).

All of them carried the same core message of tawhid, which is why believers make no distinction between them in belief (2:285), even though God raised some above others in particular gifts (2:253). God took a covenant from the prophets to support one another's message (3:81).

Their stories share a pattern: a call to worship God alone, rejection by the powerful, patience, and God's help in the end. The pattern is told to strengthen the heart of the Prophet ﷺ and of believers in every age (11:120). Muhammad ﷺ is the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (33:40), sent as a mercy to the worlds (21:107).
lessons: Guidance has always been available; every people received a warner.
Prophets were human, which makes them real examples to follow.
Believe in all of them, without distinction in faith.
Their stories are told to give patience to those who carry truth today.

p.l: We sent to every nation a messenger: worship God and avoid false gods
Messengers bringing good tidings and warnings, so people have no argument against God
We would never punish until We sent a messenger
There was no nation but a warner passed among them
Every messenger spoke the language of his people
I am only a man like you, to whom it has been revealed that your god is one
We sent before you only messengers who ate food and walked in the markets
We sent messengers before you and gave them wives and descendants
Am I anything but a human messenger?
A messenger who recites His verses, purifies them and teaches the Book and wisdom
A witness, bringer of good tidings, warner, and one who invites to God
Convey what has been revealed to you
I am a trustworthy messenger; I ask no payment for it
Ibrahim and the line of prophets after him: these are those God guided, so follow their guidance
A gallery of prophets in Surah al-Anbiya, from Musa to Isa and his mother
Ibrahim, Musa, Harun, Ismail and Idris: those God favoured among the prophets
Among them are those whose stories We have related to you, and those We have not
We make no distinction between any of His messengers
Those messengers: some We caused to exceed others
The covenant of the prophets: believe in and support the messenger who comes
We took from the prophets their covenant, from you, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa
Messengers before you were denied, but were patient until Our victory came
No messenger came to them but they ridiculed him
Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you
Each of the stories We relate to you is to make firm your heart
Muhammad is the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets
We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds
We have not sent you except to all of mankind

themes.title: Adam
themes.hook: The first human: honoured with knowledge, tested in the garden, forgiven, and sent as a successor on earth.
overview: Adam's story opens with God announcing to the angels that He will place a successor (khalifah) on earth. The angels ask whether He will place there one who causes corruption; God answers: "I know what you do not know" (2:30). He then teaches Adam the names of all things, and Adam names them when the angels cannot. Knowledge is the first sign of human dignity.

God created Adam from clay, shaped him and breathed into him of His spirit, and commanded the angels to prostrate. All did except Iblis, out of pride (7:11-12). Adam and his wife lived in the garden with one prohibition: do not approach this tree. Satan whispered, swore he was a sincere adviser, and they ate. Their nakedness became apparent to them (7:19-22).

What follows defines the human way: Adam received words from his Lord and repented, and God accepted his repentance (2:37). Their prayer is preserved: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will be among the losers" (7:23). The Qur'an says Adam forgot and had no firm resolve (20:115), and that his Lord then chose him and guided him (20:122).

They were sent down to earth, with the promise that guidance would come and that whoever follows it will not go astray (20:123). The story continues in his sons: one killed the other out of envy, and learned burial from a crow (5:27-31).
lessons: Knowledge is the first mark of human honour.
Falling is human; Adam's way is to admit it and return to God.
Satan's first weapon was a false promise of eternity and power.
Every child of Adam is invited to the same guidance and warned of the same enemy.

p.l: I will make upon the earth a successor; I know what you do not know

subs.t: Created from clay, given the spirit

p.l: Man from sounding clay; when I breathe into him of My spirit, fall in prostration
I am going to create a human being from clay
The example of Isa is like that of Adam: created from dust, then He said Be
Prostrate before Adam; they prostrated, except Iblis
I am better than him; the respite, and the oath to mislead
They prostrated except Iblis; he refused
Dwell in the garden, but do not approach this tree
Satan whispered, swore he was an adviser, and they ate; their nakedness appeared
O Adam, this is an enemy to you; shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?
Adam received words from his Lord, and He accepted his repentance
Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us we will be losers
We had taken a promise from Adam before, but he forgot
Then his Lord chose him, turned to him in forgiveness, and guided him

subs.t: Descent and the promise of guidance

p.l: Whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them
On earth you will have a dwelling and provision for a time
Whoever follows My guidance will not go astray; whoever turns away will have a straitened life
The two sons of Adam: one accepted, one killed out of envy, and the crow
Whoever kills a soul, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely
O children of Adam, do not let Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise
The children of Adam testify: Are You not our Lord?
We have honoured the children of Adam

themes.title: Idris
themes.hook: A truthful prophet, patient, raised by God to a high station.
overview: Idris is mentioned only twice in the Qur'an, and both times briefly. In Surah Maryam he is described as "a man of truth and a prophet", whom God "raised to a high station" (19:56-57). In Surah al-Anbiya he is named among the patient, alongside Ismail and Dhul-Kifl, and among those admitted into God's mercy as righteous (21:85-86).

The Qur'an does not tell his story, and the app follows its lead: the message is in the qualities named. Truthfulness, patience and righteousness are what raised him. Much else that is said about Idris comes from later reports that are not authenticated, and is left out under the app's content rules.
lessons: A few words from God about a person can be the highest praise: truthful, patient, righteous.
Rank with God comes from character, not from how much is told about you.

subs.t: A man of truth raised high

p.l: Idris was a man of truth and a prophet, and We raised him to a high station
Ismail, Idris and Dhul-Kifl: all were of the patient

themes.title: Nuh
themes.hook: 950 years of calling his people by day and night, the ark, the flood, and a father's grief.
overview: Nuh called his people for nine hundred and fifty years (29:14). Surah Nuh records his own account of the effort: he called them night and day, publicly and privately, and told them to seek forgiveness so that God would send rain, wealth and children (71:5-12). They put their fingers in their ears and covered themselves with their garments.

The leaders mocked his followers as the lowest of people and demanded he drive them away; he refused (11:27-31). When God told him that no more of his people would believe, he was commanded to build the ark under God's eyes. The chiefs laughed as they passed by (11:38).

The flood came: water burst from the sky and the earth, and the ark sailed on waves like mountains. Nuh called to his son, who had stayed apart, "O my son, come aboard with us"; the son said he would take refuge on a mountain, and a wave came between them (11:42-43). Nuh pleaded for his son as part of his family; God told him the son was not of his family in faith, and Nuh sought refuge in God from asking what he had no knowledge of (11:45-47). His wife too is named as an example of one who was close to a prophet yet did not believe (66:10).
The ark came to rest on al-Judi, and Nuh descended with peace and blessings. His story is held up as a sign for all who come after (29:15; 54:15).
lessons: Persistence in calling to good does not depend on results.
Faith is not inherited: a prophet's son and wife could still refuse.
A parent's love is real, but it bows to God's knowledge.
The weak who believe are not to be driven away to please the powerful.

p.l: Worship God; I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous Day
If my staying among you is difficult for you, I rely on God
Worship God; the chiefs said he is only a man like you
I am a trustworthy messenger; I ask no payment from you

subs.t: His methods: day and night, openly and privately

p.l: I invited them night and day; seek forgiveness and He will send rain

subs.t: The weak believers and the arrogant chiefs

p.l: We do not see you followed except by the lowest of us
Shall we believe you while the lowest follow you? I will not drive away the believers
Construct the ship under Our eyes; whenever the chiefs passed they ridiculed him
Construct the ship under Our observation and Our inspiration
When the oven overflowed: embark, in the name of God is its course and anchorage
We opened the gates of heaven with pouring water and caused the earth to burst with springs
O earth, swallow your water; and the ark came to rest on al-Judi
O my son, come aboard with us; he said I will take refuge on a mountain
My son is of my family; He said: he is not of your family
The wives of Nuh and Lut were under two righteous servants but betrayed them
My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house a believer
Praise be to God who saved us; my Lord, let me land at a blessed landing place
I am overpowered, so help

subs.t: A sign for all who come after

p.l: He remained among them a thousand years minus fifty; We made it a sign for the worlds
Peace upon Nuh among the worlds

themes.title: Hud
themes.hook: Sent to the mighty people of 'Ad, who built monuments and asked "Who is greater than us in strength?"
overview: Hud was sent to his own people, 'Ad, a powerful nation in the region of al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes. They were given strength and stature, built lofty monuments on every height as if they would live forever, and seized others with tyranny (26:128-130).

Hud called them to worship God alone, to seek His forgiveness so He would send abundant rain and add strength to their strength (11:52). He asked for no payment.
