They replied that he had brought no clear proof, that they would not abandon their gods on his word, and that one of their gods had possessed him with evil (11:53-54). Hud answered with complete trust: "I have relied upon God, my Lord and your Lord; there is no creature but He holds its forelock" (11:56).

Their pride is summed up in a single question: "Who is greater than us in strength?" The Qur'an replies: "Did they not see that God who created them was greater than them in strength?" (41:15). They saw a cloud approaching their valleys and rejoiced, thinking it rain; it was a furious wind that blew for seven nights and eight days, leaving them like the trunks of hollow palm trees (46:24-25; 69:6-8). Hud and those who believed with him were saved.
lessons: Strength and monuments do not protect a people from God.
Trust in God frees the one who calls to truth from fear.
What people hope for can be the very thing that destroys them.

p.l: To 'Ad their brother Hud: worship God; remember when He made you successors after Nuh
Seek forgiveness of your Lord, then repent; He will send rain and add strength
I am a trustworthy messenger; I ask no payment
Do you construct on every elevation a sign, and take for yourselves palaces?
Iram, who had lofty pillars, the like of which had not been created in the lands
I rely upon God; there is no creature but He holds its forelock
The brother of 'Ad warned his people in al-Ahqaf
They said: who is greater than us in strength?
They saw a cloud and said this is rain; it was a wind with a painful punishment
A screaming violent wind for seven nights and eight days
A violent wind on a day of continuous misfortune
We sent against them the barren wind

themes.title: Salih
themes.hook: Sent to Thamud, who carved homes in mountains; their test was a she-camel they were told not to harm.
overview: Salih was sent to Thamud, successors of 'Ad, who carved homes from the mountains with skill and built palaces in the plains (7:74). He called them to worship God, reminding them that He produced them from the earth and settled them in it (11:61).

Thamud demanded a sign, and God sent a she-camel as a clear proof, with a condition: she would have her share of water on one day and they on another, and they must not touch her with harm (26:155-156). The camel became a test of whether they would accept God's limits.

The arrogant chiefs mocked the believers among them. Nine men in the city "who caused corruption and did not reform" plotted to kill Salih and his family at night (27:48-49). The most wretched of them hamstrung the camel, and the people agreed to it (91:12-14). Salih told them to enjoy themselves in their homes for three days (11:65). Then a shout or tremor seized them, and they lay fallen in their homes (7:78). Salih and the believers were saved.
The Qur'an notes that Salih turned away from them saying "I conveyed to you my Lord's message and advised you, but you do not like advisers" (7:79).
lessons: A sign from God is also a test of obedience.
A few corrupt people can lead a whole community to ruin when others go along.
Skill and wealth do not replace gratitude.

p.l: Worship God; this is the she-camel of God as a sign; remember when He made you successors
He produced you from the earth and settled you in it, so ask forgiveness
Will you be left secure in gardens and springs, carving homes in the mountains?
She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn on a known day; do not touch her with harm
We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her
We are sending the she-camel as a trial for them
Nine family heads in the city who caused corruption plotted to attack him at night
The most wretched of them was sent forth, and they hamstrung her
They hamstrung the she-camel and were insolent toward the command of their Lord
Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days
The earthquake seized them; Salih said: you do not like advisers
We sent upon them one blast
Thamud preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt seized them
The companions of al-Hijr denied the messengers

themes.title: Ibrahim
themes.hook: The friend of God who reasoned his way to tawhid, broke the idols, survived the fire, and built the Ka'bah with his son.
overview: Ibrahim is called a nation in himself (16:120) and the intimate friend of God (4:125). His story is the story of tawhid lived to its fullest.

As a young man among idol-worshippers, he reasoned aloud about a star, the moon and the sun: each rose and set, and he would not take as lord anything that disappears. "I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth" (6:76-79). He called his father with gentle words, "O my father", four times, and when threatened with stoning he replied "Peace be upon you; I will ask forgiveness for you" (19:41-48).

He broke his people's idols, leaving the largest, and told them to ask it who had done it. They threw him into a fire, and God said: "O fire, be coolness and safety for Ibrahim" (21:68-69). He debated a king who claimed to give life and death, silencing him with the rising of the sun from the east (2:258).

In old age he received honoured guests, angels who brought news of Ishaq, and Sarah laughed (11:69-73). He left Hajar and their infant Ismail in a barren valley by God's house, praying for them (14:37). He saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son; the son said "O my father, do as you are commanded", both submitted, and the son was ransomed with a great sacrifice (37:102-107). Father and son raised the foundations of the Ka'bah and prayed for a messenger from their descendants (2:127-129).
The Qur'an presents him as the model for all believers (60:4), neither Jew nor Christian but upright in submission to God (3:67).
lessons: Faith can begin with honest reasoning about creation.
Even when disagreeing, speak to parents with gentleness and peace.
Submission to God may ask for what we love most, and God provides.
Pray for your children and for the generations after them.

p.l: The star, the moon, the sun: I do not like those that disappear
His people argued with him; that was Our argument which We gave Ibrahim
O my father, why do you worship what does not hear? Peace be upon you
What do you worship? It is the Lord of the worlds who created me and guides me
I am free of what you worship except He who created me
Ibrahim's request of forgiveness for his father was only because of a promise

subs.t: Breaking the idols and the fire

p.l: He broke them into fragments; O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim
He turned upon them, striking with his right hand; they planned a building for him
Ibrahim's call and his people's answer: kill him or burn him
God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west
My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead: take four birds
They brought good news; his wife laughed; then he argued for the people of Lut
The honoured guests: he brought a fat calf; a knowledgeable boy
Ibrahim's guests: do not despair; who despairs of his Lord's mercy except the astray?

subs.t: Hajar and Ismail in the valley

p.l: My Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley near Your sacred House
O my son, I have seen in a dream that I sacrifice you; do as you are commanded
Ibrahim and Ismail raising the foundations, praying: accept from us
Proclaim the pilgrimage among the people
The first House established for mankind; in it is the standing place of Ibrahim
My Lord, give me wisdom and join me with the righteous
Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have returned
God took Ibrahim as an intimate friend
Ibrahim was a nation, devoutly obedient, inclining toward truth
There has already been for you an excellent example in Ibrahim
Ibrahim was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but inclining toward truth, a Muslim
Who would be averse to the religion of Ibrahim except a fool?

themes.title: Lut
themes.hook: Sent to a people who openly committed indecency; saved with the believers while his wife stayed behind.
overview: Lut believed in Ibrahim and migrated with him (29:26), then was sent as a prophet to a people who committed an indecency no one in the worlds had done before them: approaching men with desire instead of women, committing highway robbery and doing evil openly in their gatherings (7:80-81; 29:28-29). When he called them, they said: "Expel them from your town; they are people who keep themselves pure" (7:82).

The angels who visited Ibrahim came next to Lut as guests, and he was distressed for them. His people rushed to his house. He pleaded with them, offering his "daughters", understood by scholars as the women of the nation available through marriage, and asked: "Is there not among you a man of reason?" (11:78). The angels revealed who they were: "They will never reach you" (11:81).

Lut was told to leave by night with his family, and that none should look back except his wife, who would be struck by what struck them. At dawn the city was turned upside down and stones of baked clay rained on it (11:81-83). His wife is named with the wife of Nuh as an example: close to a prophet, yet not of the believers (66:10). The ruins were left as a sign for those who reflect (29:35; 15:75-77).
lessons: Normalising open wrongdoing and mocking those who stay pure is a mark of a corrupt society.
Calling to good continues even when one stands alone.
Closeness to a righteous person does not save someone who does not believe.

p.l: Do you commit an immorality no one in the worlds has done before you?
Do you approach males among the worlds and leave your wives?
Do you commit immorality while you are seeing?
You cut off the road and commit evil in your meetings

subs.t: Expel them for keeping themselves pure

p.l: Evict them from your city; they are people who keep themselves pure
Expel the family of Lut from your city
He was anxious for them; his people came hastening; is there not among you a man of reason?
The messengers came to the family of Lut
Set out with your family during a portion of the night, and let none look back except your wife
Follow behind them and let none of you look back
The wives of Nuh and Lut betrayed them
We saved him and his family, except his wife
We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones of baked clay
Except the family of Lut; We saved them before dawn
You pass by them in the morning and at night; will you not reason?
We have left of it a clear sign for a people who use reason
In that are signs for those who discern
To Lut We gave judgement and knowledge and saved him from the city

themes.title: Ismail
themes.hook: The son who submitted to God's command, helped build the Ka'bah, and was true to his promise.
overview: Ismail is the elder son of Ibrahim, through Hajar. As an infant he was left with his mother in the barren valley of Makkah by God's command, with Ibrahim's prayer that hearts would incline toward them and they would be provided with fruits (14:37).

When he was old enough to work with his father, Ibrahim told him of the dream in which he was sacrificing him. Ismail answered: "O my father, do as you are commanded; you will find me, if God wills, of the steadfast" (37:102). Most scholars understand the son of the sacrifice to be Ismail, since the good news of Ishaq comes after the sacrifice in the same passage (37:112). God ransomed him with a great sacrifice.

Ismail joined his father in raising the foundations of the Ka'bah, and together they prayed: "Our Lord, accept this from us", asking for a submissive nation from their descendants and a messenger from among them (2:127-129), a prayer the Qur'an presents as answered in the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

God describes Ismail as true to his promise, a messenger and prophet, who enjoined prayer and charity on his family and was pleasing to his Lord (19:54-55). He is named among the patient (21:85) and the best (38:48).
lessons: Submission to God can be shown by the young as well as the old.
Keeping promises is a prophetic quality.
Lead your family in prayer and charity.

p.l: My Lord, I have settled some of my descendants in an uncultivated valley
O my father, do as you are commanded; you will find me among the steadfast

subs.t: Building the Ka'bah with his father

p.l: Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations: our Lord, accept this from us
He was true to his promise, a messenger and prophet, and enjoined prayer on his family

subs.t: Among the patient and the best

p.l: Ismail, Idris and Dhul-Kifl: all were of the patient
Remember Ismail, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl; all are among the outstanding
Ismail, Elisha, Yunus and Lut: each We preferred over the worlds
The God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq

themes.title: Ishaq
themes.hook: The son promised to Ibrahim and Sarah in old age, and father of a line of prophets.
overview: Ishaq is the son of Ibrahim and Sarah, born when both were old. Angels brought the news to Ibrahim, and Sarah laughed in astonishment: "Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this my husband is an old man?" The angels answered: "Do you wonder at the decree of God? The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house" (11:71-73).

The good news included more than a son: "and after Ishaq, Yaqub" (11:71), a grandson as an extra gift (21:72). Ishaq is described as a prophet among the righteous (37:112), and God blessed him and Ibrahim (37:113).

He is named with Ibrahim and Yaqub as men "of strength and vision", chosen and among the best (38:45-47), and his name appears in the testimony of Yaqub's sons: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq" (2:133).
lessons: Nothing is too late or too hard for God's decree.
Righteous lineage is a gift to be carried, not a guarantee.

subs.t: The good news of his birth

p.l: We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Yaqub
They gave him good tidings of a learned boy; his wife struck her face
We give you good tidings of a learned boy
We gave him good tidings of Ishaq, a prophet among the righteous
We gave him Ishaq and Yaqub in addition, and made them leaders guiding by Our command
We gave him Ishaq and Yaqub, and each We made a prophet
Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub, those of strength and vision
We gave him Ishaq and Yaqub; all We guided
We gave him Ishaq and Yaqub, and placed prophethood in his descendants
The God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq

themes.title: Yaqub
themes.hook: A father tested by the loss of his son, who answered with "beautiful patience" and never despaired.
overview: Yaqub, also called Israel, is the son of Ishaq and the father of twelve sons. His story in the Qur'an is mostly told within Surah Yusuf, and it is the story of a father's patience.

When the young Yusuf told him his dream, Yaqub warned him not to tell his brothers, knowing their envy (12:5). When the brothers returned with a shirt stained with false blood, he did not believe them: "Your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting, and God is the one sought for help" (12:18). Years later, when they asked to take Binyamin to Egypt, he made them swear an oath and advised them to enter by separate gates, while saying that his advice could not avail against God's decree (12:66-67).

When Binyamin was held in Egypt, his grief for both sons returned. His eyes became white from sorrow, yet he said: "I only complain of my suffering and grief to God" and told his sons: "Do not despair of relief from God" (12:84-87). When Yusuf's shirt was cast over his face, his sight returned, and when his sons asked him to seek forgiveness for them, he promised to (12:96-98).
At his death he gathered his sons and asked: "What will you worship after me?" and they answered: "Your God and the God of your fathers" (2:133).
lessons: Beautiful patience means grief without complaint to people, only to God.
Never despair of God's relief, however long the loss lasts.
Take precautions, then trust God with the outcome.
A parent's last concern should be the faith of their children.

p.l: O my son, do not relate your vision to your brothers

subs.t: The false blood and beautiful patience

p.l: Patience is most fitting, and God is the one sought for help
I will not send him until you give me a promise by God; enter from different gates
I only complain of my suffering and grief to God; do not despair of relief from God

subs.t: The shirt and the return of sight

p.l: Cast it over my father's face; he returned seeing
He raised his parents upon the throne and they fell down in prostration
When death approached Yaqub: what will you worship after me?
Yaqub given in addition; leaders guiding by Our command
Each We made a prophet, and gave them a mention of high honour
All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful for himself

themes.title: Yusuf
themes.hook: "The best of stories": envy, betrayal, temptation, prison, power and forgiveness in a single surah.
overview: Surah Yusuf tells one story from start to finish, and God calls it "the best of stories" (12:3). It follows a young man from his father's lap to a well, a household, a prison and a throne, and every stage tests a different virtue.

As a boy he dreamed of eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing to him. His brothers, jealous of their father's love, threw him into a well and brought back his shirt with false blood. Travellers sold him for a few silver coins in Egypt, where al-Aziz took him into his house (12:4-21).

As a young man he was tempted by the wife of his master. He refused: "I seek refuge in God; he is my master who has made good my residence" (12:23). When she gathered the women of the city, he prayed: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to" (12:33). Innocent, he was imprisoned anyway, and in prison he called his companions to tawhid before interpreting their dreams (12:37-41).

The king's dream of seven fat and seven lean cows brought him out. He refused to leave until his innocence was declared, then asked to be put in charge of the storehouses: "I am a knowing guardian" (12:50-55). His management saved the land through famine, and brought his brothers to him needing grain.

He tested them, kept Binyamin with him through the episode of the king's cup, and finally revealed himself: "I am Yusuf, and this is my brother." When they admitted their sin, he said: "No blame upon you today; God will forgive you" (12:90-92). The family came to Egypt and bowed before him, fulfilling the dream. His closing prayer asks only to die in submission and be joined with the righteous (12:101).
lessons: Envy within families can lead to great harm; guard against it early.
Chastity and loyalty are worth prison if needed.
Use any position, even prison, to call to God.
Competence and trustworthiness belong together in leadership.
Forgive fully when you have the power to punish.

p.l: We relate to you the best of stories
I saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to me

subs.t: The brothers' plot and the well

p.l: Kill Yusuf or cast him out; put him into the bottom of the well
They sold him for a reduced price, a few dirhams; the one who bought him from Egypt
I seek refuge in God; his shirt torn from behind
My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than that to which they invite me
O my two companions of prison, are separate lords better or God, the One?
Seven fat cows eaten by seven lean, and Yusuf's interpretation
Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; I am a knowing guardian
His brothers came and he recognised them, but they did not recognise him
He put the drinking cup into the bag of his brother
Do not despair of relief from God
I am Yusuf and this is my brother; no blame upon you today

subs.t: The shirt and his father's sight

p.l: I find the smell of Yusuf; he returned seeing
This is the interpretation of my vision; cause me to die a Muslim
In their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding
Yusuf came to you before with clear proofs

themes.title: Ayyub
themes.hook: The prophet of patience, who called on God in his suffering and was restored.
overview: Ayyub is the Qur'an's example of patience under prolonged hardship. He was afflicted in his body and lost his family and wealth, and the Qur'an records his prayer, notable for its restraint: "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful" (21:83). He did not demand or complain; he described his state and named God's mercy.

God answered him: "Strike the ground with your foot; this is a cool bath and drink" (38:42). His affliction was removed, and his family was restored with as many again, as mercy and a reminder for worshippers (21:84; 38:43).

The Qur'an adds a detail about an oath: he was told to take a bundle of thin grass and strike with it, and not break his oath (38:44), a gentle fulfilment that scholars connect to an oath he had made during his illness. God's verdict on him: "We found him patient, an excellent servant; he was one who repeatedly turned back" (38:44).
lessons: Make your need known to God with humility, and name His mercy.
Patience does not mean silence before God; it means not despairing of Him.
God can restore more than was lost.

p.l: Adversity has touched me, and You are the most merciful of the merciful
Satan has touched me with hardship and torment
We responded and removed his adversity, and gave him his family and the like with them
Strike the ground with your foot: a cool bath and drink; We gave him back his family
Take in your hand a bunch and strike with it; We found him patient, an excellent servant
We revealed to Ibrahim, Ismail, Ishaq, Yaqub, Isa, Ayyub, Yunus, Harun and Sulayman
Of his descendants: Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa and Harun

themes.title: Shu'ayb
themes.hook: Sent to Madyan, a people who cheated in weights and measures; faith and fair trade go together.
overview: Shu'ayb was sent to Madyan and to the companions of the Thicket. Their characteristic sin was economic: they gave short measure and weight, deprived people of their rightful goods, and sat on roads to threaten travellers and turn people from God's way (7:85-86).

His call joined worship and honest dealing: "Worship God; you have no other god. Do not decrease the measure and the weight. I see you in prosperity, but I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing Day" (11:84). He told them that what remains with God is better for them (11:86).

Their reply exposes a common attitude: "Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we please?" (11:87). They saw religion and money as separate. Shu'ayb answered that he did not want to do himself what he forbade them: "I only intend reform as much as I am able, and my success is only through God" (11:88).
They threatened to stone him and expel the believers, and were seized by an earthquake and a blast, and the companions of the Thicket by a day of shadow (7:91; 11:94; 26:189).
lessons: Faith reaches into business: honest weights and fair dealing are worship.
Wealth is not "mine to do with as I please" outside God's limits.
Reform as far as you are able, and practise what you call to.

subs.t: His call: worship and honest measure

p.l: Give full measure and weight, and do not deprive people of their due
Do not decrease the measure; what remains from God is best for you
Give full measure, weigh with an even balance, and do not deprive people
Does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped or what we do with our wealth?
I only intend reform as much as I am able; my success is only through God
We will evict you or you must return to our religion; the earthquake seized them
Were it not for your family we would have stoned you; the shriek seized them
The punishment of the day of the black cloud seized them
To Madyan their brother Shu'ayb; they denied him
The companions of the Thicket were wrongdoers

themes.title: Musa
themes.hook: The most frequently told story in the Qur'an: from a basket on the river to the parting of the sea, the Tablets and the journey with Khidr.
overview: Musa is mentioned more than any other prophet, and his story appears in many surahs, each emphasising a different stage.

He was born while Pharaoh was killing the sons of Bani Israel. God inspired his mother to place him in a basket on the river and promised to return him; Pharaoh's own household picked him up, his sister followed, and he refused all nurses until he was returned to his mother (28:7-13). As a young man he struck an Egyptian who was fighting an Israelite and killed him unintentionally; he repented and fled to Madyan, where he helped two women water their flock, married one of them and worked for her father for years (28:14-28).

On the way back he saw a fire at Mount Tur and was called: "I am God; there is no god but Me" (20:14). He was given signs, the staff and the shining hand, and sent with his brother Harun to Pharaoh, to speak gently (20:42-44). Pharaoh's magicians were defeated and believed. Plagues came and went. Musa led Bani Israel out; the sea parted, and Pharaoh drowned (26:52-68).

In the desert came the springs from the rock, manna and quails, and the forty nights at the mountain where Musa received the Tablets. In his absence the people worshipped a golden calf made by as-Samiri (20:83-97). Later came the command to slaughter a cow, the refusal to enter the Holy Land, and forty years of wandering.

His journey with Khidr taught that God's wisdom lies behind events that look wrong (18:60-82). Musa's prayers, "My Lord, expand my chest" and "My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send me", remain among the most loved in the Qur'an.
lessons: God's protection can work through the household of one's enemy.
Speak gently even to a tyrant.
Leaders must stay alert; communities can slide into idolatry quickly.
Humility in learning: even a great prophet followed a teacher with patience.
Ask God for an open heart and ease in your task.

p.l: Pharaoh divided the people into factions, killing their sons
Put him into the river; Pharaoh's family picked him up; We returned him to his mother
We restored you to your mother that she might be content
Musa struck him and killed him; my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me
He watered their flock; one of them came walking shyly; the hire of eight years
I am your Lord; remove your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa
A fire at the mountain; O Musa, I am God, Lord of the worlds
Blessed is whoever is at the fire; throw down your staff
His Lord called him in the sacred valley of Tuwa: go to Pharaoh
Speak to him with gentle speech, that perhaps he may be reminded
Did we not raise you among us as a child?
He threw his staff and it became a serpent; he drew out his hand and it was white
Throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have crafted
The magicians fell down in prostration: we believe in the Lord of the worlds
Do you kill a man because he says my Lord is God?
The flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood as distinct signs
Pharaoh: is not the kingdom of Egypt mine?

subs.t: The exodus and the parting of the sea

p.l: Strike the sea with your staff; it parted, each portion like a great mountain
Strike for them a dry path through the sea
Today We will save you in body, that you may be a sign
We parted the sea for you and drowned the people of Pharaoh

subs.t: In the desert: water, manna and quails

p.l: We shaded you with clouds and sent down manna and quails
Strike the stone with your staff; twelve springs gushed forth

subs.t: The forty nights and the Tablets

p.l: My Lord, show me Yourself; We wrote for him on the Tablets
As-Samiri led them astray: a calf, a body with a lowing sound
They took a calf; he threw the Tablets and seized his brother
You took the calf while you were wrongdoers
God commands you to slaughter a cow

subs.t: Refusal to enter and the wandering

p.l: Go, you and your Lord, and fight; forbidden to them for forty years
May I follow you so you teach me? The boat, the boy and the wall
Qarun was from the people of Musa, but he tyrannised them
My Lord, expand for me my chest and ease for me my task
My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me
Do not be like those who abused Musa; he was distinguished in the sight of God
Musa was chosen, a messenger and prophet; We called him from the right side of the mount

themes.title: Harun
themes.hook: Musa's brother, eloquent helper and deputy, who stood firm when his people turned to the calf.
overview: Harun is known through his brother. When Musa was sent to Pharaoh, he asked God to make his brother his minister: "Increase through him my strength and let him share in my task, that we may glorify You much" (20:29-34). He described Harun as more eloquent in speech (28:34), and God granted the request: "We will strengthen your arm through your brother" (28:35). Harun is therefore a prophet given as a gift to another prophet (19:53).

When Musa went to the mountain for forty nights, he left Harun as his deputy: "Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters" (7:142). In his absence the people made the golden calf. Harun warned them: "You are only being tested by it; your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my order" (20:90). They refused.

When Musa returned in anger and seized him, Harun answered with "O son of my mother", explaining that he feared being blamed for causing division among Bani Israel (20:94), and that the people had overpowered him and nearly killed him (7:150). Musa then prayed for forgiveness for himself and his brother (7:151).
lessons: Asking for help in a great task is wisdom, not weakness.
A good deputy keeps to the trust given to him.
Siblings can be partners in faith and work.

p.l: Appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun my brother
My brother Harun is more fluent than me in tongue; We will strengthen your arm
Send for Harun
We gave him out of Our mercy his brother Harun as a prophet
We appointed with him his brother Harun as an assistant
We gave Musa and Harun the criterion and a light
Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters
You are only being tested by it; O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard
The people overpowered me and were about to kill me; my Lord, forgive me and my brother
We conferred favour upon Musa and Harun; peace upon Musa and Harun

themes.title: Dhul-Kifl
themes.hook: Named twice among the patient and the best; known by his virtues rather than his story.
overview: Dhul-Kifl is one of the prophets whose names the Qur'an gives with very little detail. He appears twice: among the patient with Ismail and Idris, admitted into God's mercy as righteous (21:85-86), and among "the outstanding" with Ismail and al-Yasa' (38:48).

His name may mean "the one with the portion" or "the one who kept his pledge", and many later stories have been attached to it, but none is authenticated, so the app keeps to what the Qur'an says. As with Idris, the lesson is in the words chosen: patience and goodness are what earned him a place in God's book.
lessons: Patience is one of the qualities God names most in His prophets.
A life can be honoured by God without its details being told.

p.l: Ismail, Idris and Dhul-Kifl; all were of the patient
Remember Ismail, Elisha and Dhul-Kifl; all are among the outstanding

themes.title: Dawud
themes.hook: The young warrior who killed Jalut, a king and prophet given the Psalms, iron and judgement, quick to repent.
overview: Dawud first appears as a young soldier in the army of Talut. When the small believing army faced the giant Jalut and his forces, they prayed for patience and steadiness, and "Dawud killed Jalut, and God gave him kingship and wisdom and taught him what He willed" (2:250-251).

He became both king and prophet. God gave him the Zabur (4:163; 17:55), and the mountains and birds glorified God with him (34:10; 38:18-19). God made iron soft for him and taught him to make coats of mail: "Make full coats of mail and calculate the links, and work righteousness" (34:10-11), so he is also a model of skilled, honest work.

He is praised as a man of strength who constantly turned back to God (38:17). Two disputants once climbed into his prayer chamber with a case about ewes; Dawud judged quickly, then realised he had been tested, sought forgiveness, fell down bowing and repented (38:21-25). God then told him: "We have made you a successor on earth, so judge between people in truth and do not follow desire" (38:26). He and his son Sulayman also judged together in the case of the field, and God gave Sulayman the better understanding while giving both judgement and knowledge (21:78-79).
lessons: God can raise the young and unknown to defeat what seems unbeatable.
Skilled work done with integrity is part of righteousness.
Judge with truth, not desire, and listen to both sides.
Those in power should be quickest to repent.

p.l: How many a small company has overcome a large one; Dawud killed Jalut
Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength; We strengthened his kingdom and gave him wisdom
To Dawud We gave the Zabur
We preferred some prophets over others, and to Dawud We gave the book

subs.t: Mountains and birds glorify with him

p.l: O mountains, repeat praises with him, and the birds
We subjected the mountains to exalt with Dawud, and the birds

subs.t: Iron and the coats of mail

p.l: We made iron pliable for him: make full coats of mail, and work righteousness
We taught him the fashioning of coats of armour

subs.t: The test of judgement and his repentance

p.l: The two disputants and the ewes; he asked forgiveness and fell down bowing
We have made you a successor on earth, so judge with truth and do not follow desire
We gave understanding of the case to Sulayman, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge
We gave Dawud and Sulayman knowledge; Sulayman inherited Dawud
To Dawud We gave Sulayman; an excellent servant
Cursed were those who disbelieved on the tongue of Dawud and Isa

themes.title: Sulayman
themes.hook: A prophet-king given command of wind and jinn and the speech of birds, who said: "This is from my Lord's favour, to test me."
overview: Sulayman inherited from Dawud knowledge and prophethood and was given a kingdom like no other: the wind blew at his command, the jinn built for him, and he was taught the speech of birds (27:16; 34:12-13). Yet the constant note of his story is gratitude.

Marching with his army of jinn, men and birds, he came to the valley of the ants and heard an ant warn the others to enter their homes lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush them unknowingly. He smiled and prayed: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour" (27:18-19). Inspecting the birds, he noticed the hoopoe was missing; it returned with news of a queen in Saba' and her people who worshipped the sun (27:20-26).

He sent her a letter beginning "In the name of God, the Most Merciful", inviting her to submit. She consulted her council, sent a gift to test him, and he refused it. Her throne was brought to him in the blink of an eye, at which he said: "This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful or ungrateful" (27:40). When she came and saw his palace with its glass floor, she said: "I submit with Sulayman to God, Lord of the worlds" (27:44).

The Qur'an also defends him: it was not Sulayman who disbelieved through magic, but the devils (2:102). He died leaning on his staff, and the jinn did not realise until a creature of the earth ate through it, showing they never knew the unseen (34:14).
lessons: Power and wealth are tests of gratitude.
A leader notices even the smallest member of his realm.
Invitation to faith can be made with letters, diplomacy and wisdom.
Refuse gifts that are meant to buy you off the truth.

subs.t: Inheritance and the speech of birds

p.l: We have been taught the language of birds and given from all things
O ants, enter your dwellings; he smiled and prayed: enable me to be grateful
I found a woman ruling them; she and her people prostrate to the sun

subs.t: The letter and the queen's council

p.l: It is from Sulayman, and it is: in the name of God, the Most Merciful
Do you provide me with wealth? What God has given me is better

subs.t: The throne brought in a blink

p.l: This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me whether I will be grateful

subs.t: The palace of glass and her submission

p.l: I submit with Sulayman to God, Lord of the worlds

subs.t: Wind and jinn in his service

p.l: To Sulayman the wind; the jinn worked for him; work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude
To Sulayman the wind, blowing forcefully by his command
We subjected to him the wind and the devils, builders and divers
My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom such as will not belong to anyone after me
We gave understanding of the case to Sulayman

subs.t: Cleared of the charge of magic

p.l: It was not Sulayman who disbelieved, but the devils
When We decreed his death, nothing indicated it except a creature eating his staff

themes.title: Ilyas
themes.hook: A messenger who confronted the worship of Ba'l: "Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators?"
overview: Ilyas is named in Surah as-Saffat as one of the messengers. He asked his people: "Will you not fear God? Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators, God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers?" (37:124-126). Ba'l was an idol worshipped in the region.

They denied him, and the Qur'an says they will be brought to account, except God's sincere servants (37:127-128). God left for him a good mention among later generations: "Peace upon Ilyasin. Thus do We reward the doers of good; he was of Our believing servants" (37:129-132). In Surah al-An'am he is listed with Zakariya, Yahya and Isa as "all of the righteous" (6:85).
lessons: Idols change names across history; the call to worship the Creator alone does not change.
A truthful call is remembered with peace even when rejected.

p.l: Do you call upon Ba'l and leave the best of creators?
Peace upon Elias; he was of Our believing servants
Zakariya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas: all were of the righteous

themes.title: Al-Yasa'
themes.hook: Named among the outstanding and those preferred over the worlds.
overview: Al-Yasa' (Elisha) is named twice in the Qur'an, each time in a list of prophets. In Surah al-An'am he appears with Ismail, Yunus and Lut: "each We preferred over the worlds" (6:86). In Surah Sad he is named with Ismail and Dhul-Kifl: "all are among the outstanding" (38:48).
The Qur'an tells nothing more of his life, and the app keeps to its account. His inclusion shows that God's honour extends to prophets whose deeds are known to Him even if they are not told to us.
lessons: To be counted among "the outstanding" by God is the measure that matters.

p.l: Ismail, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut; each We preferred over the worlds
Remember Ismail, al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl; all are among the outstanding

themes.title: Yunus
themes.hook: The prophet who left his people in anger, called out from the darkness of the whale, and was forgiven; his people were the one nation saved by repenting.
overview: Yunus, also called Dhun-Nun, "the man of the fish", left his people in anger before God gave him leave, thinking God would not restrict him (21:87). He boarded a laden ship; lots were drawn, he lost, and he was cast into the sea, where a great fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy (37:140-142).

In the layers of darkness he called out: "There is no god but You, glory be to You; I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87). The Qur'an says that had he not been of those who glorify God, he would have remained in its belly until the Day of Resurrection (37:143-144). God answered him and saved him from distress, "and thus do We save the believers" (21:88).
He was cast onto open land while ill, and God made a gourd plant grow over him (37:145-146). He was then sent again to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed (37:147-148).

His people are singled out: "Why was there not a town that believed so its faith benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace" (10:98). The Prophet ﷺ is told: "Be patient for the decision of your Lord, and do not be like the companion of the fish" (68:48).
lessons: Do not abandon your duty in frustration; patience is the prophetic way.
In any darkness, the prayer of Yunus is a door: tawhid, glorification and confession.
Repentance can lift even a punishment that has begun to approach.

p.l: Dhun-Nun, when he went off in anger and thought We would not decree anything upon him
He ran away to the laden ship, drew lots, and the fish swallowed him
There is no deity except You; exalted are You; I have been of the wrongdoers
Had he not been of those who exalt God, he would have remained inside its belly
Do not be like the companion of the fish when he called out in distress
We threw him onto the open shore while he was ill, and caused a gourd vine to grow over him

subs.t: Sent again to a hundred thousand

p.l: We sent him to a hundred thousand or more, and they believed

subs.t: The people who repented in time

p.l: Except the people of Yunus: when they believed, We removed the punishment of disgrace
Ismail, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut
We revealed to Ayyub, Yunus, Harun and Sulayman

themes.title: Zakariya
themes.hook: An elderly prophet who prayed quietly for an heir, and whose prayer was answered with Yahya.
overview: Zakariya was the guardian of Maryam. Whenever he entered her prayer chamber he found provision with her, and when he asked where it came from she said: "It is from God; God provides for whom He wills without account" (3:37). Moved by what he saw, he prayed there and then for a child of his own (3:38).

Surah Maryam opens with his prayer, which God calls a secret call: "My Lord, my bones have weakened and my head has filled with white, and never have I been unhappy in my prayer to You" (19:3-4). He feared for those who would succeed him, since his wife was barren, and asked for an heir who would inherit from him and from the family of Yaqub (19:5-6).

The angels called him while he stood praying: God gives you good news of Yahya, confirming a word from God, noble, chaste and a prophet (3:39). He asked how, being old and his wife barren; the answer was that it is easy for God (19:8-9). His sign was that he would not speak to people for three nights except by gestures (19:10).
The Qur'an praises the whole family: "They used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us" (21:90).
lessons: Seeing God's generosity to others can inspire your own prayer.
Pray quietly and humbly, naming your weakness before God.
Nothing is impossible for God, even in old age.

p.l: Whenever Zakariya entered upon her in the prayer chamber, he found provision with her
When he called to his Lord a private supplication: my bones have weakened
There Zakariya called upon his Lord: grant me from Yourself good offspring
My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors
The angels called him while he was standing in prayer
O Zakariya, We give you good tidings of a boy whose name will be Yahya

subs.t: A family that hastened to good

p.l: They used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear
Zakariya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas: all were of the righteous

themes.title: Yahya
themes.hook: Given wisdom as a child, tender-hearted, pure, dutiful to his parents: peace on the day he was born, died and will be raised.
overview: Yahya (John) was the son granted to Zakariya in old age, and God chose his name, one given to no one before him (19:7). He was told as a child: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination", and was given judgement while still a boy (19:12).

The Qur'an's description of him is a portrait of character: affection and purity from God, God-conscious, dutiful to his parents, and not a disobedient tyrant (19:13-14). He confirmed a word from God, understood as Isa, and was noble, chaste and a prophet from among the righteous (3:39).

His description closes with a blessing over his whole existence: "Peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive" (19:15). The same words are later spoken by Isa about himself (19:33).
lessons: Wisdom and seriousness about faith can begin in childhood.
Tenderness, purity and kindness to parents are prophetic qualities.

p.l: A boy whose name will be Yahya; We have not assigned to any before this name
O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination; We gave him judgement while yet a boy
Affection from Us and purity; he was fearing God and dutiful to his parents
Confirming a word from God, a leader, chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous
Peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive
We gave him Yahya and amended for him his wife
Zakariya, Yahya, Isa and Ilyas

themes.title: Isa
themes.hook: Born of Maryam without a father, a word from God, a messenger with miracles, raised to God, and a sign of the Hour.
overview: Isa son of Maryam holds a high place in the Qur'an. The angels gave Maryam good news of "a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near" (3:45). He was born without a father, and the Qur'an compares his creation to Adam's: created from dust, then God said "Be" (3:59).

He spoke from the cradle to defend his mother: "I am the servant of God; He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet... and dutiful to my mother" (19:30-32). He was sent to Bani Israel with signs by God's permission: a bird of clay given life, healing the blind and the leper, raising the dead, and telling people what they ate and stored in their homes (3:49). He confirmed the Torah, made lawful some things forbidden to them, and was given the Gospel (3:50; 5:46). His disciples declared themselves helpers of God, and asked for a table spread from heaven (5:111-115).

The Qur'an states that he was not killed and not crucified, "but it was made to appear so to them", and that God raised him to Himself (4:157-158). It rejects the claim that he is God or the son of God, and records his own testimony on the Day of Judgment that he told people only to worship God, his Lord and theirs (5:116-117). He gave good news of a messenger to come after him named Ahmad (61:6), and he will be a sign of the Hour (43:61).
lessons: Isa is honoured in Islam as a mighty messenger, the Messiah, born of a chaste mother.
His miracles were by God's permission; he called to worship God alone.
Respect for Isa and Maryam is part of a Muslim's faith.

p.l: A word from Him whose name is the Messiah, Isa son of Maryam
I am only the messenger of your Lord to give you a pure boy
She withdrew to a remote place; the pains of childbirth drove her to the palm trunk
The example of Isa is like that of Adam: created from dust, then Be
I am the servant of God; He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet
I make for you from clay a bird; I cure the blind and the leper and give life to the dead
You made from clay a bird, by My permission
Who are my supporters for God? The disciples said: we are supporters of God
O Isa, can your Lord send down to us a table spread from heaven?
Be supporters of God, as Isa said to the disciples
We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light, confirming the Torah
We gave him the Gospel and placed in the hearts of those who followed him compassion and mercy

subs.t: Not killed, not crucified, but raised

p.l: They did not kill him nor crucify him; God raised him to Himself
O Isa, I will take you and raise you to Myself
The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God
The Messiah son of Maryam was no more than a messenger; they both used to eat food
That is Isa son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute
They have taken the Messiah son of Maryam as a lord besides God
I said to them only what You commanded: worship God, my Lord and your Lord
Bringing good tidings of a messenger after me whose name is Ahmad
He is a sign for the Hour, so do not doubt it

themes.title: Muhammad ﷺ
themes.hook: The Messenger of God and seal of the prophets: his life, mission and character as the Qur'an describes them.
overview: The Qur'an speaks to the Prophet ﷺ and about him throughout his twenty-three years of mission. It recalls his early life with tenderness: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter, and find you lost and guide you, and find you poor and make you self-sufficient?" (93:6-8). It records the first revelation in the cave, "Read", and his commissioning to warn (96:1-5; 74:1-7).

His mission is described as universal: a mercy to the worlds (21:107), sent to all people (34:28), as witness, bringer of good news, warner and lamp spreading light (33:45-46). He is the seal of the prophets (33:40). Yet he is human: "I am only a man like you, to whom it is revealed" (18:110), and he would die like every soul (39:30; 3:144).

His character is praised by God Himself: "You are of a great moral character" (68:4). He was gentle, which drew people to him (3:159), grieved by people's hardship and anxious for their good (9:128), and is the excellent example for those who hope in God (33:21).

The Qur'an records the hardships: mockery and plots to imprison, kill or expel him (8:30), the Night Journey (17:1), the migration with his companion in the cave (9:40), and the battles that followed. It commands believers to obey him, love him above themselves (33:6), and send blessings upon him (33:56).
lessons: His life shows that orphanhood and hardship do not limit what God can make of a person.
Gentleness, concern for people and patience are the heart of his example.
Following him is the path to God's love.
Send blessings on him often, as God and His angels do.

p.l: Did He not find you an orphan and give refuge?
Did We not expand for you your breast and remove your burden?

subs.t: The first revelation and the call

p.l: Read in the name of your Lord who created
Arise and warn, and your Lord glorify
Warn your closest kindred
We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds
We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind
A witness, bringer of good tidings, warner, and an illuminating lamp
Muhammad is the Messenger of God and the seal of the prophets
I am only a man like you, to whom it has been revealed
Muhammad is not but a messenger; messengers have passed on before him
You will die, and they will die
You are truly of a great moral character
By mercy from God you were lenient with them; had you been harsh they would have left you
Grievous to him is what you suffer; concerned over you, kind and merciful
In the Messenger of God you have an excellent example
When those who disbelieved plotted to restrain you, kill you or evict you
Declare what you are commanded; We are sufficient against the mockers
They do not call you untruthful; it is the verses of God the wrongdoers reject
Glory to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa
He saw him at another descent, at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary
The second of two, when they were in the cave: do not grieve, God is with us
If you love God, follow me
Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed God
The Prophet is more worthy of the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers
God and His angels send blessings on the Prophet; send blessings on him
Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet
O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women

themes.title: Non-prophet figures
themes.hook: Sages, kings, tyrants and unnamed believers: people who were not prophets but whose stories teach.
overview: Alongside the prophets, the Qur'an tells the stories of other people whose lives carry lessons. Some are righteous: Luqman the wise, who advised his son (31:12-19); Khidr, the servant of God given knowledge from Him, whom Musa followed (18:65-82); Dhul-Qarnayn, a just ruler who travelled east and west and built a barrier against Gog and Magog (18:83-98); Talut, chosen as king for his knowledge and strength (2:247); and the youths of the Cave, who fled persecution for their faith (18:9-26).

Some are unnamed believers who stood up at great cost: the believing man from Pharaoh's family who concealed his faith and then spoke out (40:28-45); the man who came running from the far end of the town to support the messengers (36:20-27); the man who passed by a ruined town, died for a hundred years and was raised to see how God gives life (2:259).

Others are warnings: Pharaoh, the archetype of the tyrant; Haman his minister; Qarun, whose wealth swallowed him (28:76-82); as-Samiri, who made the golden calf (20:85-97); and Abu Lahab, the Prophet's uncle and enemy (surah 111).
Under the app's message-first rule, names and identities beyond the Qur'an's own words (for example, who Khidr or Dhul-Qarnayn were historically) are left to the tafsir.
lessons: Righteousness and wisdom are not limited to prophets.
One brave believer speaking up can matter, even inside a tyrant's household.
Wealth, power and cleverness without faith lead to ruin.

p.l: Luqman, given wisdom, advising his son
A servant of God given mercy and knowledge from Us, followed by Musa
Dhul-Qarnayn: his journeys and the barrier against Gog and Magog
Talut chosen as king for knowledge and stature; the river test
Youths who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance
A believing man from the family of Pharaoh who concealed his faith
A man came running from the farthest end of the city: follow the messengers
One who passed by a township fallen into ruin, and God caused him to die for a hundred years
Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people
O Haman, ignite for me a fire upon the clay and make me a tower
Pharaoh said: I am your most exalted lord

subs.t: Those ruined by wealth or cunning

p.l: Qarun: the earth swallowed him and his home
As-Samiri led them astray
The man with two gardens who said: I do not think this will ever perish
May the hands of Abu Lahab be ruined
Leave Me with the one I created alone: he thought and deliberated
Are they better or the people of Tubba'?
The Jews say 'Uzayr is the son of God
Ibrahim said to his father Azar

themes.title: Women in the Qur'an
themes.hook: Maryam, Asiyah, the mothers of Musa and Isa, the Queen of Saba' and others: women of faith, courage and warning.
overview: The Qur'an tells the stories of many women, and holds some up as examples for all believers, men and women alike. Two are named as models: the wife of Pharaoh, who prayed for a house in Paradise and rescue from Pharaoh and his deeds (66:11), and Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity and believed in her Lord's words (66:12). Maryam is the only woman named in the Qur'an, and a surah carries her name. The angels told her: "God has chosen you, purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds" (3:42).

Other women are central to the stories of prophets: Musa's mother, who placed her baby in the river trusting God's promise; Musa's sister, who followed the basket; the wife of Imran, who vowed her child to God; Sarah, who laughed at the news of Ishaq; Hajar, left in the valley of Makkah; the daughters of Madyan; and the Queen of Saba', a wise ruler who consulted her council and submitted to God with Sulayman.

Some are warnings: the wives of Nuh and Lut, who were close to prophets but did not believe (66:10), the wife of al-Aziz, and the wife of Abu Lahab. And some women of the Prophet's time are honoured by having their concerns answered in revelation, like the woman who argued about her husband (58:1). The Qur'an states plainly that men and women who believe and do good receive equal reward (33:35; 3:195).
lessons: Women are held up in the Qur'an as models of faith for everyone.
Faith is personal: a believing woman married to a tyrant, and unbelieving wives of prophets.
God heard a woman's complaint and answered it in His book.

p.l: The wife of Pharaoh: my Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise
Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity and believed
O Maryam, God has chosen you and purified you above the women of the worlds
Musa's mother: put him into the river and do not fear
The wife of Imran: I have pledged what is in my womb to You
Maryam and the birth of Isa
Ibrahim leaves his family in the barren valley
Sarah laughed at the good news
Musa's sister: follow him
Two women who said: we do not water until the shepherds leave
The Queen of Saba': her council, her gift and her submission with Sulayman

subs.t: The wife of al-Aziz and the women of the city

p.l: The wife of al-Aziz sought to seduce him; the women of the city cut their hands
The wife of al-Aziz: now the truth has become evident; it was I who sought to seduce him
The wives of Nuh and Lut betrayed them
His wife, the carrier of firewood
God has heard the speech of the one who argues with you about her husband
When the believing women come to you as emigrants, and when they pledge allegiance
O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other women
Muslim men and women, believing men and women: God has prepared forgiveness and great reward
I will not allow the work of any worker to be lost, whether male or female

themes.title: Miracles of the prophets
themes.hook: Signs God gave His messengers: a staff that split the sea, fire made cool, the dead raised, and the Qur'an itself.
overview: The Qur'an calls miracles "signs" (ayat), the same word used for its verses. They were given by God's permission to prove a messenger's truth, usually in a form his people would recognise.

Musa's staff became a serpent and swallowed the magicians' illusions; his hand shone white; the sea parted when struck; twelve springs burst from a rock. Ibrahim was thrown into a fire that God made cool and safe. Salih's people were given a she-camel from God as a sign. Isa made a bird from clay and breathed into it, healed the blind and the leper, and raised the dead, each "by God's permission". Sulayman commanded the wind and jinn and understood the speech of birds; Dawud's mountains and birds glorified God with him and iron softened in his hands. Yunus survived inside a fish. Maryam was provided for in her prayer chamber and fed with fresh dates.

For the Prophet ﷺ, the Qur'an itself is the central miracle: "Is it not sufficient for them that We sent down to you the Book which is recited to them?" (29:51). It also mentions the splitting of the moon (54:1) and the Night Journey (17:1). When the Quraysh demanded particular miracles, he was told to answer: "Glory be to my Lord; am I anything but a human messenger?" (17:93). The Qur'an notes that past peoples who were given the signs they demanded still denied them (17:59).
lessons: Miracles come by God's permission; the prophets never claimed them as their own power.
The Qur'an is a living sign that remains, unlike past miracles.
Demanding signs is not the same as seeking truth.

p.l: He threw his staff and it became a serpent; he drew out his hand, white
What is that in your right hand? Throw it down
Strike the sea with your staff; it parted
Strike the stone with your staff; twelve springs
O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim
Take four birds, then call them; they will come to you in haste
This is the she-camel of God for you as a sign
I make from clay a bird and it becomes a bird by God's permission
You healed the blind and the leper and brought forth the dead by My permission
A table spread from heaven
We made iron soft for Dawud, and gave Sulayman the wind
We have been taught the language of birds
The throne brought before the blink of an eye
The ark built under Our eyes, and the flood
The fish swallowed him, then cast him out
Take this shirt of mine and cast it over my father's face
Provision found with Maryam in her chamber
Shake the trunk of the palm toward you; it will drop ripe fresh dates
A son in old age: it is easy for Me
We struck their ears in the cave for a number of years
Look at your donkey; We will make you a sign for the people
Is it not sufficient for them that We revealed to you the Book?
The Hour has come near and the moon has split
The Night Journey to al-Masjid al-Aqsa
Nothing prevented Us from sending signs except that the former peoples denied them
They said: we will not believe until you make a spring gush forth
Even if We sent down the angels and the dead spoke to them, they would not believe
You are only a warner, and for every people is a guide

themes.title: Destroyed nations
themes.hook: The people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud, Lut, Madyan, Pharaoh and Saba': why they fell, and what their ruins still say.
overview: The Qur'an repeatedly asks its listeners to look at the ruins of earlier nations and learn. It names the people of Nuh, drowned in the flood; 'Ad, destroyed by a wind; Thamud, seized by a blast; the people of Lut, whose cities were overturned; Madyan, struck by an earthquake; Pharaoh and his army, drowned in the sea; and Saba', whose great dam burst after they turned away (34:15-17). It also mentions the companions of the Thicket, of the Well, of the Elephant, of the Ditch, and the people of Tubba'.

Their sins differ: idolatry, arrogance about their strength, cruelty to the weak, sexual immorality, cheating in trade, tyranny and ingratitude. What they share is denying their messengers and persisting after warning. "Each We seized for his sin" (29:40).

The Qur'an sets two limits on this pattern. God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers (11:117), and He does not punish until He has sent a messenger (17:15). The stories are not told to entertain but as signs: "Have they not travelled through the land, so that they have hearts to reason with?" (22:46).
lessons: No power or wealth makes a nation secure against God's justice.
Corruption, injustice and ingratitude bring down societies.
Reformers within a community are a protection for it.

p.l: 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh and Haman: each We seized for his sin
Such is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they commit wrong
We opened the gates of heaven with rain pouring down
Destroyed by a screaming violent wind
Iram, with lofty pillars
Their Lord brought down upon them destruction for their sin
Thamud were destroyed by the overpowering blast
We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon them stones
The shriek seized those who had wronged
How much they left behind of gardens and springs; the heaven and earth did not weep for them
Pharaoh: I believe; Now? Today We will save your body
Two gardens, the flood of the dam, and their gardens replaced with bitter fruit
Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?
Cursed were the companions of the trench, the fire full of fuel
'Ad, Thamud, the companions of the well, and many generations between them
The people of Nuh, the companions of the well, Thamud, 'Ad, Pharaoh, Lut, the Thicket and Tubba'

subs.t: Why nations fall, and why some are spared

p.l: When We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent but they defiantly disobey
Your Lord would not destroy cities unjustly while their people were reformers
How many a city which was insolent in its livelihood We destroyed
Have they not travelled through the land, so that they have hearts to reason with?
Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?

themes.title: The history of Bani Israel
themes.hook: A people chosen and favoured, tested by covenants, the Sabbath and their own failures, with the righteous among them honoured.
overview: The Children of Israel are addressed directly in the Qur'an more than any other earlier people, and their history is told as a lesson for every community that receives revelation.

God reminds them of His favours: rescue from Pharaoh, the parting of the sea, shade from clouds, manna and quails, water from the rock, and being preferred over the worlds of their time (2:40-57). He took covenants from them: to worship God alone, honour parents, care for relatives, orphans and the poor, speak well to people, pray and give charity, and not shed one another's blood (2:83-84).

The Qur'an also records failures: the golden calf, demanding to see God openly, changing the words they were told to say, complaining about manna, hardened hearts, refusing to enter the Holy Land, and breaking the Sabbath through a trick (7:163-166). It describes two periods of corruption on earth, each followed by punishment (17:4-8).

At the same time it is careful to be fair: "They are not all the same; among the People of the Book is a community standing in prayer, reciting God's verses" (3:113). Among the people of Musa is a community that guides by truth and establishes justice by it (7:159). The lesson for Muslims is explicit: favour brings responsibility, and the same failures can befall any people.
lessons: Being chosen by God is a responsibility, not a privilege of birth.
Tricks to get around God's commands are themselves disobedience.
Judge communities fairly: the righteous among any people are honoured.
What happened to earlier people of the Book is a warning to Muslims.

p.l: O Children of Israel, remember My favour; We saved you from Pharaoh's people
We shaded you with clouds and sent down manna and quails
Remember the favour of God upon you when He saved you from Pharaoh's people
We gave the Children of Israel the Scripture, judgement and prophethood
We saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment
We took your covenant and raised over you the mount
Worship none but God, be good to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy
God took a covenant from the Children of Israel and We appointed twelve leaders
You took the calf; you said: we will never believe until we see God outright
They changed the words they were told to say; they asked for garlic, lentils and onions
Your hearts hardened after that, being like stones or even harder
Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are sitting right here
The town by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath
You knew those who transgressed concerning the Sabbath
We said to them: do not transgress on the Sabbath
The Sabbath was only appointed for those who differed over it
You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice
Among the people of Musa is a community which guides by truth
They are not all the same: a community standing in prayer
We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient
Among them are a moderate community

themes.title: The Prophet's life and battles in sequence
themes.hook: The events of the Prophet's mission as the Qur'an records them, from the cave of Hira to the farewell pilgrimage.
overview: This theme follows the Prophet's life in order, using the passages revealed about each event. Read in sequence, they show how revelation accompanied the community through every stage.

In Makkah: the first revelation (96:1-5), the command to warn his kin (26:214), years of mockery and pressure, plots to imprison, kill or expel him (8:30), and the Night Journey (17:1). Then the Hijrah, with his companion in the cave: "Do not grieve, God is with us" (9:40).

In Madinah: the first permission to fight for those who had been wronged (22:39-40); the battle of Badr, where a small force was supported by angels (3:123; 8:9-12); Uhud, where disobedience of the archers turned victory into loss and the Qur'an consoled and corrected the believers (3:121-175); the expulsion of Banu Nadir (59:2-6); the siege of the Trench, when "eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats" (33:9-27); the slander against Aisha and her vindication (24:11-20).

Then the treaty of Hudaybiyah, called a "clear victory" though it looked like a setback (48:1-29); the conquest of Makkah and people entering God's religion in crowds (surah 110); Hunayn, where pride in numbers nearly brought defeat (9:25-26); Tabuk, the test of the hypocrites and of the three who stayed behind (9:38-118); the completion of the religion (5:3); and the reminder that Muhammad ﷺ is a messenger who would pass on like those before him (3:144).
lessons: Revelation guided the community through victory and defeat alike.
Disobedience and pride cost the believers even when God was with them.
What looks like a setback can be a clear victory.
The mission continues after the Messenger; faith is in God, who does not die.

subs.t: Makkah: the call and the opposition

p.l: Read in the name of your Lord
Warn your closest kindred, and lower your wing to the believers
When the disbelievers plotted to restrain you, kill you or evict you
The Night Journey
The second of two in the cave: do not grieve, God is with us
Permission is given to those who are fought, because they were wronged
Fighting in the sacred month is great, but preventing from God's way is greater
Your Lord took you out of your home for the truth; the angels and the sleep of security
The day the two armies met; you were on the near side of the valley
God had already given you victory at Badr while you were few
It is not for a prophet to have captives until he inflicts a massacre; the captives
When you left your family in the morning to post the believers at their stations
Do not weaken and do not grieve; when you fell into disagreement and disobeyed
When a disaster struck you; those who responded to God after injury
He expelled the disbelievers among the People of the Book from their homes
When armies came at you; eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats
Those who came with falsehood are a group among you
We have given you a clear conquest
God was pleased with the believers when they pledged under the tree
You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in safety
When the victory of God has come and the conquest
On the day of Hunayn your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you
What is wrong with you that when told to go forth you cling heavily to the earth?
Those who remained behind rejoiced in their staying
Those who took a mosque for causing harm
God turned to the Prophet, the emigrants and the helpers, and to the three left behind
Today I have perfected for you your religion
Muhammad is not but a messenger; if he died, would you turn back?

themes.title: The family of Imran
themes.hook: A chosen family: a mother's vow, Maryam's upbringing, Zakariya's prayer, and the birth of Isa.
overview: "God chose Adam, Nuh, the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran over the worlds, descendants one of another" (3:33-34). The third surah of the Qur'an is named after this family, and tells its story across three generations of faith.

It begins with a mother's vow. The wife of Imran pledged her unborn child to God's service. When she gave birth to a girl, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered a female", and named her Maryam, seeking refuge for her and her descendants from Satan. "Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good manner" (3:35-37).

Zakariya became Maryam's guardian, and found provision with her whenever he entered her chamber. That sight moved him to pray for his own child, and he was given Yahya (3:37-41). Then the angels told Maryam she was chosen and purified above the women of the worlds, and gave her the news of a son, Isa, the Messiah (3:42-47).

Surah Maryam tells the birth itself: her withdrawal, the pains under the palm, the voice that comforted her, and the infant who spoke to defend her (19:16-34). She is called "sister of Harun" (19:28), in the sense of her lineage of piety. God presents her as an example for all believers (66:12).
lessons: A parent's sincere intention for a child can shape generations.
God accepted a daughter's dedication with "good acceptance"; His choice is not by gender.
Faith can be passed through a family, and also through guardians and teachers.

p.l: God chose the family of Imran over the worlds, descendants one of another
My Lord, I have pledged to You what is in my womb; I have delivered a female
Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance, and put her in Zakariya's care
There Zakariya called upon his Lord

subs.t: Chosen above the women of the worlds

p.l: God has chosen you, purified you and chosen you above the women of the worlds
A word from Him whose name is the Messiah
She withdrew from her family to a place toward the east
O sister of Harun, your father was not a man of evil
Maryam, daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity
We made her and her son a sign for the worlds
We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign, and sheltered them

themes.title: Death, its scenes and wills
themes.hook: Every soul will taste death; the Qur'an describes the moment, the regret of those unprepared, and the will to leave behind.
overview: Death is the one certainty the Qur'an returns to most: "Every soul will taste death, and you will only be paid your full reward on the Day of Resurrection" (3:185). No one escapes it: "The death from which you flee will meet you" (62:8), even inside lofty towers (4:78). Every person has an appointed term that cannot be delayed or advanced by an hour (7:34).

The Qur'an describes the moment itself: the soul reaching the throat while those around watch helplessly (56:83-87), the stupor of death bringing the truth (50:19). For the wrongdoers, angels stretch out their hands; for the righteous, the angels greet them with peace and good news of Paradise (16:32; 41:30).

The most repeated scene is regret: "My Lord, send me back, that I might do righteousness in what I left behind" (23:99-100), and "If only You would delay me a short time, I would give charity and be among the righteous" (63:10). The answer is that the term will not be delayed.

Practical guidance accompanies this. The believer is told to write a will for parents and relatives (2:180), to have it witnessed (5:106), and that inheritance is divided after any bequest or debt is settled (4:11-12). Those who die in God's cause are not called dead; they are alive with their Lord (3:169). And those struck by loss are taught to say: "We belong to God, and to Him we will return" (2:156).
lessons: Prepare now; the request to be "sent back" is never granted.
Give charity and settle affairs before death comes.
Write a will and settle debts; it protects your family.
Meet loss with "We belong to God and to Him we return".

p.l: Every soul will taste death, and you will be paid in full on the Day
The death from which you flee will meet you
Wherever you are, death will overtake you, even in lofty towers
The intoxication of death will bring the truth
For every nation is a term; when it comes they cannot delay it an hour
He defers them for a specified term
Spend before death comes and one says: if only You would delay me a little
When the soul reaches the throat, We are nearer to him than you
When it reaches the collarbones, and he is certain it is the parting
The angels extend their hands: discharge your souls
The angels take the disbelievers, striking their faces and backs
How will it be when the angels take them in death, striking their faces?
Those whom the angels take in death while wronging themselves
The angels take them, being good, saying: peace be upon you, enter Paradise
The angels descend: do not fear and do not grieve
My Lord, send me back that I might do righteousness; behind them is a barrier
Prescribed for you when death approaches, if he leaves wealth, is a bequest
Testimony among you when death approaches, at the time of bequest, two just men
Shares of inheritance, after any bequest or debt

subs.t: Those who die in God's cause

p.l: Do not say about those killed in God's way: dead; they are alive
They are alive with their Lord, receiving provision, rejoicing
Those who say when disaster strikes: we belong to God and to Him we return

themes.title: Barzakh and the signs of the Hour
themes.hook: What lies between death and resurrection, and how the Qur'an describes the approach and arrival of the Hour.
overview: Between death and resurrection lies the barzakh, a barrier (23:100). The Qur'an gives only glimpses of it: Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, before the greater punishment on the Day (40:46); the people of Nuh were drowned and "made to enter a Fire" (71:25); those killed in God's way are alive and provided for (3:169).

The Hour itself is unknown to anyone but God: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord; none will reveal its time except Him" (7:187). Yet it is near (54:1; 21:1), and its indications have already come (47:18). Among the signs named are the release of Gog and Magog, the Beast that speaks to people, a smoke covering the sky, and Isa son of Maryam as a sign for the Hour.

When it arrives, the Qur'an describes a cosmic undoing. The sun is wrapped up, the stars fall, the mountains move like clouds and become like carded wool, the seas are set aflame, the sky splits open, and the earth is shaken with its final quake and throws out its burdens (81; 82; 99; 101). The Horn is blown and all in the heavens and earth fall dead except whom God wills; then it is blown again and they stand, looking on (39:68).
These passages are among the earliest Makkan revelations, short and forceful, meant to shake the listener into taking life seriously.
lessons: No one knows the time of the Hour; the wise prepare instead of predicting.
The world's permanence is an illusion; even mountains will be carded wool.
Each person meets their own "hour" at death; that is the nearest Hour.

p.l: Behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected
The Fire, they are exposed to it morning and evening
Because of their sins they were drowned and put into the Fire

subs.t: Its time is with God alone

p.l: They ask you about the Hour: its knowledge is only with my Lord
People ask you about the Hour; perhaps it is near
They ask you about the Hour; to your Lord is its finality
God has knowledge of the Hour
The Hour has come near and the moon has split
Their account has approached for the people while they turn away
Its indications have already come
When Gog and Magog are released
We will bring forth a creature from the earth
Watch for the Day when the sky brings a visible smoke
He (Isa) is a sign of the Hour
On the day some of your Lord's signs come, faith will not benefit
When the sun is wrapped up and the stars fall
When the sky breaks apart and the seas are erupted
When the sky has split and the earth has been extended
When the earth is shaken with its final earthquake
People like moths dispersed and mountains like wool fluffed up
When vision is dazzled and the moon darkens
My Lord will blow them away with a blast and leave the earth a level plain
When the Occurrence occurs; the mountains broken down
The Horn will be blown and all will fall dead; then it will be blown again
It will be only one blast, and at once they are all brought present
The Day the Horn is blown and you will come forth in multitudes

themes.title: Resurrection and Judgment
themes.hook: The Creator who made you the first time will raise you again; every deed will be weighed, and your own limbs will testify.
overview: The Qur'an answers the objection "Who will give life to bones when they have rotted?" with a simple argument: "He will give them life who produced them the first time" (36:78-79). Creating a second time is no harder than the first (30:27). The earth that is dead and revived by rain is shown as a picture of resurrection (22:5; 30:19), and God says He is able to restore even the fingertips (75:3-4).
