On the Day, people come out of their graves hurrying as if to a goal (70:43), like scattered locusts (54:7). Each is handed a record: "Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant" (17:14). Those given it in the right hand rejoice; those given it in the left wish it had never been given (69:19-29).

Justice is exact. "We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged at all; even if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth" (21:47). Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it, and an atom's weight of evil will see it (99:7-8).

Witnesses come from within: tongues, hands, feet, hearing, sight and skin testify (24:24; 36:65; 41:20-21). No one carries another's burden (6:164); a man flees his brother, mother, father, wife and children (80:34-37). Intercession exists only by God's permission (2:255; 20:109). Every person will be questioned about what they were given (102:8; 17:36).
lessons: The One who created you once can surely do it again.
Nothing is too small to be weighed: neither good nor bad.
Your own body will speak on the Day; use it in what you will be glad to hear.
No relationship will carry your burden for you.

p.l: Who will give life to bones when they have rotted? He who produced them the first time
If you are in doubt about the resurrection: We created you from dust
He brings the living out of the dead and gives life to the earth after its death
Does man think We will not assemble his bones? We are able to proportion his fingertips
When we are bones and crumbled particles, will we be resurrected?
When we have died and become dust? That is a distant return; We revive a dead land
The Day they emerge from the graves rapidly as if hurrying to an erected idol
Like locusts spreading
Voices will be stilled before the Most Merciful
We will gather them and not leave behind anyone; presented to your Lord in rows
Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as accountant
Here, read my record; I wish I had not been given my record
Whoever is given his record in his right hand
What is this book that leaves nothing small or great except it has enumerated it?
We place the scales of justice; no soul will be treated unjustly at all
The weighing that Day will be the truth
As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it
That Day We will seal their mouths, and their hands will speak to Us
Their hearing, their eyes and their skins will testify
Their tongues, hands and feet will bear witness
How will it be when We bring from every nation a witness?
No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another
The Day a man will flee from his brother, his mother and father, his wife and children
No friend will ask anything of a friend; the criminal will wish to ransom himself with his children
A Day when no father will avail his son
Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?
That Day no intercession will benefit except for one to whom the Most Merciful has given permission
Fear a Day when no soul will suffice for another, and no intercession will be accepted
How many an angel whose intercession will not avail except after God permits
We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent
We will surely question them all about what they used to do
The hearing, the sight and the heart: about all those one will be questioned
You will surely be asked that Day about pleasure

themes.title: Paradise
themes.hook: Gardens as wide as the heavens and earth, rivers that never change, reunion with loved ones, peace, and the pleasure of God.
overview: The Qur'an describes Paradise (al-Jannah, the Garden) in more detail than almost any other subject, to awaken longing. Its width is that of the heavens and the earth (3:133). It has rivers of water that never stagnates, of milk whose taste never changes, of wine that is delicious and causes no intoxication, and of purified honey (47:15). There are gardens with shade, fruits within reach, couches, cups of crystal and silver, and garments of silk.

Yet the deepest descriptions are not material. In Paradise there is no idle talk or sin, only "Peace, peace" (56:25-26). God removes all resentment from hearts, and people sit facing one another as brothers (15:47). There is no fatigue and no grief (35:34-35). Believers are joined with their righteous parents, spouses and children (13:23; 52:21). And the greatest gift: some faces will be radiant, "looking at their Lord" (75:22-23), and for those who did good is the best reward "and more" (10:26), with God's pleasure being greater than all (9:72).

Paradise is eternal, and no one wishes to leave it (18:108). Still, the Qur'an says that what lies there is beyond description: "No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for eyes" (32:17).
It is for those who believe and do good: who restrain anger, pardon people, spend in ease and hardship, and seek forgiveness after a fault (3:133-136).
lessons: Paradise is described to stir longing that drives good deeds.
Its greatest joys are peace of heart, reunion with loved ones, and God's pleasure.
Its door is open to anyone who believes, does good and repents.

subs.t: As wide as the heavens and earth

p.l: A garden as wide as the heavens and earth, prepared for the righteous
Race toward forgiveness and a garden whose width is like the heavens and earth
Rivers of water unaltered, milk, wine delicious to drinkers, and purified honey
Gardens beneath which rivers flow; this is what we were provided before
For him who fears standing before his Lord are two gardens
The foremost, brought near, in gardens of pleasure
They will be given to drink a cup whose mixture is camphor and ginger
The righteous will be in pleasure, given drink of pure wine sealed
In an elevated garden, where they hear no unsuitable speech
Their greeting therein will be: peace
Peace, a word from a merciful Lord
They will not hear therein ill speech, only the saying: peace, peace
Peace be upon you; you have become pure, so enter it to abide eternally
We will remove whatever is in their breasts of resentment, brothers on thrones facing each other
Praise to God who has removed from us all sorrow
We will remove whatever is in their breasts of resentment
Those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith, We will join with them their descendants
Gardens of perpetual residence; they will enter with whoever were righteous among their fathers, spouses and descendants
Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, delighted

subs.t: The vision of God and His pleasure

p.l: Some faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord
For those who have done good is the best reward and extra
The approval from God is greater; that is the great attainment
They will have whatever they wish therein, and with Us is more
No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for eyes
The gardens of Paradise as a lodging, wherein they abide eternally; they will not desire any transfer

themes.title: Hell
themes.hook: The Qur'an's warnings of the Fire: its fuel, its gates, its torment, and the regret of those who refused every warning.
overview: The Qur'an describes Hell (Jahannam, the Fire) so that people will avoid it. Its fuel is people and stones (66:6), and over it are angels stern and severe, nineteen in number (74:30). It has seven gates, each with an assigned portion (15:44). Those who enter are asked by its keepers: "Did no warner come to you?" and they answer: "Yes, a warner came, but we denied" (67:8-9).

The punishments are described vividly: garments of fire, boiling water poured over heads, the tree of Zaqqum as food, drink like molten metal, skins replaced as they are burned so that the pain continues (4:56; 22:19-22; 37:62-67). There is no death in it and no life (20:74; 87:13).

Much of the description is dialogue and regret. The people of the Fire admit: "Had we listened or reasoned, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze" (67:10). Followers and leaders blame one another; Satan disowns them (14:22). The wrongdoer bites his hands and wishes he had taken a path with the Messenger and had not taken so-and-so as a friend (25:27-28). The disbeliever wishes he were dust (78:40).

The people of Paradise call to the people of the Fire, and between them is a barrier; on its heights are people who know each group by their marks (7:44-49). The repeated message is that the Fire is the result of choices made after warning: "We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves" (11:101).
lessons: The warning is given so that it never has to be fulfilled for you.
Listening and reasoning now are what the people of the Fire wished they had done.
Choose your friends with the Hereafter in mind.

p.l: A Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are angels stern and severe
Fear the Fire, whose fuel is people and stones, prepared for the disbelievers
Saqar: it lets nothing remain; over it are nineteen
Hell has seven gates; for every gate is a portion
The disbelievers driven to Hell in groups; did there not come to you messengers?

subs.t: Did no warner come to you?

p.l: Had we only listened or reasoned, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze
Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins
Garments of fire, scalding water poured over their heads
The tree of Zaqqum is food for the sinner, like murky oil boiling in bellies
Is that better or the tree of Zaqqum?
Their food will be only from a bitter thorny plant
If they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like murky oil
He will neither die therein nor live
What put you into Saqar? We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor
He did not believe in God, nor encourage the feeding of the poor
Our Lord, remove us; we will do righteousness, other than what we were doing
Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us; remove us from it
The wrongdoer will bite on his hands: I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger
The disbeliever will say: I wish I were dust

subs.t: Leaders and followers blaming one another

p.l: Those followed disassociate from those who followed them
We obeyed our masters and dignitaries, and they led us astray
Those oppressed will say to the arrogant: if not for you, we would have been believers
The companions of Paradise call to the companions of the Fire; on the elevations are men
A wall with a door between them; its interior has mercy and its exterior torment
We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves

themes.title: Names of the Day of Judgment
themes.hook: The Striking Calamity, the Inevitable Reality, the Overwhelming, the Day of Regret: each name shows a side of that Day.
overview: The Qur'an names the Day of Judgment in many ways, and each name works like a window onto it. Several surahs are named after them.

Yawm ad-Din, the Day of Recompense (1:4), is when every deed is repaid. Al-Qari'ah, the Striking Calamity, strikes hearts with terror (101:1-3). Al-Haqqah, the Inevitable Reality, is the Day that will certainly come and make all truths clear (69:1-3). Al-Ghashiyah, the Overwhelming, covers everyone (88:1). At-Tammah al-Kubra, the Great Overwhelming Event (79:34), and as-Sakhkhah, the Deafening Blast (80:33), describe its force. Al-Waqi'ah, the Occurrence, is the event no one can deny once it falls (56:1-2).

Other names describe what happens on it: the Day of Gathering (64:9), the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain, when people discover who truly lost (64:9); the Day of Meeting (40:15); the Day of Emergence from the graves (50:42); the Day of Sorting (77:13-14; 44:40); the Day of Threat (50:20); the Day of Calling, when people call to one another (40:32); and the Day of Regret (19:39), when the matter is decided while people were heedless.
Studying the names is a way to reflect on the Day from many angles: as justice, as shock, as reunion, as sorting and as regret.
lessons: Each name of the Day calls for a different preparation: justice, fear, hope, sincerity.
The "Day of Mutual Loss" redefines success: who truly gained and who truly lost.

p.l: Sovereign of the Day of Recompense
They will enter it on the Day of Recompense; the Day no soul will have power for another
The Striking Calamity: what is the Striking Calamity?
The Inevitable Reality: what is the Inevitable Reality?
Has there reached you the report of the Overwhelming?
When the greatest Overwhelming Calamity comes
When the Deafening Blast comes
When the Occurrence occurs, there is no denial of its occurrence

subs.t: The Day of Gathering and of Mutual Loss

p.l: The Day He will assemble you for the Day of Assembly; that is the Day of Deprivation

subs.t: The Day of Meeting and of Calling

p.l: To warn of the Day of Meeting; warn them of the Approaching Day
I fear for you the Day of Calling

subs.t: The Day of Emergence and of Threat

p.l: The Horn will be blown; that is the Day of the threat
That is the Day of Emergence
For what Day was it postponed? For the Day of Judgement
The Day of Judgement is the appointed time for them all
This is the Day of Judgement which you used to deny
Warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will be concluded
That is the True Day
The convulsion of the Hour is a terrible thing

themes.title: Glad tidings and warnings
themes.hook: The Prophet came as bearer of good news and warner; the Qur'an pairs hope and fear so neither is lost.
overview: One of the Prophet's titles is "bearer of glad tidings and warner" (bashir wa nadhir), and the Qur'an itself is described the same way: it guides to what is most upright, gives good news to believers who do righteous deeds, and warns those who do not believe in the Hereafter (17:9-10).

The glad tidings are many: gardens beneath which rivers flow (2:25), God's mercy and pleasure (9:21), good news for the patient who say "We belong to God" (2:155-157), for the friends of God who have no fear and no grief (10:62-64), for those who listen and follow the best of it (39:17-18), and from the angels to those who stand firm (41:30).

The warnings are as clear: a painful punishment for those who deny, a Day that turns children grey-haired, and the regret of those who did not heed. Many passages place the two side by side, so the listener never takes one without the other. The Qur'an asks believers to call on God "in fear and hope" (7:56; 32:16), and God describes Himself as Forgiving and Merciful and also severe in punishment (15:49-50).
The balance matters: hope without fear leads to carelessness, and fear without hope leads to despair, which the Qur'an forbids (39:53).
lessons: Keep both hope and fear alive; each protects you from the danger of the other.
Good news is for those who act on it; warnings are for those who still have time.

subs.t: The bearer of good news and warner

p.l: We have sent you as a witness, bringer of good tidings and warner
We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner
We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner

subs.t: The Qur'an as good news and warning

p.l: This Qur'an guides to what is most suitable and gives good tidings to the believers
To warn of severe punishment and give good tidings to the believers
We have made it easy in your tongue to give good tidings and warn
Give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds
Give good tidings to the patient
The allies of God: no fear upon them, nor will they grieve; for them are good tidings
For them are good tidings; so give good tidings to My servants who listen
Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy, approval and gardens
Your good tidings today are of gardens
We have warned you of a near punishment
Warn the people of a Day when the punishment will come
How can you fear, if you disbelieve, a Day that will make the children white-haired?
Woe to every sinful liar; give him tidings of a painful punishment
I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and My punishment is the painful punishment
God is severe in penalty and God is Forgiving and Merciful
Invoke Him in fear and aspiration
They supplicate their Lord in fear and aspiration
He fears the Hereafter and hopes for the mercy of his Lord

themes.title: Purification and prayer
themes.hook: Prayer is established at its times, prepared for with purity, and meant to shape the whole life.
overview: Prayer (salah) is mentioned more than any other act of worship, almost always with the verb "establish": to perform it fully and keep it standing in one's life. The believers are those who establish prayer (2:3), and prayer is prescribed at fixed times (4:103), with verses pointing to its times from dawn to the darkness of night (17:78; 11:114; 30:17-18).

Purity comes first. Before prayer, believers wash their faces, hands to the elbows, wipe their heads and wash their feet; after major impurity they bathe; and if water cannot be found, they use clean earth (5:6). "God does not intend to make difficulty for you, but He intends to purify you" (5:6).

The Qur'an describes what prayer should do: it restrains from immorality and wrongdoing (29:45), it is a help alongside patience (2:45), and it protects against the anxiety and stinginess of human nature (70:19-23). Success belongs to those who are humbly focused in their prayers (23:1-2), and woe to those who pray carelessly or for show (107:4-6).

Prayer adapts to circumstances: it may be shortened when travelling, performed in fear while walking or riding (2:239; 4:101-102), and the Friday prayer calls believers to leave trade for God's remembrance (62:9). Night prayer is praised as the practice of the devoted (73:1-6; 32:16). Believers are told to enjoin prayer on their families and be patient in it (20:132).
lessons: Prayer is not a ritual on the side; it is meant to restrain wrongdoing in daily life.
Focus (khushu') is the measure of a successful prayer.
Purity of body prepares purity of heart.
Lead your family in prayer, gently and patiently.

p.l: When you rise to prayer, wash your faces and forearms; if you find no water, seek clean earth
Do not approach prayer while intoxicated or in a state of impurity
God loves those who purify themselves
Your clothing purify
He sent down rain from the sky to purify you
Prayer has been decreed upon the believers at specified times
Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of night, and the Qur'an of dawn
Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and the approach of night
Exalt God when you reach the evening and the morning
Maintain the prayers, and the middle prayer
Prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing
Seek help through patience and prayer
Man was created anxious, except the observers of prayer
Successful are the believers who are during their prayer humbly submissive
Woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show
When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people
No blame upon you for shortening the prayer when you travel
If you fear, pray on foot or riding
When the call is made for prayer on Friday, proceed to the remembrance of God
Turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram
Arise in the night, except a little
Your Lord knows that you stand almost two thirds of the night
From the night, pray with it as additional worship for you
Their sides part from their beds, supplicating their Lord
They used to sleep but little of the night, and in the hours before dawn seek forgiveness
O you who believe, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord
Prostrate and draw near
Their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration
When you call to prayer, they take it in ridicule
There came after them successors who neglected prayer and followed desires
What put you into Saqar? We were not of those who prayed
Enjoin prayer upon your family and be steadfast therein
Ismail used to enjoin on his people prayer and zakah

themes.title: Zakat and charity
themes.hook: Giving purifies wealth and soul: obligatory zakat, voluntary charity, and the rights of the poor in what we own.
overview: Zakat is joined with prayer in dozens of verses: "Establish prayer and give zakat" (2:43). The word means both purification and growth, and the Qur'an uses both senses: "Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them increase" (9:103). The eight categories who may receive zakat are named precisely: the poor, the needy, those who administer it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, freeing captives, those in debt, God's cause, and the stranded traveller (9:60).

Beyond zakat, the Qur'an encourages generous spending of every kind. Charity grows like a grain that produces seven hundred (2:261). God calls charity a "goodly loan" to Him that He multiplies (2:245; 57:11). Give from what you love (3:92) and from the good of what you have earned, not the worthless (2:267). Giving secretly is better, though giving openly is also good (2:271).

The Qur'an also guards charity from being spoiled. Do not cancel it with reminders of your generosity or with hurt (2:264). Do not give to be seen (4:38). Give in moderation, neither tight-fisted nor wasteful (17:29; 25:67).

The poor have a "known right" in the wealth of the righteous (70:24-25). Hoarding gold and silver is condemned (9:34-35), and the Qur'an counts failing to feed the poor among the signs of denying the religion (107:1-3).
lessons: Zakat is worship and a right owed to others, not a favour.
Give from what you love, and give secretly when you can.
Never spoil a gift by reminding or hurting the one who received it.
Feeding the hungry is central to faith.

p.l: Establish prayer and give zakah
Whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with God
If they repent, establish prayer and give zakah, they are your brothers
Zakah is for the poor, the needy, those employed for it, those whose hearts are to be reconciled, captives, debtors, God's cause and the traveller
Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them
The most righteous, who gives his wealth to purify himself
A grain that grows seven ears; those who spend and do not follow with reminders
Who will loan God a goodly loan so He may multiply it many times?
Who will loan God a goodly loan?
If you loan God a goodly loan, He will multiply it
You will not attain righteousness until you spend from what you love
Spend from the good things you have earned, not the defective
If you disclose your charities, that is good; but if you conceal them and give to the poor, it is better
Those who spend their wealth by night and day, secretly and publicly
Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury
Those who spend their wealth to be seen by people
Do not make your hand chained to your neck or extend it completely
Those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy
They ask you what they should spend: the excess
In their wealth was the right of the beggar and the deprived
In whose wealth is a known right for the petitioner and the deprived
Give the relative his right, and the poor and the traveller
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way
Those who withhold what God has given them of His bounty
Woe to every scorner who collects wealth and counts it
They give food, in spite of love for it, to the needy, the orphan and the captive
The steep path: freeing a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan or a needy person
You do not honour the orphan, nor encourage feeding the poor
Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? He drives away the orphan

themes.title: Fasting
themes.hook: Prescribed as it was for those before, so that you may gain taqwa; Ramadan, the month of the Qur'an.
overview: The main passage on fasting is a single section of Surah al-Baqarah (2:183-187), and it explains both the rule and its purpose. "Fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may become God-conscious" (2:183). Fasting is not new to Islam, and its aim is taqwa.

The fast is in the month of Ramadan, "in which the Qur'an was revealed, a guidance for people" (2:185). The sick and travellers may make up missed days later; those who cannot fast at all may feed a poor person for each day. "God intends ease for you and does not intend hardship" (2:185).

In the middle of this legal passage comes a verse about prayer: "When My servants ask you about Me, I am near; I answer the call of the caller" (2:186). Its placement links fasting with closeness to God and supplication.
The nights of Ramadan are permitted for eating, drinking and marital relations until the dawn thread is distinct (2:187). The Night of Decree, better than a thousand months, falls within it (97:1-3).
Fasting also appears as an expiation (for broken oaths, accidental killing, zihar and violations during Hajj) and among the qualities of believing men and women who fast (33:35).
lessons: The goal of fasting is taqwa, not hunger.
Ease is part of the law; exemptions are a mercy to be used, not ignored.
Ramadan is the month of the Qur'an; fast with it.
Fasting draws you near to God; make du'a.

themes.title: Hajj and Umrah
themes.hook: The pilgrimage to the House built by Ibrahim and Ismail: its rites, its limits and its spirit.
overview: The Hajj goes back to Ibrahim. God showed him the site of the House and commanded him to purify it for those who pray, and to "proclaim the pilgrimage among the people: they will come to you on foot and on every lean camel from every distant pass" (22:26-27). The Ka'bah is "the first House established for mankind", blessed and a guidance, containing the station of Ibrahim; whoever enters it is safe (3:96-97).

Pilgrimage is a duty on those able to make the journey (3:97). Its months are known; once a person enters ihram there is to be no sexual relations, no wrongdoing and no quarrelling, and "take provision, but the best provision is taqwa" (2:197). Hunting is forbidden in ihram (5:95). The Qur'an mentions the walk between Safa and Marwa as among God's symbols (2:158), the standing at Arafat and the remembrance at al-Mash'ar al-Haram (2:198), the counted days of remembrance afterwards (2:203), and shaving or shortening the hair (48:27).

The sacrifice is given its meaning directly: "Their meat will not reach God, nor their blood, but what reaches Him is taqwa from you" (22:37). Pilgrims eat from it and feed the poor and those who ask (22:28; 22:36).
The Hajj also has a social side: it is permitted to seek bounty through trade (2:198), and pilgrims are told to leave Arafat with the rest of the people, without claims to privilege (2:199).
lessons: Hajj is a journey back to Ibrahim's tawhid.
Its rules train the soul: no quarrelling, no wrongdoing, patience in crowds.
The sacrifice is about taqwa, not meat and blood.
All pilgrims are equal; leave with the people.

themes.title: Remembrance of God (Dhikr)
themes.hook: "In the remembrance of God do hearts find rest": remembrance as the life of the heart, for all of creation and at all times.
overview: Remembrance (dhikr) is the simplest form of worship and one of the most emphasised. "O you who believe, remember God with much remembrance, and exalt Him morning and evening" (33:41-42). God promises: "Remember Me and I will remember you" (2:152). The prayer itself is established "for My remembrance" (20:14), and "the remembrance of God is greater" (29:45).

Its effect is named: "Those who believe and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of God; unquestionably, by the remembrance of God hearts are assured" (13:28). The believers are those whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned (8:2), and whose skins shiver and then soften at His word (39:23).

All of creation glorifies God: the seven heavens, the earth and whatever is in them, though people do not understand their glorification (17:44). Several surahs open by declaring that everything in the heavens and earth exalts Him (57:1; 59:1; 61:1; 62:1; 64:1).

Remembrance is not only for the mosque. People of understanding remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides (3:191). Believing men are those whom neither trade nor sale distracts from remembrance (24:37). And forgetting has a cost: whoever turns away from God's remembrance will have a straitened life (20:124), and Satan becomes the companion of one who is blind to it (43:36).
lessons: Remembrance is the quickest path to a calm heart.
Remember God in every posture and every activity, not only in prayer.
Forgetting God invites anxiety and bad company.

themes.title: Supplications of the prophets
themes.hook: The prayers prophets made in their hardest moments, preserved word for word so we can pray them too.
overview: The Qur'an preserves many prayers (du'a) in the exact words of prophets and righteous people, and each one belongs to a moment.

Adam, after his slip: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves" (7:23). Nuh, defeated by his people: "I am overpowered, so help" (54:10), and later "My Lord, forgive me and my parents" (71:28). Ibrahim, settling his family in a barren valley, praying for them, for the city and for himself (14:35-41), and with Ismail as they built the Ka'bah: "Our Lord, accept from us" (2:127). Yusuf, facing temptation: "Prison is dearer to me" (12:33), and at the height of his success: "Cause me to die a Muslim and join me with the righteous" (12:101).

Musa's prayers mark every stage of his life: forgiveness after the killing (28:16), rescue from wrongdoers as he fled (28:21), "I am in need of whatever good You send down to me" when alone in Madyan (28:24), and "Expand my chest and ease my task" when sent to Pharaoh (20:25-28). Ayyub in illness: "Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful" (21:83). Yunus in the darkness of the fish: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; I have been among the wrongdoers" (21:87). Zakariya, old and childless, praying quietly (19:3-6). Sulayman, smiling at an ant: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful" (27:19).

The Prophet ﷺ is taught "My Lord, increase me in knowledge" (20:114), and the believers are given the closing prayer of al-Baqarah (2:286). Learning these prayers means learning what to say in every circumstance.
lessons: Each prophet's prayer fits a situation; learn which prayer belongs to which need.
Admitting fault is the opening of forgiveness.
Even at the height of success, ask for a good end.

themes.title: Supplications for people
themes.hook: Qur'anic prayers grouped by who or what they ask for: parents, children, spouses, fellow believers, knowledge, ease and a good end.
overview: This theme regroups the Qur'an's prayers by purpose, so that a person can find the right words for a need.

For parents: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small" (17:24). For children and spouses: "Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes, and make us leaders of the righteous" (25:74). For fellow believers, including those who came before: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put no resentment in our hearts toward those who believe" (59:10). The angels themselves pray for the believers and their families (40:7-9).

For oneself: forgiveness, guidance and steadfastness ("Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us", 3:8), knowledge (20:114), ease in one's task (20:25-28), the good of both worlds ("Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the Fire", 2:201), protection from Satan, and a good death (12:101).

The Qur'an also shows prayers that were not granted: Nuh's for his son, Ibrahim's for his father, and the Prophet's for the hypocrites. They teach that prayer is a request to a wise Lord, not a command. And it teaches how to pray: humbly, privately, in fear and hope (7:55-56), with the promise "Call upon Me; I will respond to you" (40:60).
lessons: Make your parents, children and the whole community part of your daily prayers.
Pray for those who came before you, without resentment.
Ask for both worlds, and for a good end.
Pray humbly and trust God's wisdom in how He answers.

themes.title: Repentance and second chances
themes.hook: The door of return stays open: God loves those who repent, and turns evil deeds into good.
overview: Repentance (tawbah) means turning back to God, and the Qur'an makes it available to everyone, whatever they have done. "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of God's mercy; God forgives all sins" (39:53). Even those guilty of shirk, murder and adultery are told that whoever repents, believes and does good, "God will replace their evil deeds with good" (25:70).

True repentance is described as sincere (66:8): stopping the wrong, regretting it, and resolving not to return, often joined with putting right what was harmed. It should come soon after a wrong done in ignorance; it is not accepted from one who keeps sinning until death arrives and only then says "Now I repent" (4:17-18). Pharaoh's last-minute declaration as he drowned is the Qur'an's clearest example of repentance too late (10:90-91).

The prophets show what repentance looks like: Adam and his wife admitting their wrong (7:23), Musa after killing a man (28:16), Dawud bowing in repentance (38:24), Yunus in the fish (21:87). Communities too: the people of Yunus, who repented in time (10:98), and the three companions who stayed behind from Tabuk, until "the earth, broad as it was, became narrow for them", and God accepted their repentance (9:118).
God does not merely tolerate repentance; He loves those who repent (2:222), and He is called at-Tawwab, the One who constantly accepts repentance.
lessons: No sin is too great for God's forgiveness while life remains.
Repent soon, sincerely, and repair what you can.

themes.title: Faith, taqwa and trust
themes.hook: What faith is, how God-consciousness shapes a life, and how trust in God frees the heart.
overview: The Qur'an defines faith by its contents and its effects. Its contents: belief in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets (2:177; 4:136). Its effects: giving wealth to relatives, orphans, the poor and those who ask, freeing captives, establishing prayer, keeping promises, and patience in hardship. "Righteousness is not that you turn your faces east or west" (2:177): faith is belief that shows in conduct.

It distinguishes submission (islam) from faith (iman) that has entered the heart (49:14), and describes true believers as those who believe without doubt and strive with their wealth and lives (49:15), whose hearts tremble when God is mentioned and whose faith increases when His verses are recited (8:2). Faith can increase (48:4; 9:124).

Taqwa, God-consciousness, is the quality the Qur'an seeks above all: the Book is guidance for the muttaqin (2:2), fasting is so that you gain taqwa (2:183), and the noblest in God's sight is the one with the most taqwa (49:13). It is carried "as much as you are able" (64:16), and its promise is a way out of difficulty and provision from where one does not expect (65:2-3).

Tawakkul, trust in God, completes the picture: "Whoever relies on God, He is sufficient for him" (65:3). Trust follows effort: "Once you have decided, rely on God" (3:159). Sincerity (ikhlas) holds it all together: "My prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God, Lord of the worlds" (6:162).
lessons: Faith is proven in conduct: generosity, prayer, keeping promises, patience.
Taqwa is the real measure of nobility.

themes.title: Psychology, emotions and the self
themes.hook: Grief, fear, anxiety, anger, envy, hope and peace: the Qur'an speaks honestly about the inner life and how to heal it.
overview: The Qur'an does not pretend that believers feel no pain. Yaqub's eyes turned white from grief (12:84); the Prophet ﷺ was so distressed by people's rejection that he was told not to destroy himself with sorrow (18:6), and God knew that his chest was constrained by what they said (15:97). Grief is human. The Qur'an's guidance is where to take it: "I only complain of my suffering and my grief to God" (12:86).

It describes human nature candidly: created anxious, fretful when evil touches him and withholding when good touches him (70:19-21); hasty (17:11; 21:37); ungrateful (100:6); weak (4:28); and inclined to transgress when he sees himself self-sufficient (96:6-7).

And it offers remedies. Remembrance brings rest to hearts (13:28). Prayer and patience give strength (2:45). Hope is never cut off: "Do not despair of relief from God" (12:87), and with hardship comes ease (94:5-6). Anger is restrained and people are pardoned (3:134; 42:37). Envy is guarded against by seeking refuge (113:5) and by not coveting what God has given others (4:32). The believer is taught to hold the world lightly: "so that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you" (57:23).
God's own words of comfort, such as "Your Lord has not taken leave of you, nor is He displeased" (93:3) and "Do not grieve; God is with us" (9:40), are meant to be heard by every anxious heart.
lessons: Grief is not a lack of faith; complain to God, not about Him.
Know your own nature: anxious, hasty, ungrateful; and work on it.
Remembrance, prayer and patience are the Qur'an's remedies for the heart.

themes.title: Sacred times
themes.hook: The Night of Decree, Ramadan, Friday, the sacred months, the days of Hajj, and the hours of the day God swears by.
overview: God gives some times special honour, and the Qur'an asks believers to notice them. The Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), on which the Qur'an was sent down, is "better than a thousand months"; the angels descend in it and it is peace until dawn (97:1-5). It falls in Ramadan, the month of fasting and of the Qur'an (2:185).

Friday has its congregational prayer, for which believers leave their trade and hasten to remembrance (62:9). The year has twelve months, four of them sacred, in which wronging oneself is especially warned against (9:36); fighting in them is a grave matter (2:217). The days of Hajj, the "known days" and "counted days", are times of remembrance (2:197-203; 22:28), and God swears by "ten nights" (89:2), which many scholars understand as the first ten of Dhul-Hijjah.

Each day has its own sacred times: prayers from dawn to night (17:78; 11:114), glorification before sunrise and sunset (50:39), and the hours before dawn when the righteous seek forgiveness (51:18). God swears by time itself, by the dawn, the forenoon, the night and the afternoon (103; 89; 93; 92), as if to say: time is the material of a life, and it is passing.
The calendar is lunar: the new moons are measures of time for people and for the Hajj (2:189), and the moon's phases help people know the number of years (10:5).
lessons: Seek the Night of Decree; one night can outweigh a lifetime.
Honour the sacred months by guarding against wrongdoing.
Every day has sacred moments; especially dawn and the hours before it.
Time itself is a sign; by it, mankind is in loss except those who believe and do good.
