We made the night and day two signs, that you may know the number of years

themes.title: Ethics and character
themes.hook: Justice, truthfulness, patience, humility and forgiveness: the character the Qur'an builds, and the vices it warns against.
overview: The Qur'an praises the Prophet ﷺ with one sentence that sums up its moral aim: "You are of a great moral character" (68:4). Faith in the Qur'an is never only belief; it is meant to become character.

Its central virtues are named again and again. Justice, even against oneself or one's relatives (4:135), and even toward those one dislikes (5:8). Truthfulness: "Be with those who are truthful" (9:119). Keeping promises and returning trusts (17:34; 4:58). Patience, which God loves and rewards without measure (39:10). Humility: the servants of the Most Merciful walk gently on the earth (25:63). Forgiveness and pardon: "Let them pardon and overlook; would you not like God to forgive you?" (24:22). And returning good for evil: "Repel evil with what is better, and your enemy will become like a devoted friend" (41:34).

The vices are named as clearly: arrogance, envy, stinginess, extravagance, lying, mockery, suspicion, spying and backbiting (49:11-12). One verse gathers the whole ethic: "God commands justice, excellence and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression" (16:90).
The measure is moderation. The community is described as a middle nation (2:143), and believers spend neither wastefully nor stingily but in between (25:67).
lessons: Character is the proof of faith; the Prophet's character was his greatest example.
Be just even when it costs you or those you love.
Answer harm with good; it can turn an enemy into a friend.
Watch the "small" sins of the tongue: mockery, suspicion and backbiting.

p.l: You are truly of a great moral character
Had you been rude and harsh in heart, they would have dispersed from you
In the Messenger of God you have an excellent example
God commands justice, good conduct and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality and oppression
Stand firm for justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and relatives
Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just; be just, that is nearer to righteousness
When you speak, be just, even if it concerns a near relative
Fear God and be with those who are truthful
Speak words of appropriate justice
The one who brought the truth and those who believed in it: they are the righteous
Fulfil every commitment; the commitment will be questioned
God commands you to render trusts to whom they are due
Those who are to their trusts and their promises attentive
Seek help through patience and prayer; God is with the patient
Be patient, endure and remain stationed
The patient will be given their reward without account
If you are patient, it is better for the patient
The servants of the Most Merciful walk upon the earth easily
Do not turn your cheek in contempt, nor walk exultantly
You will never tear the earth apart or reach the mountains in height
The home of the Hereafter is for those who do not desire exaltedness on earth

subs.t: Forgiveness and returning good for evil

p.l: Let them pardon and overlook; would you not like God to forgive you?
Whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with God
Repel evil by that which is better, and the enemy will become a devoted friend
Take what is given freely, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant
Do good to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, neighbours, companions and travellers
Speak to people good words
Do good as God has done good to you

subs.t: Vices of the tongue and heart

p.l: Do not ridicule, insult, use offensive names, spy or backbite
Woe to every scorner and mocker
God seals over every heart of an arrogant tyrant
From the evil of an envier when he envies
Whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, those are the successful
Let not those who withhold think it is better for them
Do not spend wastefully; the wasteful are brothers of the devils
Eat and drink, but be not excessive
They only invent falsehood who do not believe in the verses of God
Why do you say what you do not do?
We made you a just community
Those who, when they spend, are neither excessive nor stingy

themes.title: Lists of virtues
themes.hook: The Qur'an's own checklists: the servants of the Most Merciful, the successful believers, the ten qualities, and more.
overview: Several passages in the Qur'an gather virtues into a single list. They work as checklists that a believer can measure themselves against, and they overlap in instructive ways.

The servants of the Most Merciful (25:63-77) walk humbly, answer the ignorant with peace, spend the night in prayer, are moderate in spending, avoid shirk, unjust killing and adultery, do not bear false witness, pass by idle talk with dignity, and pray for their families. The successful believers (23:1-11) are focused in prayer, turn from vain talk, give zakat, guard their chastity, and keep trusts and promises.

Surah al-Isra contains a long series of commands (17:22-39): worship God alone, honour parents, give to relatives and the poor, avoid waste, do not kill children, approach no adultery, do not take life unjustly, protect the orphan's wealth, keep promises, measure fairly, do not follow what you do not know, and do not walk in arrogance. Surah al-An'am gives a similar ten-point list (6:151-153).

Others focus on specific settings: the ten qualities shared by men and women alike (33:35), the steadfast worshippers who are not anxious or stingy (70:22-35), those who hasten to forgiveness (3:133-135), the people of understanding (13:19-24), and those whose affairs are by consultation (42:36-43).
lessons: Pick one list and review yourself against it each week.
The same qualities appear in every list: prayer, honesty, chastity, generosity, humility.
Virtues are given equally to men and women.

subs.t: The servants of the Most Merciful

p.l: They walk humbly, spend the night in prayer, are moderate, and do not testify falsely
Humble in prayer, turning from vain talk, giving zakah, guarding chastity, keeping trusts
Worship God alone, honour parents, do not approach adultery, keep promises, measure justly

subs.t: The ten commands of Surah al-An'am

p.l: Do not associate, be good to parents, do not kill children, approach no immorality

subs.t: Ten qualities of men and women

p.l: Muslim men and women, believing, obedient, truthful, patient, humble, charitable, fasting, chaste, remembering God
Except the observers of prayer, in whose wealth is a known right
Those who spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, pardon people, and seek forgiveness
Those who fulfil God's covenant, join what God commanded to be joined, are patient and repel evil with good
They avoid major sins, forgive when angry, and conduct their affairs by consultation
Belief, giving wealth, freeing slaves, prayer, zakah, keeping promises, patience

subs.t: The believers who sold themselves to God

p.l: The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, who enjoin right and observe God's limits
They used to sleep little at night, sought forgiveness before dawn, and gave the deprived their right
They fulfil vows, fear a Day, and give food to the needy for God's sake
Forceful against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves, bowing and prostrating

themes.title: Communication and speech
themes.hook: Straight words, gentle words, noble words, good words: how the Qur'an teaches us to speak and to listen.
overview: The Qur'an pays close attention to words. It names different kinds of good speech for different situations. Speak "straight words" that are accurate and fair (33:70). Speak "gentle words", even to a tyrant like Pharaoh (20:44). Speak "noble words" to aged parents (17:23). Speak "kind and fitting words" to those in your care (4:5). Speak "words of ease" when you cannot give what is asked (17:28). Speak "good words" to all people (2:83). And speak "penetrating words" that reach the heart of one who needs warning (4:63).

The basic rule: "Tell My servants to say what is best, for Satan sows discord among them" (17:53). Lower your voice (31:19). Argue only in the best way (16:125; 29:46). Turn away from idle talk (23:3), and when the ignorant address you harshly, answer "peace" (25:63).

The Qur'an forbids mockery, insulting nicknames, suspicion, spying and backbiting, comparing backbiting to eating the flesh of one's dead brother (49:11-12). It forbids false testimony (22:30) and spreading rumours without verifying them (49:6; 24:15). Secret conversations are blameworthy unless they are for charity, good or reconciliation (4:114).
Listening is part of speech: when the Qur'an is recited, listen and be silent (7:204), and the guided are those who listen to speech and follow the best of it (39:18). Every word is recorded (50:18).
lessons: Match your words to the situation: gentle, noble, easy, straight.
Say what is best; harsh words open the door to Satan.
Verify before you share, and never backbite.
Listening well is part of speaking well.

p.l: Speak words of appropriate justice
Speak to him with gentle speech
Speak to them a noble word
Speak to them words of appropriate kindness
Speak to them a gentle word
Speak to people good words
Speak to them a far-reaching word
Speak words of appropriate justice
Tell My servants to say that which is best; Satan induces dissension
A good word is like a good tree
To Him ascends good speech
Lower your voice
Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet
Argue with them in a way that is best
Do not argue with the People of the Scripture except in a way that is best
They turn away from ill speech
When they hear ill speech, they turn away from it: peace be upon you
When they pass near ill speech, they pass by with dignity
When the ignorant address them harshly, they say words of peace

subs.t: Verify before you speak or share

p.l: If a disobedient one comes to you with information, investigate
You received it with your tongues and said with your mouths what you had no knowledge of
Those who like that immorality should spread among believers
Do not ridicule or insult; avoid suspicion; do not spy or backbite
Woe to every scorner and mocker
Avoid false statement
Those who do not testify to falsehood
No good in their private conversation except for charity, good, or reconciliation
When you converse privately, do not converse about sin and aggression
When you are greeted, greet in return with one better or equal
When you enter houses, give greetings of peace
When the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and pay attention
Those who listen to speech and follow the best of it
For one who has a heart or who listens while he is present
Not a word does he utter but there is an observer prepared
The hearing, the sight and the heart will be questioned

themes.title: Etiquette, hospitality and gifts
themes.hook: Asking permission, making room, returning greetings, honouring guests and refusing bribes: the manners of daily life.
overview: The Qur'an gives detailed guidance on everyday manners, because how people treat one another in small things shapes a community.

Homes are protected: do not enter houses other than your own until you have asked permission and greeted their people; if told to go back, go back (24:27-28). Within the household, servants and children who have not reached puberty ask permission at three times of privacy: before dawn prayer, at midday rest and after the night prayer (24:58-59). Enter houses by their doors (2:189).

In gatherings, make room for others when asked, and rise when asked to rise (58:11). Return a greeting with a better one or at least the same (4:86). Do not leave a collective matter without permission (24:62).

Hospitality is shown through Ibrahim: when guests arrived, he hurried to his family and brought a roasted fat calf and placed it near them (51:24-27). Yusuf describes himself as "the best of hosts" (12:59). Eating together or separately in the homes of relatives and friends is permitted (24:61).

Gifts have a place, but not bribes. The Queen of Saba' sent Sulayman a gift to test him, and he refused what was meant to buy his silence (27:35-36). Bribing judges to consume others' property is forbidden (2:188). There is also etiquette with the Prophet ﷺ: not raising voices above his, not calling him as people call one another, and not overstaying in his home (49:1-5; 24:63; 33:53).
lessons: Ask permission before entering, and accept a "no" without offence.
Make room for others; it is a small act God promises to repay with room for you.
Honour your guests with what is best, and quickly.
A gift that is meant to buy you is a bribe; refuse it.

p.l: Do not enter houses other than your own until you ascertain welcome and greet their inhabitants
Enter houses from their doors
Let those whom your right hands possess and those not yet of age ask permission at three times
When you are told to make space in assemblies, make space
When they are with him for a matter of common interest, they do not depart until they ask permission
Greet with one better than it or return it equally
When you enter houses, give greetings of peace upon each other
He went to his family and came with a fat calf and placed it near them
He did not delay in bringing a roasted calf
Do you not see that I give full measure and that I am the best of accommodators?
No blame in eating together or separately, in the houses of relatives and friends
I will send them a gift; do you provide me with wealth?
Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly or send it to the rulers
Give the women their bridal gifts graciously
We have given you clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment; the clothing of righteousness is best
Take your adornment at every mosque; who has forbidden the adornment of God?
Do not walk exultantly; be moderate in your pace and lower your voice
Do not walk upon the earth exultantly
Do not put yourselves before God and His Messenger; do not raise your voices
Do not make the calling of the Messenger like the calling of one another
Do not enter the Prophet's houses except when permitted, and when you have eaten, disperse

themes.title: Father and son
themes.hook: Fathers and sons across the Qur'an: Luqman's counsel, Ibrahim and Azar, Nuh's lost son, Yaqub's patience, and the bond's limit on the Day.
overview: The father–son relationship appears in the Qur'an through the stories of prophets and righteous men, and through direct commands. Read together, they show a relationship of guidance and duty running in both directions.

Fathers are shown as teachers of faith. Luqman gives his son a complete curriculum, beginning with tawhid and ending with manners (31:12-19). Ibrahim and Yaqub, at their deaths, urge their sons to remain in submission to God (2:132-133). Yaqub guides Yusuf to keep his dream private, and bears his own grief with beautiful patience. A father's righteousness can even protect his children after his death, as in the treasure kept for two orphans "because their father was righteous" (18:82).

Sons are shown in their response. Ismail answers his father's dream with "O my father, do as you are commanded" (37:102). Yusuf honours his father in reunion. Ibrahim, as a son, calls his idol-worshipping father four times with "O my father", gently and respectfully, before parting with peace. Nuh's son refuses the ark, and a father's plea for him is answered with "he is not of your family" in faith (11:46).

The forms of address carry the tenderness: fathers say "ya bunayya", "O my dear son", and sons say "ya abati", "O my father". Yet the Qur'an also sets the bond's limit: obedience ends at disobedience to God, and on the Day of Judgment no father can help his son, nor son his father (31:33).
lessons: A father's first gift is faith, given with love and in a wise order.
Speak to a parent with respect even in disagreement, as Ibrahim did.
A child's faith is their own; a prophet's son could still refuse.
A righteous father's goodness can reach his children after him.

p.l: The father's authority comes from God-given wisdom, shown first as gratitude
A father gives his son the best he has, and the best is tawhid
Inside the father's speech, God names the son's duty to both parents, the mother's sacrifice first
Obedience to parents stops at disobedience to God; kindness to them never stops
The father plants accountability: no deed is too small or hidden
From belief to action: prayer, calling to good, and the patience it needs
Faith shows in how you face people: no contempt, no arrogance
The last lesson is small habits: measured steps and a lowered voice
Ibrahim challenges his father Azar for taking idols as gods
Four gentle "O my father" appeals; threatened, he parts with "peace be upon you"
He questions his father and people about their statues
Debate with father and people; he prays "forgive my father"
He asks his father and people what they worship
He declares himself free of what his father worships
Why Ibrahim stopped seeking forgiveness for his father
Ibrahim as the model, with his promise to his father as the one exception
The sacrifice dream; "O my father, do as you are commanded"
He asks leadership for his descendants; father and son raise the Ka'bah and pray together
He prays for his offspring in the barren valley, and for his parents
Ibrahim and Yaqub enjoin their sons to die as Muslims
The son refuses the ark and drowns; Nuh pleads; "he is not of your family"
Yusuf tells his dream; Yaqub's protective advice
The brothers plot; false blood on the shirt; Yaqub's beautiful patience
Binyamin requested; Yaqub's oath and advice to enter by different gates
Grief and lost sight; "do not despair of God's mercy"
The shirt restores his sight; his sons ask him to seek forgiveness for them
Reunion; Yusuf: "O my father, this is the fulfilment of my dream"
Yaqub's deathbed question: "What will you worship after me?"
Father and son judge the same case; Sulayman given the understanding
Sulayman inherits Dawud
Sulayman described as God's gift to Dawud
Prays for an heir; Yahya born, described as dutiful to his parents
The same prayer, Madinan account
Short account, linked to his wife
The boy who would have burdened his believing parents; treasure kept because their father was righteous
The families of Ibrahim and Imran, "offspring one of another": faith passed from father to child
Prophets guided along with their fathers, descendants and brothers
Prophets from the descendants of Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Israel
What a son owes his ageing father: not even "uff", and a prayer for him
Two sons contrasted: one thanks God for his parents at forty, the other rebukes them
What a father owes his child from birth: provision for the nursing mother and the baby
A father's fear of poverty is no excuse; God provides for him and his children
Do not kill your children for fear of poverty; We provide for them and for you
A son as his father's test: love for children must not override obedience to God
Among your spouses and children are enemies to you; wealth and children are a trial
The father's prayer: children who are a comfort to the eyes
A believing father's reward: his believing children joined with him in Paradise
The limit of the bond: on the Day no father can help his son, nor son his father
The bond broken by terror: on the Day a man flees his father and his sons

themes.title: Mother and son
themes.hook: Musa's mother and the river, Maryam and the infant who defended her, and the mother's sacrifice named in God's own command.
overview: The mother–son relationship in the Qur'an is defined by sacrifice on one side and duty on the other. God names the mother's burden in His own command to honour parents: she carried the child in weakness upon weakness, bore him with hardship and delivered him with hardship, and carrying and weaning him took thirty months (31:14; 46:15).

Two stories show the bond from the mother's side. Musa's mother was inspired to nurse her baby and, when she feared for him, to place him in the river, with God's promise to return him. Her heart became empty with worry and she nearly revealed him, but God strengthened her heart. He refused every wet nurse until he was returned to her, "that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve" (28:7-13).

Maryam bore Isa alone, in pain beneath a palm tree, wishing she had died before this. She was comforted with water and fresh dates. When her people accused her, she pointed to the infant, who spoke to defend her: "He made me dutiful to my mother, and did not make me a wretched tyrant" (19:22-33).

From the son's side, the duty is constant: kindness, gratitude, and prayer for her. Even a believing son must not obey a mother who presses him to shirk, yet must keep her company with kindness (31:15).
lessons: A mother's sacrifice is named by God Himself; remember it.
Trust in God can ask a mother to let go, and He returns what is entrusted to Him.
A dutiful son defends and honours his mother.

subs.t: The mother's burden, named by God

p.l: His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness
His mother carried him with hardship and gave birth with hardship; thirty months
Nurse him, then cast him into the river; We returned him to his mother
We inspired your mother; We restored you to your mother so she might be content
The pains of childbirth drove her to the palm tree; do not grieve
He made me dutiful to my mother
Remember My favour upon you and upon your mother
We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign
A mother and infant settled in a barren valley by God's house
Do not say to them "uff"; my Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me
We have enjoined upon man goodness to parents; but if they strive to make you associate, do not obey
Accompany them in this world with kindness
Mothers may nurse their children two complete years
If they nurse for you, give them their payment
Every nursing mother will be distracted from what she was nursing

subs.t: The son who rebuked his believing parents

p.l: One who says to his parents: uff to you
The Day a man will flee from his brother and his mother and his father

themes.title: Husband and wife
themes.hook: Created as a pair for tranquillity, with affection and mercy; the Qur'an's marriages show love, trial, faith and failure.
overview: "Among His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them, and He placed between you affection and mercy" (30:21). The Qur'an presents marriage as a sign of God and its purpose as tranquillity (sakinah), sustained by love (mawaddah) and mercy (rahmah). Spouses are "garments" for one another (2:187): covering, protecting, close and comforting.

The rules aim at fairness: wives have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable (2:228); husbands are told to live with their wives in kindness, "for perhaps you dislike a thing and God makes in it much good" (4:19). Disputes are resolved through counsel, arbitration by a representative from each family, and reconciliation, which is "best" (4:35; 4:128).

The Qur'an's marriages are varied. Adam and Hawwa were tempted together and repented together. Ibrahim and Sarah shared the astonishing news of a son in old age. Zakariya's wife was "amended" for him, and the couple hastened to good together (21:90). Musa married after an honest agreement with his father-in-law. Ayyub kept his oath gently. But there are also believing wives of tyrants (Pharaoh's wife), disbelieving wives of prophets (Nuh's and Lut's), a wife who tried to seduce her husband's servant, and a couple united in hostility to God's Messenger (Abu Lahab and his wife).
The Prophet's own household is addressed directly, and believing couples are promised reunion in Paradise (36:56; 43:70).
lessons: Seek tranquillity, affection and mercy in marriage; they are its purpose.
Be "garments" for each other: protect, cover and comfort.
Live with kindness even through dislike; good may be hidden in it.
Faith is individual; it does not pass automatically between spouses.

p.l: Mates that you may find tranquillity in them; affection and mercy between you
Created you from one soul and created from it its mate
He created from it its mate that he might dwell in security with her
They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them
They have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable
Live with them in kindness; perhaps you dislike a thing and God makes in it much good
Lodge them where you dwell; let a man of wealth spend from his wealth
If you fear dissension, appoint an arbitrator from his people and from hers
Settlement is best; if they separate, God will enrich each from His abundance
Adam and his wife: tempted together, repenting together
Ibrahim's wife standing, laughing at the good news
His wife approached with a cry and struck her face
We amended for him his wife; they hastened to good deeds
I wish to wed you to one of my daughters; Musa travelled with his family
Ayyub's oath fulfilled gently
The wives of Nuh and Lut betrayed their husbands
The wife of Pharaoh asked for a house in Paradise
The wife of Pharaoh: a comfort of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him
The wife of al-Aziz and Yusuf
Abu Lahab and his wife, carrier of firewood
O Prophet, say to your wives: if you desire the worldly life
Why do you prohibit what God made lawful to you, seeking the approval of your wives?
The woman who argued about her husband
When Zayd had no longer need of her, We married her to you
Among your wives and children are enemies to you, so beware; but if you pardon, God is Forgiving
Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes
They and their spouses in shade, reclining on couches
Enter Paradise, you and your kinds, delighted
Whoever were righteous among their fathers, spouses and descendants

themes.title: Brothers
themes.hook: Habil and Qabil, Yusuf and his brothers, Musa and Harun, and the brotherhood of faith.
overview: The Qur'an's first story after Adam is about brothers: the two sons of Adam. Both offered a sacrifice; one was accepted. The other threatened to kill him, and the righteous brother answered: "If you stretch your hand to kill me, I will not stretch my hand to kill you; I fear God" (5:28). Envy led to the first murder, and a crow taught the killer how to bury his brother, leaving him full of regret (5:31).

Envy drives the brothers of Yusuf too: their father loved Yusuf and his brother more, so they threw him into a well (12:8-15). Years later, when they stood before him in need, Yusuf revealed himself and forgave them completely: "No blame upon you today" (12:92). The same story shows the bond between Yusuf and his full brother Binyamin, kept close to him in Egypt.

Musa and Harun show brothers as partners: Musa asks God to make his brother his helper and share his task (20:29-32). Even their one quarrel, over the golden calf, ends with Musa praying for both of them (7:151).

Finally, the Qur'an widens the word: "The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers" (49:10). Many prophets are introduced as "their brother" to the people they were sent to, and on the Day of Judgment a man will flee even from his brother (80:34).
lessons: Envy between siblings is dangerous; parents and siblings must both guard against it.
Forgive family fully when you have the upper hand.
A sibling can be your strongest partner in good work.
Every believer is your brother or sister; make peace between them.

p.l: If you stretch your hand to kill me, I will not stretch mine to kill you
Whoever kills a soul, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely
Yusuf and his brother are more beloved to our father than we are
His brothers came and he recognised them
I am your brother, so do not despair over what they used to do
If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before
I am Yusuf and this is my brother; no blame upon you today
After Satan had induced estrangement between me and my brothers
Appoint for me a minister from my family, Harun my brother
We will strengthen your arm through your brother
Take my place among my people
O son of my mother; my Lord, forgive me and my brother
O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard

subs.t: Prophets as brothers to their people

p.l: To 'Ad their brother Hud
To Thamud their brother Salih
To Madyan their brother Shu'ayb
When their brother Nuh said to them: will you not fear God?
The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your brothers
By His favour you became brothers
If they repent and establish prayer, they are your brothers in religion
Forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith
Would one of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when dead?
The Day a man will flee from his brother
He would ransom himself with his children, his wife and his brother

themes.title: Teacher and student
themes.hook: Musa following Khidr, the Prophet taught by Jibril, Adam taught the names: knowledge passed with humility and patience.
overview: The Qur'an presents God as the first teacher: He taught Adam the names (2:31), taught by the pen (96:4), and taught the Qur'an and speech (55:1-4). The Prophet ﷺ was "taught by one intense in strength", Jibril (53:5), and was himself sent as a teacher who recites, purifies and teaches the Book and wisdom (2:151; 62:2).

The most detailed teacher–student story is Musa and Khidr (18:60-82). Musa, a great prophet, sets out with determination to find a servant of God given knowledge from Him. He asks politely: "May I follow you, on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught of right guidance?" The teacher warns him he will not be able to be patient. Three times Musa objects to what he sees, and three times he is reminded. In the end the teacher explains each act and parts from him. The story teaches humility, patience, asking permission, and that a teacher may know what a student cannot see.

Other passages show teaching in families and communities: Luqman counselling his son (31:13), Yaqub teaching his sons at his death (2:132), Yusuf telling his prison companions "this is from what my Lord has taught me" (12:37). A group from every community should go out to gain understanding of religion and return to teach their people (9:122). And the student's prayer is constant: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge" (20:114).
lessons: Even the greatest should seek teachers, with humility.
Patience is the price of learning.
Teach what you know, and attribute it to God.
Communities need people dedicated to learning and teaching.

p.l: He taught Adam the names of all things
Who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know
The Most Merciful taught the Qur'an, created man and taught him eloquence
Taught to him by one intense in strength
A messenger from among you, teaching you what you did not know
Teaching them the Book and wisdom
Reciting His verses, purifying them and teaching them
I will not cease until I reach the junction of the two seas
May I follow you on condition that you teach me? You will never be able to have patience with me
The boat, the boy and the wall; this is parting between me and you
The explanation of what you could not bear with patience
Luqman said to his son while instructing him
Ibrahim instructed his sons, and so did Yaqub
Your Lord will teach you the interpretation of narratives
That is from what my Lord has taught me
We gave understanding of the case to Sulayman, and to each We gave judgement and knowledge
A party from every group should go forth to obtain understanding in religion and warn their people
Ask the people of the message if you do not know
My Lord, increase me in knowledge

themes.title: Friendship
themes.hook: The companion in the cave, the friend you regret, the friends who become enemies, and the friendships that last into Paradise.
overview: The Qur'an treats friendship as a choice with lasting consequences. "Close friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous" (43:67). Friendships built on God continue into the Hereafter; others turn into blame.

One of the most moving scenes is the regret of a man on the Day of Judgment: "Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a friend; he led me away from the remembrance after it had come to me" (25:28-29). In Paradise, another man remembers a companion who mocked belief in the resurrection, looks down, and sees him in the Fire: "By God, you almost ruined me" (37:51-57).

The model of friendship is the Prophet ﷺ and his companion in the cave during the migration: "Do not grieve, God is with us" (9:40). The Prophet is told to keep himself patiently with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face, and not to look past them for the adornments of worldly life (18:28).

The Qur'an's word for a close ally is wali, and it describes believers as allies of one another (9:71). It permits kindness and justice to non-Muslims who do not fight believers or drive them from their homes (60:8). It also shows friendship's heights: God took Ibrahim as an intimate friend, khalil (4:125). And it promises that through good conduct even an enemy can become a devoted friend (41:34).
lessons: Choose friends who remind you of God; it will matter on the Day.
A true friend comforts you with faith in hard times.
Stay with the sincere even if they are poor or unknown.
Kindness and justice are owed to peaceful people of every faith.

p.l: Close friends that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous
I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a friend
On the Day you will deny one another and curse one another
I had a companion who would say: are you among those who believe?
He said to his companion: do not grieve; God is with us
Keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening
Do not send away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening
Whoever obeys God and the Messenger: they will be with the prophets, the truthful and the righteous; excellent are they as companions
The believing men and women are allies of one another
God does not forbid you from being righteous and just toward those who do not fight you
Repel evil with that which is better, and the one with enmity will become a devoted friend
God took Ibrahim as an intimate friend
We have no intercessors and no devoted friend
No friend will ask anything of a friend
He has no devoted friend here this Day
No blame on you to eat from the house of a friend

themes.title: Employer and worker
themes.hook: "The best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy": fair work, fair pay and honest dealing.
overview: The clearest description of a good worker comes from a young woman in Madyan, speaking of Musa: "O my father, hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy" (28:26). Competence and honesty together are the Qur'an's standard for anyone given a job. Yusuf asks for responsibility on the same basis: "Put me over the storehouses of the land; I am a knowing guardian" (12:55).

The employment agreement in that story is clear: eight years of work, with ten as a favour; "whichever term I fulfil, there is no injustice to me" (28:27-28). Agreements should be explicit and fair. Workers deserve payment: nursing mothers who nurse for a father are to be paid (65:6; 2:233), and when Musa and Khidr rebuilt a wall, Musa said "you could have taken a payment for it" (18:77).

The Qur'an condemns cheating in measure: "Woe to those who give less, who demand full measure when they receive and give less when they give" (83:1-3), the sin of Shu'ayb's people. It forbids consuming wealth unjustly (4:29), and treats trusts as sacred (4:58). In the story of Sulayman, the jinn worked for him on buildings, statues and vessels, and their work is presented as a blessing to be met with gratitude (34:13).
The Qur'an also notes that God made people dependent on each other, raising some above others in provision so that they employ one another (43:32), a structure that brings duties to both sides.
lessons: Hire for strength and trustworthiness; be both when you are hired.
Make agreements clear and fair from the start.
Pay what is due; cheating in measure is condemned.
Work is a blessing to be done with gratitude and excellence.

p.l: The best one you can hire is the strong and the trustworthy; eight years or ten
Appoint me over the storehouses of the land; I am a knowing guardian
If they nurse for you, give them their payment
No blame if you pay what you give according to what is acceptable
If you wished, you could have taken for it a payment
Woe to those who give less than due
Give full measure and weight in justice
Give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance
Establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance
Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, but only in lawful business by mutual consent
Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly
Render trusts to whom they are due, and judge with justice
Do not betray God and the Messenger, or betray your trusts
They made for him what he willed; work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude
We have raised some above others in degrees that they may make use of one another for service

subs.t: Writers and witnesses not to be harmed

p.l: Let no scribe or witness be harmed

themes.title: Believers among themselves
themes.hook: Brothers who make peace, cooperate in goodness, consult each other, and are merciful among themselves.
overview: The Qur'an describes the believing community as one body bound by faith. "The believers are but brothers" (49:10). They are "merciful among themselves" (48:29), "allies of one another, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong" (9:71), and like "a solid structure" when they stand together (61:4).

It gives this brotherhood concrete rules. When two groups of believers fight, make peace between them justly (49:9). Do not ridicule one another, use insulting names, assume the worst, spy or backbite (49:11-12). Cooperate in righteousness and piety, not in sin and aggression (5:2). Settle affairs by consultation (42:38). Greet with a better greeting (4:86). Think well of one another when rumours spread (24:12).

The model is the first community of Madinah: the Ansar, who loved those who emigrated to them and preferred them over themselves even when in need (59:9), and the Muhajirun, who left everything for God. The Qur'an reminds them that they were enemies until God united their hearts, and tells them to hold together to God's rope and not divide (3:103). Disputing causes failure and loss of strength (8:46).
Those who came later are taught to pray for those who came before, asking God to leave no resentment in their hearts toward any believer (59:10).
lessons: Make peace between believers; it is a duty, not a favour.
Guard the community from mockery, suspicion and backbiting.
Prefer others where you can, as the Ansar did.
Unity is a gift of God; division brings failure.

p.l: The believers are but brothers, so make peace between your brothers
Allies of one another, enjoining what is right
Merciful among themselves
In a row as though they are a single structure
If two factions among the believers fight, make settlement between them justly
No good in much private talk except one who orders reconciliation between people
Fear God and amend that which is between you
Do not ridicule, insult, suspect, spy or backbite
Why, when you heard it, did the believers not think good of one another?
Those who harm believing men and women for what they have not earned
Cooperate in righteousness and piety, not in sin and aggression
Whose affair is determined by consultation among themselves
They give preference over themselves, even if they are in need
Those who emigrated and those who gave shelter and aided: allies of one another
Hold firmly to the rope of God all together and do not become divided
Do not be like those who became divided and differed
Do not dispute and lose courage and your strength would depart
Those who have divided their religion and become sects: you are not of them
We made you a just community, that you will be witnesses over the people
You are the best nation produced for mankind: you enjoin what is right
When you are greeted with a greeting, greet in return with one better
Do not say to one who gives you peace: you are not a believer

themes.title: Rights of parents, relatives and neighbours
themes.hook: Kindness to parents comes right after worshipping God; then relatives, orphans, the needy and neighbours near and far.
overview: In the Qur'an, duty to parents is placed immediately after the worship of God: "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, good treatment" (17:23). The same pairing appears again and again (2:83; 4:36; 6:151; 31:14). When parents reach old age, the child must not say even "uff" to them, nor repel them, but speak to them nobly, lower the wing of humility out of mercy, and pray: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small" (17:23-24). The mother's hardship in pregnancy and nursing is named specifically (31:14; 46:15).
This kindness has one limit: if parents strive to make their child associate partners with God, he must not obey them, yet he must still accompany them in this world with kindness (29:8; 31:15).

The circle then widens. The verse of rights (4:36) lists, after God and parents: relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbour, the distant neighbour, the companion at one's side, the traveller, and those in one's care. Giving to relatives is part of righteousness (2:177), and relatives have their right (17:26; 30:38). Among relatives, blood kin have a stronger claim (8:75).
The prophets are praised for this duty: Yahya was "dutiful to his parents" (19:14), and Isa "dutiful to my mother" (19:32).
lessons: Honour to parents is second only to worship of God.
In their old age, even a sigh of impatience is too much.
Obedience has a limit; kindness does not.
Your neighbours, near and far, have rights over you.

subs.t: Second only to worship of God

p.l: Do not say to them "uff"; lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy
Worship none but God, and to parents do good
Do not associate anything with Him, and to parents good treatment
Worship God and associate nothing with Him, and to parents do good
His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness
His mother carried him with hardship and delivered him with hardship
If they endeavour to make you associate with Me, do not obey them
But accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness
Dutiful to his parents, and he was not a disobedient tyrant
He made me dutiful to my mother
Enable me to be grateful for Your favour upon me and my parents
One who says to his parents: uff to you
Giving wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans and the needy
Give the relative his right
Give the relative his right, and the needy and the traveller
Whatever you spend of good is for parents and relatives
Those of blood relationship are more entitled to each other
God commands giving to relatives
The near neighbour, the neighbour farther away, the companion at your side

themes.title: Father and daughter
themes.hook: The man of Madyan and his daughters, Lut's "daughters", the buried girl, and daughters as God's gift.
overview: The Qur'an's most complete father–daughter story is set in Madyan. Two young women held back their flock until the shepherds had gone, explaining "our father is a very old man" (28:23). After Musa watered their flock, one of them came to him "walking with shyness" to invite him to their father, who wanted to reward him. She advised her father: "Hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy" (28:26). Her father listened, and proposed that Musa marry one of his daughters (28:27). The story shows daughters who are dutiful, modest, perceptive and trusted, and a father who listens to them.

Against this the Qur'an sets the pre-Islamic attitude it condemned. "When one of them is given news of a female, his face becomes dark and he suppresses grief. He hides from people because of the bad news: should he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the dust? Evil is what they decide" (16:58-59). On the Day of Judgment, the girl buried alive will be asked "for what sin she was killed" (81:8-9), a question that indicts those who killed her.

The Qur'an answers with a reminder that every child is a gift: God gives females to whom He wills and males to whom He wills, or both, and makes barren whom He wills (42:49-50). Daughters inherit by divine command (4:11). Lut's words "these are my daughters" (11:78) are generally understood by scholars as referring to the women of his nation available through lawful marriage.
lessons: A daughter is a gift from God, not a burden.
Listen to your daughters; their counsel can be wise.
The cruelty of past cultures toward girls is condemned in the strongest terms.

subs.t: The man of Madyan and his daughters

p.l: Our father is an old man; one of them came walking with shyness
O my father, hire him; I wish to wed you to one of my two daughters
These are my daughters; they are purer for you
These are my daughters, if you would be doers
When one of them is informed of the birth of a female, his face becomes dark
Has He taken daughters, and chosen sons for you?
When the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed
Lost are those who killed their children in foolishness
He gives to whom He wills females and to whom He wills males
For the male, what is equal to the share of two females; if only daughters
Prohibited to you are your mothers, your daughters
O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers
Maryam, the daughter of Imran

themes.title: Mother and daughter
themes.hook: A small theme: the wife of Imran and Maryam, Musa's mother and her daughter, and the rights of mothers and daughters in law.
overview: The Qur'an has few direct mother–daughter scenes, and the app presents this theme honestly as a small one. Its centre is the wife of Imran. She vowed her unborn child to God's service; when she gave birth to a girl she said, "My Lord, I have delivered a female, and the male is not like the female," named her Maryam, and sought God's protection for her and her descendants from Satan. "Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good manner" (3:35-37). A mother's prayer and dedication shaped one of the greatest women in history.

A second scene is brief but telling. Musa's mother, having placed her son in the river, turned to her daughter: "Follow him." The daughter watched from a distance without being noticed, then offered Pharaoh's household a family to nurse the baby, bringing him back to his mother (28:11-13; 20:40). A mother and daughter worked together, in trust and courage, to carry out God's plan.

The legal passages complete the picture: mothers and daughters are both named among prohibited marriage relations (4:23), daughters and mothers both inherit (4:11), and women's earnings belong to them (4:32).
lessons: A mother's dedication and prayer can shape her daughter's whole life.
Mothers and daughters can be partners in great tasks.
God accepted a daughter's dedication fully; the Qur'an honours girls from birth.

subs.t: The wife of Imran and Maryam

p.l: My Lord, I have pledged what is in my womb; I have delivered a female
Her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and caused her to grow in a good manner
O sister of Harun, your mother was not unchaste
She said to his sister: follow him
When your sister went and said: shall I direct you to someone who will take charge of him?
Prohibited to you are your mothers, your daughters
Shares of daughters and of the mother
For women is a share of what they have earned

subs.t: Mother and daughter in God's sight

p.l: The believing women, the patient women, the charitable women
Whether male or female, you are of one another

themes.title: Brother and sister, and sisters
themes.hook: Musa's watchful sister, Maryam "sister of Harun", the two sisters of Madyan, and sisters in the law.
overview: The Qur'an's clearest brother–sister story is Musa's sister. Sent by her mother to follow the basket carrying her baby brother on the river, she watched from a distance, unseen. When the baby refused every wet nurse in Pharaoh's household, she stepped forward with a plan: "Shall I direct you to a household that will take care of him for you?" (28:11-12). Her quiet courage brought her brother home.

Maryam is addressed by her people as "O sister of Harun" (19:28), which scholars explain as a reference to her lineage of piety or to a righteous brother; either way, the address reminds her of a family name for goodness.
The two daughters of Madyan appear as sisters who work together, shepherding their flock and protecting their dignity until Musa helps them (28:23-26).

The law gives sisters clear rights. They inherit from a brother who dies without children or parents (4:12; 4:176). A man may not marry two sisters at the same time (4:23). Sisters' homes are among those one may eat in without blame (24:61), and brothers and sisters are among those before whom a woman need not cover in the same way (24:31).
lessons: A sister's courage and initiative can protect her family.
Family names carry a legacy of goodness to live up to.
Siblings, brothers and sisters, have rights over one another.

p.l: She watched him from a distance; shall I direct you to a household that will care for him?
Your sister went and said: shall I direct you to someone?
O sister of Harun
Two women keeping back their flocks; one of them said: hire him
If a man or woman leaves neither ascendants nor descendants but has a brother or sister
If a man dies leaving no child but has a sister, she will have half
Prohibited to you are your sisters, and taking two sisters together
Their brothers, their brothers' sons, their sisters' sons
Or the houses of your brothers or the houses of your sisters
No blame upon the Prophet's wives concerning their brothers and their sisters' sons

themes.title: Grandparents, ancestors and descendants
themes.hook: Yaqub as Ibrahim's grandson "in addition", the religion of one's fathers, righteous lineage, and descendants joined in Paradise.
overview: The Qur'an speaks of generations: what is passed down, what should be, and what should not be followed blindly.

Ibrahim and Sarah were given news not only of a son but of a grandson: "We gave her good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Yaqub" (11:71). The grandson is called a gift "in addition" (21:72). Yusuf, in prison, proudly names his ancestors: "I have followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub" (12:38). At Yaqub's death, his sons pledge to worship "your God and the God of your fathers" (2:133). Righteousness travels down families, as prophets are "descendants one of another" (3:34).

A righteous ancestor's goodness can bless later generations: the treasure of two orphans was preserved "because their father was righteous" (18:82), which some scholars understood as a more distant ancestor. And believing descendants will be raised to join their righteous forebears in Paradise (52:21; 13:23; 40:8).

But the Qur'an also warns against blindly following ancestors in error: "We found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following their footsteps" is the excuse of those who reject messengers (43:22-23; 2:170). Lineage is a gift and a responsibility, never a guarantee: Ibrahim asked for leadership for his descendants and was told "My covenant does not include the wrongdoers" (2:124).
lessons: Pass on faith across generations: pray for your grandchildren too.
Honour righteous ancestors by following their way, not just their name.
Never follow forefathers into error.
Your righteousness may protect descendants you will never meet.

p.l: Good tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Yaqub
We gave him Ishaq and Yaqub in addition
From your spouses children and grandchildren
I have followed the religion of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Yaqub
As He completed it upon your fathers before, Ibrahim and Ishaq
Your God and the God of your fathers
Descendants, some of them from others
From their fathers, descendants and brothers
From the descendants of Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim and Israel
And of my descendants? My covenant does not include the wrongdoers
Make from our descendants a Muslim nation
Make me an establisher of prayer, and from my descendants
Make righteous for me my offspring
Their father had been righteous, so your Lord intended that they reach maturity
We will join with them their descendants
Whoever were righteous among their fathers, spouses and descendants
Admit them to gardens with whoever was righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring
Even though their fathers understood nothing?
We found our fathers upon a religion
We found our fathers doing it
Lest you say: it was only that our fathers associated others with God before

themes.title: Uncles, cousins and extended kin
themes.hook: Ismail called a "father" by his nephews, the warning to the closest kin, the Prophet's uncle and enemy, and the rights of relatives.
overview: Extended family appears in the Qur'an in law, in stories and in the Prophet's own life.

When Yaqub asked his sons what they would worship, they answered: "Your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq" (2:133). Ismail was Yaqub's uncle, not his father, yet he is named among "your fathers". Scholars note from this that the Arabic usage can include an uncle as a father, a sign of the honour due to uncles.

The Prophet ﷺ was told to "warn your closest kindred" (26:214), and his early mission began among his extended family. Some supported him; one uncle, Abu Lahab, became an open enemy, and a whole surah addresses him (surah 111). Kinship did not save one who opposed the truth.

The law names extended relatives repeatedly. Paternal and maternal aunts are among those one may not marry (4:23), while cousins may be married (33:50). The houses of uncles and aunts are among those one may eat in freely (24:61). Relatives who attend the division of an inheritance should be given something and spoken to kindly (4:8). Giving to relatives, near and distant, is part of righteousness (4:36; 2:177; 17:26).
lessons: Honour uncles and aunts; they share in the respect due to parents.
Begin your good influence with your own family.
Kinship does not replace faith, but it carries rights.

p.l: The God of your fathers, Ibrahim, Ismail and Ishaq
Warn your closest kindred, and lower your wing to those who follow you
May the hands of Abu Lahab be ruined

subs.t: Aunts and cousins in marriage law

p.l: Prohibited are your father's sisters and your mother's sisters
The daughters of your paternal uncles and aunts, and of your maternal uncles and aunts

subs.t: The homes of uncles and aunts

p.l: The houses of your father's brothers, father's sisters, mother's brothers, mother's sisters
When relatives, orphans and the needy are present at the division, give them from it
Do good to relatives
Give the relative his right
I do not ask of you any payment except love of kinship
Those of blood relationship are more entitled to each other

themes.title: Foster, adoptive and milk relations
themes.hook: Musa raised in Pharaoh's palace, Yusuf in the house of al-Aziz, Maryam with Zakariya; the rules of adoption and of milk kinship.
overview: Some of the Qur'an's greatest figures were raised by people other than their parents. The infant Musa was picked up from the river by Pharaoh's household, and Pharaoh's wife pleaded: "A comfort of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son" (28:9). Yusuf was bought in Egypt by al-Aziz, who told his wife: "Make his residence comfortable; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son" (12:21). Maryam was raised under the guardianship of Zakariya (3:37). These stories honour those who care for children not their own.

The Qur'an then sets rules for adoption. Adopted children are not made one's biological sons: "Call them by the names of their fathers; that is more just in God's sight. If you do not know their fathers, they are your brothers in religion and your allies" (33:4-5). The case of Zayd, adopted by the Prophet ﷺ before this ruling, is addressed directly (33:37; 33:40). The aim is to preserve lineage and inheritance while keeping the care and love of fostering.

Milk kinship is also recognised. Women who nurse a child become like mothers to that child, and their children like siblings, for purposes of marriage: "your mothers who nursed you and your sisters through nursing" are prohibited in marriage (4:23). Hiring a wet nurse is permitted, with fair payment (2:233; 65:6).
lessons: Raising a child who is not your own is honoured in the Qur'an's greatest stories.
Adoption cares for a child without erasing their lineage.
Nursing creates a real bond of kinship.

p.l: A comfort of the eye for me and for you; perhaps we may adopt him as a son

subs.t: Yusuf in the house of al-Aziz

p.l: Make his residence comfortable; perhaps we may adopt him as a son
He put her in the care of Zakariya
They cast their pens as to which of them should be responsible for Maryam
Call them by the names of their fathers; if you do not know their fathers, they are your brothers
So that there not be on the believers any discomfort concerning the wives of their adopted sons
Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men
Your mothers who nursed you and your sisters through nursing
If you wish to have your children nursed by a substitute, there is no blame
If you are in discord, another woman may nurse for him
Give orphans their properties; test them until they reach marriage age

themes.title: In-laws and step-relations
themes.hook: Musa and his father-in-law, the bond of marriage that creates kinship, and the step-relations protected by law.
overview: "It is He who created from water a human being and made for him blood relationship and marriage relationship" (25:54). Marriage creates a second kind of kinship, alongside blood, and the Qur'an gives it real weight.

The best-known in-law relationship is Musa and his father-in-law in Madyan. The older man proposed the marriage himself, set fair terms of work as the bridal gift, and promised: "I do not wish to put you in difficulty; you will find me, if God wills, among the righteous." Musa agreed: "That is between me and you" (28:27-28). It is a picture of honesty and goodwill between families.

The law protects step-relations and in-laws. A man may not marry his father's former wife (4:22), his wife's mother, his stepdaughters raised in his care, or his son's wife (4:23). A woman need not cover in the same way before her husband's father or husband's sons (24:31). These rules treat in-laws and step-family as real family, owed respect.

The Qur'an also forbids guardians from preventing a divorced woman from remarrying her former husband if they agree on fair terms (2:232), a reminder that in-laws should serve a couple's good, not their own pride.
lessons: Marriage makes families; treat in-laws as true kin.
Be honest and fair in dealings between families.
Step-relations carry real protections and respect.

p.l: He made for him blood relationship and marriage relationship
I wish to wed you to one of my two daughters; I do not wish to put you in difficulty

subs.t: Step-relations and in-laws in marriage law

p.l: Do not marry those women whom your fathers married
Your wives' mothers, your stepdaughters under your guardianship, the wives of your sons
Their husbands' fathers, their husbands' sons
Do not prevent them from remarrying their husbands if they agree among themselves

subs.t: The Prophet's in-law relation by adoption

p.l: The wives of their adopted sons

themes.title: Families as a whole
themes.hook: The families of Ibrahim and Imran, Lut and Nuh, Ayyub restored, Yaqub reunited: the household as a unit of faith.
overview: The Qur'an often speaks of a family as a whole: the "people of the house" (ahl al-bayt). God chose the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran over the worlds (3:33). The angels blessed Ibrahim's household: "The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house" (11:73). The Prophet's own household is told: "God intends only to remove from you impurity, O people of the house, and to purify you thoroughly" (33:33).

Families are saved together and tested together. Nuh was saved with his family, except those whom the word had gone against (11:40). Lut was saved with his family, except his wife (11:81). Ayyub's family was restored to him "and the like of them with them" (21:84). Yaqub's scattered family was reunited in Egypt, the parents raised on the throne and the brothers bowing as the dream foretold (12:99-100).

The believer's responsibility for the family is direct: "O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire" (66:6). Enjoin prayer on your family (20:132). The families of Paradise remember how they used to be "fearful among our families" in this world (52:26), and the one given his record in the right hand returns "to his people in happiness" (84:9).

Families can also test faith: "Among your spouses and children are enemies to you" (64:14). And on the Day, each person will stand alone (80:34-36). Yet the righteous will be joined with their families in Paradise (52:21).
lessons: Faith is built at home: protect your family by teaching and example.
A family can be saved together, but each member answers for themselves.
Pray and work for a reunion with your family in Paradise.

p.l: God chose the family of Ibrahim and the family of Imran
The mercy of God and His blessings be upon you, people of the house
God intends to remove from you impurity, O people of the house
Load upon it your family, except those whom the word has preceded
We saved him and his family from the great affliction
Set out with your family, except your wife
We gave him his family and the like thereof with them
We granted him his family and a like number with them
Bring me your family, all together
He took his parents to himself and raised them on the throne
Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire
Enjoin prayer upon your family
He used to enjoin on his family prayer and zakah
Among your wives and children are enemies to you
Let not your wealth and children divert you
We were previously fearful among our people
He will return to his people in happiness
We will join with them their descendants
The Day a man flees from his family

themes.title: Orphans and guardians
themes.hook: The Prophet was an orphan; the Qur'an protects orphans' wealth, dignity and future, and condemns those who drive them away.
overview: The Qur'an speaks about orphans with unusual frequency and force, perhaps because the Prophet ﷺ was one: "Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter? So as for the orphan, do not oppress him" (93:6-9).

Orphans' property is protected in detail. Guardians must give orphans their wealth, not exchange good for bad or mix it with their own to consume it (4:2). They must test orphans' maturity before handing over their property, spend on them fairly, and witness the handover (4:5-6). A wealthy guardian should not take anything; a poor one may take only what is reasonable (4:6). "Those who consume the wealth of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies" (4:10). Do not approach the orphan's property except in the best way until he reaches maturity (6:152; 17:34).

The Qur'an also guards orphans' dignity and future. Their affairs should be improved and handled as brothers (2:220). Those who think of their own children's future should treat orphans as they would want their children treated (4:9). Orphan girls must be treated justly in marriage (4:3; 4:127).

Neglect is treated as a mark of denying religion: "Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense? That is the one who drives away the orphan" (107:1-2). The righteous feed the orphan out of love for God (76:8), and the steep path to righteousness includes feeding an orphan relative on a day of hunger (90:14-15).
lessons: Care for orphans is a test of real faith.
An orphan's money is a sacred trust; guard it as fire.
Treat orphans as you would want your own children treated.

Give to the orphans their properties, and do not substitute the defective for the good

themes.title: Kinship ties (silat ar-rahm)
themes.hook: Fear God, and the wombs: the Qur'an pairs ties of kinship with God's own name, and warns those who cut them.
overview: The opening of Surah an-Nisa pairs two things to be revered: "Fear God, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs" (4:1). The word arham, wombs, means ties of kinship. Scholars note the remarkable placement: respecting family ties is set beside respecting God Himself.

Those who keep kinship are described among the people of understanding: "those who join what God has commanded to be joined, fear their Lord and dread an evil reckoning" (13:21). Those who cut it are described with the corrupt: "those who break God's covenant after its confirmation, sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on earth: for them is the curse" (13:25; 2:27).

The Qur'an even links severing kinship with corruption in power: "Would you perhaps, if you turned away, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship? Those are the ones God has cursed" (47:22-23).

Keeping ties is practical: giving relatives their right (17:26; 30:38), spending on them (2:215), and not swearing to withhold help from them even after they have wronged you. When Abu Bakr swore to stop supporting a relative involved in the slander against Aisha, the verse came: "Let them pardon and overlook; would you not like God to forgive you?" (24:22).
lessons: Family ties are sacred; they are mentioned with God's own name.
Cutting kinship is listed with corruption and breaking God's covenant.
Keep ties even with relatives who have wronged you.

p.l: Fear God, through whom you ask one another, and the wombs

subs.t: Those who join what God commanded

p.l: Those who join what God has ordered to be joined
Those who sever what God has ordered to be joined: for them is the curse
Who break the covenant of God and sever what He ordered to be joined

Give the relative his right
Give the relative his right

God commands giving to relatives

Those of blood relationship are more entitled to each other

themes.title: A family divided by faith
themes.hook: Nuh and his son, Ibrahim and his father, Lut's wife, Pharaoh's wife: when love and faith pull apart.
overview: Some of the Qur'an's most painful stories are about families divided by faith, and they teach how to hold love and conviction together.

Nuh called his son to board the ark and was refused; he pleaded with God, and was told his son was not of his family in faith (11:42-46). Ibrahim, threatened by his father, answered with peace and a promise to pray for him, and later dissociated when it became clear his father was an enemy of God (19:46-48; 9:114). Lut was saved with his family except his wife (11:81). The wives of Nuh and Lut are given as examples of unbelief close to a prophet; the wife of Pharaoh as an example of faith beside a tyrant (66:10-11). The Prophet's own uncle Abu Lahab opposed him (surah 111).

The Qur'an's rule for such families is balanced. Faith comes first: if parents strive to make you associate partners with God, do not obey them (31:15; 29:8), and one's deepest loyalty cannot go to those who oppose God and His Messenger "even if they were their fathers, sons, brothers or kindred" (58:22). Yet kindness remains: "accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness" (31:15), and God does not forbid kindness and justice toward relatives who do not fight against the faith (60:8).
Finally, the Qur'an reminds that on the Day of Judgment relatives and children will not benefit anyone; God will judge between them (60:3).
lessons: Faith is personal; love cannot transfer it.
Disagree with parents gently and pray for them, as Ibrahim did.
Keep kindness toward relatives who do not share your faith.
Loyalty to God comes before every family loyalty.

themes.title: Marriage and divorce
themes.hook: The Qur'an's family law: whom to marry, the bridal gift, mutual rights, resolving discord, and divorce with fairness.
overview: Marriage in the Qur'an is a sign of God and a solemn covenant (4:21), entered for tranquillity, affection and mercy (30:21). Believers are encouraged to marry, including those of modest means: "If they are poor, God will enrich them from His bounty" (24:32).

The law sets clear boundaries: the relatives one may not marry are listed (4:22-24); believers may not marry polytheists (2:221) but men may marry chaste women of the People of the Book (5:5). The bride receives a bridal gift (mahr) as her own, given willingly (4:4), which the husband may not take back (4:20). A man may marry up to four, but only if he can be just; otherwise one (4:3), and the Qur'an adds that full equality of feeling is not possible (4:129).

Husbands and wives have rights over one another "according to what is reasonable" (2:228), and husbands are told to live with their wives in kindness (4:19). When discord arises, the steps are counsel, then arbitration with a representative from each family, aiming at reconciliation (4:34-35; 4:128).

Divorce is permitted but regulated to protect both sides, especially the wife. It is pronounced twice with the option of reconciliation; then the couple must either stay together honourably or part with kindness (2:229). A waiting period follows (2:228; 65:1-4), during which the wife stays in her home and is maintained. Women must not be held back to harm them (2:231), nor prevented from remarrying (2:232). Pre-Islamic practices like zihar and ila' are reformed (58:1-4; 2:226-227). Even in parting, the Qur'an says: "Do not forget graciousness between you" (2:237).
lessons: Marriage is a covenant meant for peace, love and mercy.
Justice is the condition for every right in marriage, including polygamy.
Seek reconciliation through family arbitration before separation.
If you part, part with kindness and do not forget graciousness.

p.l: That you may find tranquillity in them; affection and mercy

themes.title: Sexual ethics
themes.hook: Intimacy within marriage honoured, chastity guarded by men and women alike, and the limits that protect families and honour.
overview: The Qur'an speaks about sexuality openly and with dignity. Within marriage, intimacy is good and permitted: spouses are "garments" for one another (2:187), relations are allowed on the nights of Ramadan, and the Qur'an speaks of spouses as a "tilth" to approach as they wish while remembering God and sending good ahead for themselves (2:223). Relations are avoided during menstruation, and purification follows (2:222).

Outside marriage, the Qur'an's language is preventive. "Do not approach zina; it is an immorality and an evil way" (17:32): not only the act, but what leads to it. Men and women are both told to lower their gaze and guard their private parts (24:30-31). Chastity is among the defining qualities of successful believers, men and women (23:5-7; 33:35). Those who cannot yet marry are told to keep chaste until God enriches them (24:33). Secret lovers are forbidden (4:25; 5:5).

The law protects honour as well as morals. Zina carries a severe penalty, but it requires four witnesses, and anyone who accuses a chaste person without them is themselves punished and their testimony rejected (24:2-5). Those who love to see indecency spread among believers are warned (24:19). Forcing women into prostitution is condemned (24:33).
The stories add depth: Yusuf, who chose prison over sin (12:23-33); Maryam, who guarded her chastity (66:12); and the people of Lut, who made indecency public and ridiculed purity (7:80-82).
lessons: Intimacy in marriage is honoured; it is worship when done rightly.
Guard the gaze and the paths that lead to sin, not only the sin itself.
Never accuse without proof; honour is protected by law.
Chastity is a strength shown by prophets and the righteous, men and women.

themes.title: Inheritance
themes.hook: God Himself divides the shares: men and women both inherit, after bequests and debts are settled.
overview: Before Islam, women and children were often excluded from inheritance. The Qur'an changed this in one sentence: "For men is a share of what parents and relatives leave, and for women is a share of what parents and relatives leave, be it little or much, an obligatory share" (4:7).

The shares themselves are set out by God, not left to custom: "God instructs you concerning your children" (4:11). Verses 4:11-12 and 4:176 specify the portions for children, parents, spouses and siblings: halves, quarters, eighths, thirds, sixths and two-thirds. A son receives twice the share of a daughter; scholars connect this to the man's financial obligations, since the woman's share is hers alone while he must spend on the family. The verses close: "You do not know which of them is nearer to you in benefit. This is an obligation from God" (4:11).

Inheritance is distributed only after any bequest has been honoured and debts paid (4:11-12). Bequests are encouraged for parents and relatives (2:180), with witnesses (5:106). Relatives, orphans and the poor who are present at the division should be given something and spoken to kindly (4:8).

The law is guarded by warnings: these are God's limits; whoever obeys them enters gardens, whoever transgresses them enters a Fire (4:13-14). It is forbidden to inherit women against their will (4:19), and the Qur'an condemns those who "devour inheritance, devouring it altogether" (89:19).
lessons: Women's right to inherit is set by God and cannot be overridden.
Settle debts and honour bequests before dividing an estate.
Be generous to relatives and the needy present at the division.
The shares are God's limits; do not tamper with them.

p.l: For men is a share and for women is a share of what parents and relatives leave

themes.title: Criminal law and justice
themes.hook: Justice as a supreme command: the sanctity of life, retribution with mercy, theft and robbery, testimony, oaths and fair judges.
overview: The Qur'an's legal system rests on one principle stated many times: justice. "God commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice" (4:58). Justice must hold even against oneself or one's family (4:135), and even toward those one hates (5:8). Messengers were sent with the Book and the balance "so that people may maintain justice" (57:25).

Life is sacred: "Whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul or for corruption in the land, it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely" (5:32). For intentional killing, retribution (qisas) is prescribed with equality, "and in retribution there is life for you" (2:179), because it deters. Yet forgiveness is invited: if the victim's family pardons, blood money is paid with kindness, and "this is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy" (2:178). Accidental killing requires blood money and freeing a believing slave or fasting (4:92).

Specific penalties are set for theft (5:38), highway robbery and armed violence (5:33), unlawful sexual relations and false accusation (24:2-5). The Qur'an pairs these with repentance and reform (5:34; 5:39).

Justice depends on evidence and honest process. Write down debts and bring witnesses (2:282). Do not conceal testimony (2:283), and avoid false witness (22:30). Verify news before acting on it (49:6). Do not bribe judges (2:188). And each person bears only their own burden (6:164).
lessons: Justice is owed to everyone, including enemies and against yourself.
One life carries the weight of all humanity.
The law punishes, but it invites pardon, repentance and reform.
Fair process matters: witnesses, verification, no bribery.

themes.title: Economics, money and trade
themes.hook: Wealth as a trust: trade by consent, honest measure, written contracts, no riba, no hoarding, and wealth that circulates.
overview: The Qur'an treats wealth as something entrusted: "Spend from that in which He has made you successors" (57:7). It is a test (8:28) and an adornment of worldly life (18:46), not a measure of worth.

Trade is encouraged: after the Friday prayer, "disperse in the land and seek God's bounty" (62:10), and seeking bounty during Hajj is allowed (2:198). The basic rule is mutual consent: "Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, but only in trade by mutual consent" (4:29). Contracts must be honoured (5:1). The longest verse in the Qur'an is about recording a debt: write it down, have a fair scribe, bring witnesses, and do not be too weary to write it, whether small or large (2:282).

Riba, interest or usury, is forbidden in the strongest terms. "God has permitted trade and forbidden riba" (2:275), and those who persist are told to take notice of war from God and His Messenger (2:279). A debtor in hardship should be given time, and forgiving the debt is better (2:280).

Fair measure is a moral duty and the sin of Shu'ayb's people (83:1-3; 11:84-85). Gambling is forbidden alongside intoxicants (5:90). Hoarding gold and silver without spending in God's way is condemned (9:34), as is extravagance (17:26-27). Wealth must not circulate only among the rich (59:7), which is why zakat and charity are built into the system.
Qarun, who said "I was given it only because of knowledge I have", shows where wealth without gratitude leads (28:76-82).
lessons: Wealth is a trust from God, to be earned and spent rightly.
Trade only with consent and honesty; write down debts.
Riba is forbidden; give debtors time, and forgive if you can.
An economy should let wealth circulate, not concentrate.

subs.t: Wealth as a trust and a test
