themes.title: Work and earning
themes.hook: Seek God's bounty, eat from your own earning, and work with excellence: prophets were shepherds, shipbuilders and smiths.
overview: The Qur'an presents work as part of the life God designed. He made the earth "tame for you, so walk among its slopes and eat of His provision" (67:15), and made the day for seeking livelihood and the night for rest (78:10-11; 28:73). After the Friday prayer, believers are told to disperse in the land and seek God's bounty (62:10). Some will be "travelling in the land seeking God's bounty" alongside those who pray at night and those who strive in His cause (73:20).

Effort counts: "Man will have only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen" (53:39-40). Men and women each have a share of what they have earned (4:32). God tells the family of Dawud: "Work, O family of Dawud, in gratitude" (34:13), making work itself a form of thanks.

The prophets worked. Nuh built the ark with his own hands (11:37-38). Dawud made coats of mail, measured with care (34:10-11). Musa worked as a shepherd for years in Madyan (28:27) and carried a staff to beat down leaves for his sheep (20:18). Yusuf managed a nation's grain stores (12:55). Skill, care and honesty in work are part of their example.

The Qur'an also honours the dignity of not begging: it praises the poor who are so restrained that the ignorant think them self-sufficient, "they do not ask people persistently" (2:273), and directs charity toward them.
lessons: Earning a living is part of a life of faith, not apart from it.
Work with excellence and gratitude, as the prophets did.
Your effort will be seen and counted.
Protect your dignity, and look out for those too proud to ask.

p.l: When the prayer has concluded, disperse in the land and seek from the bounty of God

themes.title: Food, drink and hunting
themes.hook: Eat of what is lawful and good: what is forbidden, what is permitted, the name of God over slaughter, and the stages of the wine prohibition.
overview: The starting point is permission: "O mankind, eat of what is lawful and good on earth" (2:168). Believers are told not to forbid themselves the good things God has made lawful (5:87), and are asked: "Who has forbidden the adornment of God and the good things of provision?" (7:32). The rule is moderation: "Eat and drink, but do not be excessive" (7:31).

The forbidden is short and specific: carrion, blood, pork, and what is dedicated to other than God (2:173; 6:145). Surah al-Ma'idah adds animals killed by strangling, a blow, a fall or goring, those eaten by predators unless slaughtered in time, and what is sacrificed on stone altars (5:3). In necessity, without desire or excess, there is no sin (2:173).

Animals are slaughtered in God's name (6:118-121), and the food of the People of the Book is lawful (5:5). Game from the sea is lawful; hunting land game is forbidden while in ihram (5:96). Trained hunting animals may catch for you, with God's name mentioned (5:4).

Intoxicants were prohibited in stages: first a hint (16:67), then the statement that their sin outweighs their benefit (2:219), then no praying while intoxicated (4:43), and finally full prohibition with gambling: "a defilement from Satan's work, so avoid it" (5:90-91).

The Qur'an also rejects man-made food taboos, such as the pagan Arabs' rules about certain camels (5:103; 6:138-140), and notes that some foods were forbidden to Bani Israel as a consequence of their own wrongdoing (4:160; 6:146).
lessons: The default is permission; prohibitions are few and specific.
Mention God's name over your food and its slaughter.
Necessity lifts a prohibition, without excess.
Do not invent prohibitions that God did not make.

subs.t: Eat of what is lawful and good

p.l: Eat of what is lawful and good on the earth

Do not prohibit the good things God has made lawful to you

Eat of what God has provided, lawful and good, and be grateful

I do not find within what has been revealed to me anything forbidden except

Whoever is forced by necessity, neither desiring it nor transgressing, there is no sin
Except what you are compelled to
Eat of that upon which the name of God has been mentioned
Mention the name of God upon them when lined up for sacrifice

subs.t: The food of the People of the Book

p.l: The food of those given the Scripture is lawful for you
Lawful for you are the grazing livestock, except while in ihram
What your trained hunting animals catch for you, and mention the name of God
Lawful to you is game from the sea; forbidden is game of the land while in ihram

subs.t: The stages of the wine prohibition

p.l: From the fruits of the palm and grapes you take intoxicant and good provision
In them is great sin and some benefit, but their sin is greater than their benefit
Do not approach prayer while intoxicated

God has not appointed bahirah or sa'ibah
These animals and crops are forbidden, they say, by their claim

All food was lawful to the Children of Israel except what Israel made unlawful to himself
For wrongdoing on the part of the Jews, We made unlawful for them good foods
To those who are Jews We prohibited every animal of uncloven hoof
Milk, the fruits of the palm and grapes, and honey
Let man look at his food

themes.title: Human rights
themes.hook: Life, dignity, equality, freedom of belief, property, privacy, honour and justice: the rights the Qur'an guarantees to every person.
overview: The Qur'an's teaching on human rights starts from dignity given by God: "We have honoured the children of Adam" (17:70). It is not earned or granted by any state; it belongs to every human being by creation.

From this flow specific protections. The right to life: killing one person unjustly is like killing all of humanity (5:32). Equality: humanity comes from a single soul (4:1), nations and tribes exist to know one another, and the most honoured is the most righteous (49:13). Freedom of belief: "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and "Whoever wills, let him believe; whoever wills, let him disbelieve" (18:29). Property: no one may consume another's wealth unjustly (2:188; 4:29). Privacy: do not spy (49:12), and do not enter homes without permission (24:27). Honour and reputation: no mockery, insulting nicknames or false accusation (49:11; 24:4). Fair judgment: justice even against oneself, and verification before acting (4:135; 49:6).

The Qur'an names the vulnerable explicitly and gives them rights: the poor have a known right in the wealth of others (70:24-25); women have shares of inheritance and of their own earnings (4:7; 4:32); orphans' property is guarded (4:2); children may not be killed (17:31); the disabled are free from blame (24:61; 48:17); the oppressed must be defended (4:75); refugees and migrants are welcomed (59:9); and even an enemy who asks for protection must be given safe passage (9:6).
Non-Muslims who live in peace are owed kindness and justice (60:8).
lessons: Human dignity comes from God, so no one can take it away.
Freedom of belief is a Qur'anic principle.
The vulnerable have rights, not just claims on charity.
Justice and kindness are owed to peaceful people of every faith.

p.l: We have honoured the children of Adam
We created man in the best of stature

Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly
Do not spy

Let not a people ridicule another people
Those who accuse chaste women
Stand firm in justice, even against yourselves
If a disobedient one brings you information, investigate
In their wealth was the right of the beggar and the deprived
In whose wealth is a known right
For women is a share of what parents and relatives leave
For women is a share of what they have earned
They have rights similar to those upon them

Do not kill your children for fear of poverty
Give to the orphans their properties
As for the orphan, do not oppress him

themes.title: Animal rights and welfare
themes.hook: Animals are communities like us, glorify God, and are provided for by Him; the Qur'an protects them from cruelty and superstition.
overview: The Qur'an gives animals a standing of their own: "There is no creature on earth or bird that flies with its wings except that they are communities like you" (6:38). They glorify God in their own way (24:41), God provides for every one of them (11:6), and they too will be gathered (6:38; 81:5).

Animals in the Qur'an are not only resources. They are signs of God's creativity (88:17), sources of beauty, "when you bring them in at evening and send them out in the morning" (16:6), and companions in stories. The she-camel of Salih was God's sign, and the people were told: "Do not touch her with harm" (11:64); they were destroyed for hamstringing her. Sulayman's army was stopped by an ant's warning, and he smiled and thanked God, while the ant's own words show she knew the soldiers would only crush them "while they do not perceive" (27:18-19).

The law protects animals. Hunting is forbidden while in ihram (5:95). Animals are slaughtered in God's name, not for idols (6:121; 22:34-36), and sacrificial animals are treated as among God's symbols (22:36). Cutting the ears of cattle to mark them for idols is condemned as a command of Satan (4:119), and pagan rules that set some camels free from use in the name of idols are rejected (5:103).
Using animals is permitted with gratitude: for food, clothing, transport and beauty (16:5-8; 36:71-73). The relationship is one of trust, not ownership without limits.
lessons: Animals are communities with their own worship and dignity.
Cruelty to animals can bring God's anger, as Thamud learned.
Use animals with gratitude and God's name, never for idols or superstition.

p.l: No creature on earth or bird that flies except they are communities like you
The birds with wings spread, each knows its prayer and exaltation
There is not a thing except that it exalts God by His praise
Whoever is in the heavens and earth prostrates to God, and the moving creatures
There is no creature on earth but that upon God is its provision
How many a creature carries not its own provision; God provides for it and for you
Then unto their Lord they will be gathered
When the wild beasts are gathered

subs.t: The she-camel: do not touch her with harm

p.l: Leave her to feed upon God's earth and do not touch her with harm
Leave her to eat within God's land and do not touch her with harm
She has a turn of drinking, and you have a turn; do not touch her with harm
Lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they perceive not
Do not kill game while you are in ihram

subs.t: Slaughter in God's name, not for idols

p.l: Do not eat of that upon which the name of God has not been mentioned
Mention the name of God over the sacrificial animals; their meat will not reach God
I will command them so they will slit the ears of cattle
God has not appointed bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham

subs.t: Animals as blessings, used with gratitude

p.l: In them is warmth and benefits; for you in them is beauty
We subjected them to them, so some they ride and some they eat
God made for you the grazing animals that you may ride some and eat some
Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?

themes.title: Slavery and emancipation
themes.hook: The Qur'an inherited a world with slavery and made freeing slaves an act of worship, an expiation and a use of zakat.
overview: Slavery existed throughout the world when the Qur'an was revealed. The Qur'an did not create it; it built many routes out of it and regulated how enslaved people were to be treated.

Freeing a slave is named as "the steep path", the hard but noble road of righteousness (90:11-13). It is among the defining acts of true piety (2:177) and one of the eight uses of zakat (9:60). It is the first expiation listed for accidental killing (4:92), for breaking an oath (5:89) and for zihar (58:3).

Slaves who wished to buy their freedom were to be given a written contract (mukatabah) "if you know there is good in them", and helped with money from God's wealth (24:33). Owners were told to marry off righteous slaves (24:32), and marriage with believing slave women was permitted with their families' consent and a fair bridal gift (4:25); a believing slave is better than a free polytheist (2:221).

Kindness to "those your right hands possess" is listed among the duties alongside parents, relatives and neighbours (4:36), and forcing slave women into prostitution is condemned (24:33). Prisoners of war were to be freed either as a favour or for ransom (47:4).
The direction of these rulings is consistently toward freedom, which is how many scholars have read the Qur'an's intention.
lessons: Freeing a human being is one of the highest acts of righteousness.
Dignity, kindness and fair treatment are owed to everyone in one's care.
The Qur'an's direction is toward freedom.

p.l: What can make you know the steep path? It is the freeing of a slave
Righteousness is giving wealth for freeing slaves
For freeing captives
Freeing of a believing slave
Or the freeing of a slave
The freeing of a slave before they touch one another
Those who seek a contract for eventual emancipation, make a contract with them and give them from God's wealth
Marry the unmarried and the righteous among your male and female slaves
Marry them with the permission of their people and give them their due compensation
A believing slave woman is better than a polytheist, even if she pleases you

subs.t: Kindness to those in your care

p.l: Do good to those your right hands possess
Do not compel your slave girls to prostitution
Either confer favour afterwards or ransom
A slave who is owned and unable to do a thing, and one We provided good provision
Do you have among those your right hands possess any partners in what We provided?

themes.title: Children and youth
themes.hook: Children as gift, adornment and test; protected from harm, nursed, taught and prayed for; and young people of faith held up as models.
overview: Children appear in the Qur'an as a gift God gives as He wills (42:49-50), the adornment of worldly life (18:46), and a comfort to the eyes prayed for by believers (25:74). They are also a test (8:28; 64:15): love for them must not pull a parent away from God.

The Qur'an protects children firmly. It condemns killing children for fear of poverty, "We provide for them and for you" (17:31), and the buried girl will be asked for what sin she was killed (81:8-9). It guarantees two years of nursing and makes the father responsible for mother and child (2:233). Orphans' wealth is guarded until they mature (4:6), and children's inheritance is set by God (4:11).

Parents are responsible for children's faith: "Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire" (66:6). The model is Luqman's counsel to his son (31:13-19), and Ibrahim and Yaqub urging their children to stay in submission (2:132). Children below puberty ask permission at times of privacy, and after puberty as adults do (24:58-59).

Young people are shown as models of faith: the youths of the Cave, "young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance" (18:13); the young Ibrahim who reasoned against idols (21:60); Ismail, who accepted the sacrifice (37:102); Yahya, given wisdom as a child (19:12); and young Yusuf, faithful through the well and the palace. And the believing children of believers will be joined with their parents in Paradise (52:21).
lessons: Children are a gift and a trust; their faith is the parents' responsibility.
No hardship justifies harming a child.
Young people can be heroes of faith; the Qur'an shows many.
Pray for your children and teach them with love.

subs.t: A gift, an adornment and a test

p.l: He gives to whom He wills females and males
Wealth and children are adornment of the worldly life
Beautified for people is the love of women and sons

Your wealth and children are but a trial
Let not your wealth and children divert you

Do not kill your children out of poverty
When the girl buried alive is asked for what sin she was killed
Their partners made pleasing the killing of their children
That they will not kill their children
Mothers may nurse their children two complete years
Carrying him and weaning him is thirty months
Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire
O my son, do not associate anything with God
O my sons, God has chosen for you this religion
Enjoin prayer upon your family
Those who have not reached puberty ask permission at three times
Test the orphans until they reach marriage age
Grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes
My Lord, grant me a child from among the righteous
And from my descendants
Grant me from Yourself a good offspring
They were youths who believed in their Lord
We heard a young man mention them, called Ibrahim
O my father, do as you are commanded
We gave him judgement while yet a boy
When he reached maturity, We gave him judgement and knowledge
God instructs you concerning your children
We will join with them their descendants

themes.title: Gender and equal reward
themes.hook: Men and women from one soul, equal in reward and accountability, partners in faith, each with rights and duties.
overview: The Qur'an's starting point is shared origin: "O mankind, fear your Lord who created you from one soul, and created from it its mate, and spread from both of them many men and women" (4:1).

It insists on equal reward and accountability. "I will not allow the work of any worker among you to be lost, whether male or female; you are of one another" (3:195). "Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while a believer, We will give them a good life and reward them by the best of what they did" (16:97; also 4:124; 40:40). Surah al-Ahzab lists ten qualities, naming men and women separately each time: Muslim men and women, believing men and women, obedient, truthful, patient, humble, charitable, fasting, chaste and remembering God, and promises both forgiveness and a great reward (33:35).

Believing men and women are allies of one another, enjoining right, forbidding wrong, praying and giving zakat together (9:71). Both are commanded to lower their gaze (24:30-31). Women took a pledge of allegiance directly with the Prophet ﷺ (60:12), and God heard and answered a woman's argument about her husband (58:1).

Within this equality, the Qur'an assigns some different roles and shares in family and inheritance law, and says that women have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable (2:228). Each person's share of what they earn belongs to them (4:32).
lessons: Men and women come from one soul and share the same human dignity.
Reward and accountability before God are exactly equal.
Believing men and women are partners and allies in doing good.

p.l: Created you from one soul and created from it its mate, and dispersed from both many men and women
We created you from male and female
I will not allow the work of any worker to be lost, male or female; you are of one another
Whoever does righteousness, male or female, while a believer, We will give a good life
Whoever does righteous deeds, male or female, while a believer, will enter Paradise
Whoever does righteousness, male or female, will enter Paradise
Muslim men and women, believing men and women
The believing men and women are allies of one another
That He may admit the believing men and women to gardens
The Day you see the believing men and women, their light proceeding before them
Tell the believing men; tell the believing women
God has heard the speech of the one who argues with you about her husband
When the believing women come to you pledging
They have rights similar to those upon them, according to what is reasonable
For men is a share of what they have earned, and for women a share
For women is a share of what parents and relatives leave
God presents an example for those who believed: the wife of Pharaoh, and Maryam

themes.title: Equality and diversity
themes.hook: Nations and tribes to know one another; colours and languages as signs; no superiority except by righteousness.
overview: "O mankind, We created you from a male and a female, and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. The most noble of you in God's sight is the most righteous" (49:13). In one verse the Qur'an affirms common origin, explains diversity as a means of knowing one another, and sets the only measure of rank: righteousness, which only God can judge.

Human diversity is presented as a sign of God, not a problem. "Among His signs is the creation of the heavens and earth and the diversity of your languages and your colours" (30:22). The same variety appears in mountains, fruits, animals and people of different colours (35:27-28).

Even religious diversity is placed within God's will: "Had your Lord willed, He would have made mankind one community" (11:118). "For each We have made a law and a way; had God willed, He would have made you one nation, but He tests you in what He has given you, so race to good" (5:48). There is no compulsion in religion (2:256). God protects places of worship of many communities, "monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques in which God's name is much mentioned" (22:40).

The Qur'an rejects social prejudice too. The poor followers of prophets were not to be driven away to please the elite (6:52; 11:29), and the Prophet ﷺ was corrected for turning from a blind man to attend to a powerful one (80:1-10).
lessons: Differences of race, colour and language are signs of God, meant to bring people together.
No one is better than another except in righteousness, which God alone judges.
Compete in doing good, not in claiming superiority.
Never treat people by status; the poor and disabled are equal before God.

subs.t: Peoples and tribes to know one another

p.l: We made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another
From one soul
The diversity of your languages and your colours
Mountains, people, moving creatures and grazing livestock of various colours
Had your Lord willed, He could have made mankind one community
To each We prescribed a law and a method; so race to all that is good
Mankind was not but one community, but then they differed
Mankind was one community; God sent the prophets
There shall be no compulsion in religion
For you is your religion, and for me my religion
Monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques in which the name of God is much mentioned

subs.t: Honour for all children of Adam

p.l: We have honoured the children of Adam

subs.t: No prejudice against the poor or weak

p.l: Do not send away those who call upon their Lord
We do not see you followed except by the lowest of us
Should we believe you while you are followed by the lowest?
He frowned and turned away because there came to him the blind man
He raised some of you above others in degrees to test you in what He has given you
We have raised some above others in degrees

themes.title: Health and healing
themes.hook: Honey and the Qur'an as healing, Ayyub's cure, dispensations for the sick, and the duty not to destroy oneself.
overview: The Qur'an speaks of healing on two levels. For the body: honey, produced by the bee, "in it is healing for people" (16:69). For the heart: the Qur'an itself is "healing for what is in the breasts" (10:57) and "healing and mercy for the believers" (17:82). Ibrahim sums up the believer's view of illness and cure: "When I am ill, it is He who cures me" (26:80).

Illness is presented as a test met with patience and prayer, as in the story of Ayyub, whose prayer was answered with a spring to bathe in and drink from, and the restoration of his health and family (21:83-84; 38:41-44). The healing miracles of Isa, curing the blind and the leper by God's permission (3:49; 5:110), and the restoration of Yaqub's sight (12:96) show that cure belongs to God.

The law is full of concessions for health. The sick may postpone fasting (2:184-185), may use clean earth instead of water when washing would harm them (4:43; 5:6), and are relieved during Hajj (2:196). The sick, the blind and the lame are free from blame in matters that are beyond them (24:61; 48:17; 9:91). "God intends ease for you" (2:185).

Preserving health is a duty: "Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction" (2:195), "do not kill yourselves" (4:29). Moderation in eating and drinking (7:31) and avoiding intoxicants (5:90) protect the body.
lessons: All healing is from God; seek it through means and through prayer.
The Qur'an heals hearts, as honey and medicine heal bodies.
Use the concessions given to the sick; ease is God's intention.
Protect your health; harming yourself is forbidden.

p.l: From their bellies emerges a drink of varying colours, in which there is healing for people
Healing for what is in the breasts
We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy
For those who believe, it is guidance and cure

subs.t: It is He who cures me

p.l: When I am ill, it is He who cures me
We removed what afflicted him of adversity
Strike the ground with your foot: a cool bath and drink
I cure the blind and the leper, and give life to the dead, by permission of God
You healed the blind and the leper by My permission
He returned having sight
Whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days
If you are ill or on a journey and find no water, seek clean earth
Whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head
He has known that there will be among you those who are ill

subs.t: No blame on the sick and disabled

p.l: There is not upon the blind any constraint, nor upon the lame, nor upon the ill
There is not upon the blind, the lame or the ill any guilt
There is no blame upon the weak, the ill, or those who do not find anything to spend
Do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction
Do not kill yourselves
Eat and drink, but be not excessive
Among you is he who is reversed to the most decrepit old age
God created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then after strength weakness
Among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit old age

themes.title: Clothing and modesty
themes.hook: Clothing as a blessing and a cover, the garment of taqwa, modest dress and conduct for men and women, and garments of the Hereafter.
overview: Clothing first appears in the Qur'an in the story of Adam and Hawwa: when they ate from the tree, their nakedness became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves of the garden (7:22). The Qur'an then tells all of humanity: "O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your nakedness and as adornment; but the garment of righteousness (taqwa), that is best" (7:26). Clothing is both a blessing and a symbol of inner modesty.

Adornment is permitted and encouraged in worship: "Take your adornment at every place of prayer" (7:31), and "Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He produced for His servants?" (7:32). God made garments that protect from heat and from harm in battle (16:81).

Modesty applies to both sexes. Believing men lower their gaze and guard their chastity; believing women do the same, do not display their adornment except what ordinarily appears, draw their head-coverings over their chests, and may appear freely before close family listed in the verse (24:30-31). The Prophet's wives, daughters and the believing women are told to draw their outer garments close, so they will be recognised and not harmed (33:59). Older women past marriage may set aside outer garments without displaying adornment, though modesty is better for them (24:60).

The Qur'an also uses clothing as a symbol: spouses are garments for each other (2:187), and in the Hereafter the righteous wear silk and gold while the wrongdoers are given garments of fire (22:19-23).
lessons: The best clothing is taqwa; outer modesty expresses inner modesty.
Adornment is a blessing to enjoy within limits.
Modesty is required of men and of women.

p.l: Their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves leaves
They began to fasten over themselves the leaves of Paradise
Clothing to conceal your private parts and as adornment; the clothing of righteousness is best
Take your adornment at every mosque; who has forbidden the adornment of God?
You extract from the sea ornaments which you wear
He made for you garments which protect you from the heat and garments which protect you in battle
Tell the believing men to reduce their vision and guard their private parts
Not expose their adornment except what appears, and wrap a portion of their head covers over their chests
Bring down over themselves part of their outer garments, so they will be known and not abused
Women of post-menstrual age: no blame if they remove their outer clothing, but modesty is better
Do not be soft in speech; speak with appropriate speech
One of them came walking with shyness
Your clothing purify
They are clothing for you and you are clothing for them
We made the night as clothing
Their garments therein will be silk
They will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade
Upon them will be green garments of fine silk
Garments of fire will be cut out for them

themes.title: Environment and balance
themes.hook: God set the balance; do not transgress it. Corruption on land and sea comes from human hands; humans are trustees, not owners.
overview: "He raised the heaven and set up the balance, so that you do not transgress the balance; establish weight with justice and do not make the balance deficient" (55:7-9). The Qur'an presents creation as measured and balanced: everything created in measure (54:49; 15:19-21), the earth spread out with mountains, rain, plants in pairs and animals in communities. Human beings are placed on earth as successors (khalifah) and trustees (2:30; 6:165), settled in it and asked to build it (11:61).

With trusteeship comes responsibility. "Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned, so He may let them taste part of what they have done, that perhaps they will return" (30:41). "Do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation" (7:56). The corrupt person who "destroys crops and animals" is condemned (2:205).

Moderation is the practical rule: eat and drink but do not waste (7:31); give what is due at harvest and do not be excessive (6:141); the wasteful are brothers of the devils (17:27). Water is described as the source of all life (21:30), and even when twelve springs gushed for Bani Israel they were told: "Eat and drink from the provision of God, and do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption" (2:60).
The Qur'an's view of nature is reverent: all things glorify God (17:44), and the earth and its creatures are signs to be read, not just resources to be used.
lessons: Humans are trustees of the earth, not its owners.
Waste and excess break the balance God set.
Environmental harm is a form of corruption the Qur'an condemns.
Every creature glorifies God; treat creation with reverence.

p.l: He set up the balance, that you not transgress within the balance
We created everything with a measure
We caused to grow therein everything well-balanced
He created each thing and determined it with precise determination
I will make upon the earth a successive authority
It is He who has made you successors upon the earth
He produced you from the earth and settled you in it
Corruption has appeared throughout the land and sea by what the hands of people have earned
Do not cause corruption upon the earth after its reformation
He strives to cause corruption and destroy crops and animals
Do not cause corruption upon the earth after its reformation
We made from water every living thing
Eat and drink from the provision of God, and do not commit abuse on the earth
Have you seen the water that you drink? If We willed, We could make it bitter
Eat and drink, but be not excessive
Give its due on the day of harvest, and be not excessive
The wasteful are brothers of the devils
There is not a thing except that it exalts God by His praise
Whoever is in the heavens and earth prostrates to God, the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, creatures
The stars and trees prostrate

subs.t: Animals and plants as communities and signs

p.l: Communities like you
We spread the earth and made grow therein every beautiful kind

themes.title: Consultation and authority
themes.hook: Affairs decided by consultation, trusts given to the competent, obedience to authority within God's limits, and judgment with justice.
overview: The Qur'an describes the believing community as people "whose affair is consultation among themselves" (42:38). The Prophet ﷺ himself, though receiving revelation, was commanded: "Consult them in the matter; then, when you have decided, rely on God" (3:159). The verse was revealed after Uhud, where consultation had led to a costly decision, and it still says: consult them. The Queen of Saba' is shown consulting her council before acting (27:32-33).

Authority is a trust. "God commands you to render trusts to those to whom they are due, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice" (4:58). The next verse commands obedience to God, the Messenger, and those in authority, and if there is a dispute, referring it to God and the Messenger (4:59). Obedience to authority is therefore real but bounded: it is within what is right, and the final reference is revelation.

Rulers and judges are held to the same standard as everyone: judge with truth and do not follow desire (38:26), let not hatred of a people prevent justice (5:8), and do not use bribes to influence judges (2:188). News that affects public security should be referred to those with knowledge and authority instead of being spread carelessly (4:83).
Leadership is not inherited by right: when Ibrahim asked for leadership for his descendants, God answered that His covenant does not include the wrongdoers (2:124).
lessons: Consult before deciding; then act with trust in God.
Positions of authority are trusts, given to the competent and just.
Obedience to authority is within what is right, never against God.
Do not spread sensitive news; refer it to those responsible.

p.l: Whose affair is determined by consultation among themselves
Consult them in the matter; when you have decided, rely upon God
The queen: advise me in my affair; I would not decide a matter until you witness
Render trusts to whom they are due, and judge with justice
God has chosen him over you and increased him in knowledge and stature
I am a knowing guardian
Obey God, the Messenger and those in authority; if you disagree, refer it to God and the Messenger
The saying of the believers when called to God and His Messenger to judge: we hear and obey
Nor will they disobey you in what is right
Judge between people in truth and do not follow desire
Let not hatred of a people prevent you from being just
If you judge, judge between them with justice
That you may judge between the people by that which God has shown you
Do not send it to the rulers in order that you might consume a portion of others' wealth
When news comes of security or fear, they spread it; had they referred it to the Messenger and those in authority
My covenant does not include the wrongdoers

themes.title: Leadership models
themes.hook: Yusuf's competence, Sulayman's attentiveness, Dhul-Qarnayn's justice, Talut's tested army, and Pharaoh as the model of tyranny.
overview: The Qur'an teaches leadership through portraits.

Yusuf shows competence joined with trustworthiness. He interpreted the king's dream into an economic plan: seven years of planting with storage, seven of famine, then relief (12:47-49). He asked for responsibility on the basis of ability, "a knowing guardian", and managed a nation through crisis (12:55).

Sulayman shows attentiveness and gratitude. He noticed that one bird, the hoopoe, was missing, and held it to account while listening to its explanation (27:20-22). He used diplomacy with the Queen of Saba' and refused to be bought with gifts. Every display of power led him to say: "This is from the favour of my Lord, to test me" (27:40).

Dhul-Qarnayn shows justice with power. Given authority and means, he declared that wrongdoers would be punished and believers treated with ease (18:87-88). When a people asked him to build a barrier against Gog and Magog for payment, he refused payment, asked for their labour, and built it, then attributed it to God's mercy (18:94-98).

Talut shows that leadership is chosen for knowledge and strength, not wealth (2:247), and that a leader must test and refine his followers, as at the river (2:249). The Queen of Saba' shows a ruler who consulted and then submitted to truth. The Prophet's leadership is described by gentleness: "Had you been harsh, they would have dispersed from around you" (3:159).

Pharaoh is the opposite: he exalted himself, divided people into factions, oppressed the weak, killed their sons, and "made fools of his people, and they obeyed him" (28:4; 43:54). The chiefs (al-mala') who opposed every prophet show how elites protect their status against truth.
lessons: Competence and trustworthiness must come together in a leader.
Good leaders notice the smallest member and listen before judging.
Power is a test of gratitude and justice.
Tyranny works by dividing people and making them think less.

p.l: Plant for seven years; leave in the spikes what you harvest
Appoint me over the storehouses; I am a knowing guardian
Why do I not see the hoopoe? I will punish him, unless he brings a clear authority
What God has given me is better; this is from the favour of my Lord, to test me
We established him upon the earth; whoever does wrong will be punished, whoever believes will have the best reward
What my Lord has established for me is better, but assist me with strength; this is a mercy from my Lord

subs.t: Talut: chosen for knowledge and stature

p.l: God has chosen him over you and increased him in knowledge and stature; the river test

subs.t: The Queen of Saba': consultation and submission

p.l: I would not decide a matter until you witness for me
I submit with Sulayman to God
We have made you a successor; judge between people in truth
By mercy from God you were lenient with them
Concerned over you, kind and merciful to the believers
Lower your wing to those who follow you of the believers
We made them leaders guiding by Our command
We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient
Pharaoh exalted himself and made its people into factions, oppressing a sector
He bluffed his people, and they obeyed him
He proclaimed: I am your most exalted lord
I do not show you except what I see, and I do not guide you except to the way of right conduct
The eminent among his people said: we see you in clear error
We do not see you followed except by the lowest of us

subs.t: Leaders who lead to the Fire

p.l: We made them leaders inviting to the Fire
Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and dignitaries, and they led us astray
My covenant does not include the wrongdoers

themes.title: Hypocrites
themes.hook: Those who say "we believe" with their tongues but not their hearts: their signs, their tactics, and the warning to everyone.
overview: The hypocrites (munafiqun) appeared in Madinah, when it became advantageous to be seen as a Muslim. The Qur'an devotes a surah to them (al-Munafiqun) and long passages in al-Baqarah, an-Nisa', at-Tawbah and al-Ahzab, and describes them more fully than open disbelievers, because they are harder to recognise.

Their signs: they say "we believe" but are not believers; they think they deceive God and the believers but deceive only themselves; "in their hearts is a disease" (2:8-10). They claim to be reformers while causing corruption (2:11-12). They stand for prayer lazily, to be seen by people, and remember God only a little (4:142). They swear oaths to protect themselves (63:2), have impressive appearances and fine speech (63:4), and secretly side with the enemies of the believers. They enjoin wrong and forbid right, the reverse of the believers (9:67).

Their tactics appear in the battles: at Uhud they withdrew, saying "if we knew there would be fighting we would follow you" (3:167); at the Trench they said "God and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion" and asked leave to go home, claiming their houses were exposed (33:12-13); before Tabuk they made excuses not to march (9:81). They built a mosque to cause harm and division (9:107).

Their end is described in the starkest terms: the lowest depth of the Fire (4:145). Yet the door is open: "except those who repent, correct themselves, hold fast to God and make their religion sincere for God" (4:146). The Qur'an's purpose is less to label others than to warn every believer to examine themselves for these traits.
lessons: Examine yourself for hypocrisy: saying what you do not do, praying for show, swearing to cover faults.
Inconsistency between words and deeds is the core of hypocrisy.
Sincerity is the cure, and repentance remains open.

p.l: Among the people are some who say: we believe, but they are not believers; in their hearts is disease
Their example is that of one who kindled a fire, then God took away their light
When the hypocrites come to you, they say: we testify that you are the Messenger of God
When it is said to them: come, the Messenger will ask forgiveness for you, they turn their heads aside
When they stand for prayer, they stand lazily, showing off to people
Those who make show
The hypocrite men and women are of one another; they enjoin what is wrong
The hypocrites are apprehensive lest a surah be revealed; say: mock
Those who remained behind rejoiced in their staying
They said: if we had known there would be fighting, we would have followed you
God and His Messenger did not promise us except delusion; our houses are exposed
Those who took a mosque for causing harm and disbelief and division among the believers
They wish to refer legislation to false judges
When they are called to God and His Messenger to judge, a party of them turns aside
Those in whose hearts is disease look at you with a look of one overcome by death
When he is harmed for God, he considers the trial of the people as the punishment of God
The hypocrite men and women will say: wait for us that we may acquire some of your light
The hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire
Except for those who repent, correct themselves, hold fast to God and are sincere
Others have acknowledged their sins; they mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad

themes.title: Wars and battles
themes.hook: The battles recorded in the Qur'an, from Talut and Jalut to Badr, Uhud, the Trench, Hudaybiyah, Hunayn and Tabuk, and the lessons revelation drew from each.
overview: The Qur'an records wars not as heroic epics but as moral lessons, often correcting the believers' own faults.

From earlier history: Talut's small army, after a test at the river, defeated Jalut's forces when young Dawud killed Jalut, and they prayed "Our Lord, pour upon us patience" (2:249-251). Bani Israel refused to enter the Holy Land out of fear, saying "go, you and your Lord, and fight" (5:24). The Romans were defeated by the Persians, with the prophecy that they would win within a few years (30:2-5). The army of the Elephant came to destroy the Ka'bah and was destroyed by birds (surah 105). Sulayman chose diplomacy with Saba' instead of war (27:29-37).

From the Prophet's time: at Badr, a small and poorly equipped force defeated a larger one with God's help; the Qur'an attributes the victory to God, "you did not kill them, but God killed them" (8:17), and reminds them they were few (3:123). At Uhud, the archers left their post to collect spoils and the victory turned to loss; the Qur'an explains why, forgives them, and teaches that defeat is also a test (3:152-155). At the Trench, the city was besieged by confederate tribes until "eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats", and a wind and unseen forces scattered them (33:9-11). At Hudaybiyah, a treaty that looked like a concession was called "a clear victory" (48:1). At Hunayn, the believers' pride in their numbers nearly brought defeat (9:25). Tabuk tested who would answer the call in the heat and who would make excuses (9:38-49).
lessons: Victory is from God; pride in numbers or strength invites defeat.
Disobedience to leadership at a critical moment can turn victory into loss.
Patience and prayer are the soldier's real weapons.
A peace that looks like a setback can be a clear victory.

p.l: How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of God

subs.t: Bani Israel and the Holy Land

p.l: Go, you and your Lord, and fight; we are remaining right here
The Byzantines have been defeated, but they will overcome
He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay
Kings, when they enter a city, ruin it; I will send them a gift
Fighting in the sacred month is great sin, but averting people from God's way is greater
You did not kill them, but it was God who killed them
The day the two armies met
God had already given you victory at Badr while you were few
Concerning the captives
When two parties among you were about to lose courage
When you disobeyed after He had shown you what you love
When a disaster struck you, although you had struck them with twice of it
They thought their fortresses would protect them from God
When armies came at you; the eyes shifted and hearts reached the throats
The hypocrites at the Trench
When the believers saw the confederates, they said: this is what God and His Messenger promised
We have given you a clear conquest
God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree
God has promised you much booty that you will take
When the victory of God has come and the conquest
Your great number pleased you, but it did not avail you
If you do not go forth, He will punish you
The hour of difficulty, and the three who were left behind

themes.title: Laws of war and peace
themes.hook: Fight only those who fight you, do not transgress, accept peace when offered, protect the asylum-seeker, and treat captives well.
overview: The Qur'an's first permission to fight came after thirteen years of persecution: "Permission is given to those who are fought, because they were wronged" (22:39). The reason given is defence of the oppressed and of places of worship: "Were it not that God checks some people by means of others, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would have been demolished" (22:40).

The core rule: "Fight in God's way those who fight you, but do not transgress; God does not love transgressors" (2:190). Fighting is for defence and to end persecution (2:193), and stops when the aggression stops. Believers are urged to fight to rescue the oppressed men, women and children who cry for help (4:75).

Peace is preferred whenever it is genuinely offered: "If they incline to peace, incline to it as well, and rely on God" (8:61). Those who withdraw and offer peace may not be attacked (4:90). Someone who greets believers with peace must not be dismissed as an enemy for gain (4:94). Even an enemy who asks for protection must be granted it, allowed to hear God's word, and escorted to safety (9:6). Treaties are binding and must be honoured until their term (9:4); treachery is condemned (8:58).

Captives are to be released as a favour or for ransom (47:4), and feeding the captive is a mark of the righteous (76:8). Those unable to fight, the sick, the blind and the weak, carry no blame (9:91; 48:17). Kindness and justice toward non-combatant peoples is explicitly permitted (60:8-9).
lessons: War is permitted for defence and to end oppression, never for transgression.
Accept genuine peace; do not reject an offer of peace for gain.
Honour treaties; treachery is condemned.
Protect captives and asylum-seekers, even from the enemy side.

p.l: Permission is given to those who are fought because they were wronged
Why do you not fight for the oppressed men, women and children?
Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress; if they cease, there is to be no aggression
Whoever has assaulted you, assault him in the same way
If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and rely upon God
If they withdraw from you and offer you peace, God has not made for you a cause against them
Do not say to one who gives you peace: you are not a believer
If any polytheist seeks your protection, grant him protection, then deliver him to his place of safety
Except those with whom you made a treaty and who have not been deficient toward you
As long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them
If you fear treachery from a people, throw their treaty back to them on equal terms
Either confer favour afterwards or ransom
Say to whoever is in your hands of the captives
They give food to the captive
The bounties are for God and the Messenger
Whatever you take as spoils, one fifth is for God and the Messenger
What God restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns
Do not turn your backs to them
When you meet a company, stand firm and remember God much
Prepare against them whatever you are able of power, to terrify the enemy of God
When you are among them and lead them in prayer, let a group stand with you
There is no blame upon the weak, the ill, or those who do not find anything to spend
There is not upon the blind, the lame or the ill any guilt

subs.t: Those who die in God's way

p.l: Never think of those killed in the cause of God as dead; they are alive
Do not say about those killed in the way of God: they are dead
God does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion

themes.title: Relations with other faiths
themes.hook: A common word with the People of the Book, no compulsion in religion, argue only in the best way, and justice and kindness toward the peaceful.
overview: The Qur'an addresses Jews and Christians as "People of the Book", recognising that they received revelation. It invites them to "a word that is equitable between us and you: that we worship none but God and associate nothing with Him" (3:64). It tells believers: "Do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best way, except those who do wrong among them, and say: we believe in what was revealed to us and to you; our God and your God is one" (29:46).

It acknowledges righteousness among them: "They are not all the same; among the People of the Book is an upright community reciting God's verses during the night" (3:113). Some, when they hear what was revealed, weep from recognising the truth (5:83). It states that believers, Jews, Christians and Sabians who believe in God and the Last Day and do good will have their reward (2:62; 5:69), a verse whose scope scholars have discussed at length. Their food is lawful, and marriage to their chaste women is permitted (5:5).

The Qur'an also states clear theological differences: it rejects the Trinity and the divinity of Isa (4:171; 5:116), and calls on all to return to pure monotheism. Yet the principle of freedom of belief stands: "There is no compulsion in religion" (2:256), and "For you is your religion, and for me is mine" (109:6). Believers must not insult what others worship, lest they insult God in return (6:108).
Toward any people who do not fight them or drive them from their homes, believers may show kindness and justice: "God loves those who act justly" (60:8).
lessons: Begin dialogue with common ground: the worship of the One God.
Argue only in the best way, and never insult what others hold sacred.
Recognise the righteous in every community.
Freedom of belief and justice to the peaceful are Qur'anic principles.

p.l: Come to a word that is equitable between us and you
Our God and your God is one
Argue with them in a way that is best
Do not insult those they invoke other than God
They are not all the same: an upright community reciting the verses of God
Among the People of the Book are those who believe in God and what was revealed to you
Their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they recognised of the truth
Those who believed, the Jews, the Christians and the Sabeans: whoever believed in God and the Last Day
Those who believed, the Jews, the Sabeans and the Christians
The food of those given the Scripture is lawful for you, and chaste women from among them
Do not say three; desist, it is better for you
Did you say to the people: take me and my mother as deities besides God?
They have taken their scholars and monks as lords besides God
There shall be no compulsion in religion
For you is your religion, and for me is my religion
Would you compel the people until they become believers?
To each of you We prescribed a law and a method
God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection
For us are our deeds and for you your deeds; there is no argument between us and you
Monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques

subs.t: Justice and kindness to the peaceful

p.l: God does not forbid you from being righteous and just toward those who do not fight you

themes.title: Migration and travel
themes.hook: Hijrah for the sake of faith, the welcome of the Ansar, travel to reflect on history, and the journeys of the prophets.
overview: Migration is part of the story of faith. Ibrahim said "I will emigrate to my Lord" (29:26); Musa fled Egypt for Madyan (28:20-22); and the Prophet ﷺ and his companions left Makkah for Madinah, the Hijrah that begins the Islamic calendar. The Qur'an records the moment in the cave, when the Prophet told his companion "Do not grieve; God is with us" (9:40).

It teaches that one who is oppressed for their faith should not stay where they cannot practise it if they are able to leave: "Was not God's earth spacious enough for you to emigrate in it?" (4:97). And it promises: "Whoever emigrates for the cause of God will find on earth many places of refuge and abundance" (4:100). Even one who dies on the way has his reward with God.

The Qur'an honours both the migrants (muhajirun), who were driven from their homes and property seeking God's bounty and pleasure, and the hosts (ansar), who "love those who emigrated to them, find no envy in their hearts, and prefer them over themselves even if they are in need" (59:8-9). It makes them allies of one another (8:72).

Travel is also commanded for learning: "Travel through the land and see how He began creation" (29:20), and "see how was the end of those who denied" (3:137). Travel brings concessions in prayer and fasting (4:101; 2:184), and journeys by land and sea are among God's favours (16:7-8; 17:66; 43:12-13).
lessons: Faith can require leaving home; God's earth is wide.
Welcome those who migrate, as the Ansar did.
Travel with eyes open: history and creation are lessons.

p.l: Ibrahim said: I will emigrate to my Lord
I will go to my Lord; He will guide me
Musa left it, fearful and anticipating; he turned toward Madyan
He said to his companion: do not grieve, God is with us
When the disbelievers plotted against you to evict you

subs.t: The duty to migrate from oppression

p.l: Was not the earth of God spacious enough to emigrate? Whoever emigrates will find many locations
O My servants who have believed, My earth is spacious, so worship only Me
The earth of God is spacious
Those who emigrated for God after they had been wronged, We will settle them in a good place
Those who believed and emigrated and fought in the cause of God: they expect the mercy of God
Those who emigrated or were evicted from their homes
Those who believed, emigrated and strove are greater in rank
They love those who emigrated to them and give them preference over themselves
Those who believed and emigrated, and those who gave shelter and aided
Travel through the land and observe how He began creation
Travel through the land and observe how was the end of those who denied
Have they not travelled through the earth and have hearts by which to reason?
Have they not travelled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them?
Their journey of winter and summer
We placed between them and the cities visible cities and determined between them the journey
They carry your loads to a land you could not reach except with difficulty
He made for you of ships and animals those you ride
Your Lord drives the ship for you through the sea
When you travel throughout the land, there is no blame in shortening the prayer
Whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days

themes.title: Covenants
themes.hook: The covenant of all souls before birth, the covenant of the prophets, of Bani Israel, and the command to fulfil every contract.
overview: The Qur'an speaks of covenants at every level. The first is primordial: God brought forth the descendants of Adam and made them testify, "Am I not your Lord?" and they said, "Yes, we testify" (7:172). This covenant explains why every human being has a natural sense of God.

God took a covenant from the prophets: to believe in and support any messenger who came after them confirming their message (3:81), and named five of them: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ (33:7). He took a covenant from Bani Israel to worship Him alone, be good to parents, relatives, orphans and the needy, speak kindly, pray and give charity (2:83), and from the Christians as well (5:14). Their breaking of it is recorded as a warning (5:13).

For believers, covenants are binding: "O you who believe, fulfil all contracts" (5:1). "Fulfil every commitment; the commitment will be questioned" (17:34). Breaking oaths after confirming them is compared to a woman who untwists her yarn after spinning it strongly (16:92). Those who keep God's covenant are among the people of understanding (13:20); those who break it are among the losers (2:27).

The early believers made covenants with the Prophet ﷺ, such as the pledge under the tree at Hudaybiyah, about which God said: "The hand of God is over their hands" (48:10). Some believers "were true to what they promised God" (33:23).
lessons: Every soul has already testified that God is its Lord.
A promise made is a covenant before God; it will be asked about.
Breaking promises undoes your own work like unspinning yarn.

p.l: Am I not your Lord? They said: yes, we have testified
When God took the covenant of the prophets
We took from the prophets their covenant, from you, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and Isa
Fulfil My covenant upon you; I will fulfil your covenant
We took your covenant and raised over you the mount
Worship none but God and be good to parents
God took a covenant from the Children of Israel; for their breaking of the covenant
From those who say: we are Christians, We took their covenant
O you who believe, fulfil all contracts
Fulfil every commitment; the commitment is ever questioned
Those who fulfil the covenant of God and do not break the contract
Those who exchange the covenant of God and their oaths for a small price
Do not be like she who untwisted her spun thread after it was strong
Who break the covenant of God after contracting it
Those who break the covenant of God after contracting it
Those with whom you made a treaty but then they break their pledge every time
Fulfil their treaty until their term
So long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them
Those who pledge allegiance to you are pledging to God; the hand of God is over their hands
God was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance under the tree
When the believing women come to you pledging
Among the believers are men true to what they promised God

themes.title: Categories of people
themes.hook: Believers, disbelievers and hypocrites; the foremost, the companions of the right and of the left; the three levels of believers.
overview: The Qur'an often sorts people into groups, not to label individuals but to help each reader see where they stand and where they could be.

The opening of al-Baqarah sets out three groups: the God-conscious who believe in the unseen, pray, give and are certain of the Hereafter (2:2-5); those who disbelieve, whose hearts are sealed (2:6-7); and the hypocrites, who say they believe but do not (2:8-20).

Surah al-Waqi'ah divides people on the Day into three: the foremost (as-sabiqun), brought near to God; the companions of the right, in gardens of thornless lote trees and flowing water; and the companions of the left, in scorching wind and boiling water (56:7-56). The same three appear at death (56:88-94).

Among believers, there are levels: "Among them is he who wrongs himself, among them is he who is moderate, and among them is he who is foremost in good deeds by permission of God" (35:32). Some mix good deeds with bad, and are hoped for (9:102). Among the Bedouin, some said "we believe" when they had only submitted, since faith had not yet entered their hearts (49:14), while others believed and spent sincerely (9:99).

The Qur'an also contrasts pairs: the one who gives and fears God, and the one who withholds and denies (92:5-10); the one who fears standing before his Lord, and the one who transgresses (79:37-41); faces radiant and faces covered in dust (80:38-42).
lessons: Use the Qur'an's categories to examine yourself, not to judge others.
Aim to be among the foremost; the door is open to everyone.
Even those who mixed good and bad deeds have hope with God.

p.l: Those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer and spend
Those who disbelieve: God has set a seal upon their hearts
Among the people are some who say: we believe, but they are not believers

subs.t: The three groups on the Day

p.l: You become three kinds: the companions of the right, of the left, and the forerunners
The forerunners in gardens of pleasure; the companions of the right among lote trees
The companions of the left in scorching fire and scalding water
If he was of those brought near, of the companions of the right, or of the deniers
Among them is he who wrongs himself, he who is moderate, and he who is foremost in good deeds
They mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad; perhaps God will turn to them
Say: we have submitted, for faith has not yet entered your hearts
Among the Bedouins are some who believe in God and the Last Day
The first forerunners among the emigrants and the helpers
As for he who gives and fears God; as for he who withholds and denies
As for he who transgressed; as for he who feared the position of his Lord
Some faces that Day will be bright; other faces will have dust upon them
The record of the wicked and the record of the righteous
Whoever is given his record in his right hand; whoever is given it behind his back
Among the people is he who worships God on an edge
Whoever obeys God and the Messenger will be with the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous
On the elevations are men who recognise all by their marks

themes.title: Pre-Islamic practices addressed
themes.hook: Idols, female infanticide, moving the sacred months, divining arrows, animal taboos, zihar, inheriting widows: what the Qur'an reformed.
overview: The Qur'an was revealed into a specific society, pre-Islamic Arabia, which it calls the time of jahiliyyah, ignorance. Many of its rulings address that society's practices directly, and knowing them helps understand the verses.

Religious practices: the worship of idols such as al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, believed to be daughters of God (53:19-23), and earlier idols of the people of Nuh such as Wadd and Suwa' (71:23); calling the angels daughters of God (16:57); seeking refuge with jinn (72:6); clapping and whistling at the Ka'bah instead of prayer (8:35); and divining arrows to make decisions (5:3; 5:90).

Social practices: burying infant daughters alive (81:8-9; 16:58-59); killing children for fear of poverty (6:151); inheriting widows as property (4:19); marrying one's father's former wives (4:22); zihar, a form of divorce by declaring a wife like one's mother, which left women in limbo (58:2); and tribal boasting about ancestors (2:200).

Ritual and calendar practices: postponing or swapping the sacred months to suit raiding (9:37); pagan animal taboos (5:103; 6:138-139); entering houses from the back during pilgrimage as a supposed sign of piety (2:189); and performing the circuit of the Ka'bah unclothed, which 7:31 answers by commanding adornment for every place of prayer.
The Qur'an's response is not only prohibition but a new standard: the "zeal of ignorance" (48:26) is replaced by tranquillity and taqwa, and the "judgment of ignorance" (5:50) by God's judgment.
lessons: Many rulings make full sense only when you know what they replaced.
Cultural customs are judged by revelation, not the other way round.
Ignorance (jahiliyyah) is a state of mind that can return in any age.

p.l: Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza and Manat? They are not but names you have named
Never leave Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq and Nasr
They attribute to God daughters
Men from mankind sought refuge in men from the jinn
Their prayer at the House was not except whistling and handclapping
That you seek decision through divining arrows
Intoxicants, gambling, stone alters and divining arrows are defilement
When the girl buried alive is asked
Should he keep it in humiliation or bury it in the ground?
Their partners made pleasing to many of the polytheists the killing of their children
Do not kill your children out of poverty
It is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion
Do not marry those whom your fathers married, except what has already occurred
Those who pronounce zihar: they are not their mothers
Remember God like your remembrance of your fathers, or greater
When those who disbelieved had put into their hearts the zeal of the time of ignorance
The postponing of restriction within sacred months is an increase in disbelief
God has not appointed bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah or ham
These animals and crops are forbidden
Righteousness is not entering houses from the back
When they commit an immorality, they say: we found our fathers doing it; take your adornment at every mosque
Then depart from the place from where all the people depart
Is it the judgement of the time of ignorance they desire?
Do not display yourselves as was the display of the former times of ignorance
Thinking of God other than the truth, the thought of ignorance

themes.title: Human creation and purpose
themes.hook: Made from clay and a drop of fluid, shaped stage by stage, honoured with the spirit, and created for worship and stewardship.
overview: The Qur'an tells the story of human creation on two levels. The first human, Adam, was made from clay, "from sounding clay of altered black mud" (15:26), shaped by God and given life through the spirit He breathed into him (15:29). Every human after him is created through a sequence described in detail: a drop of fluid, then a clinging substance, then a lump like chewed flesh, then bones clothed with flesh, then "another creation" (23:12-14; 22:5), in three darknesses within the mother (39:6).

The human being is honoured: created "in the best of stature" (95:4), given dignity above much of creation (17:70), and offered the trust (amanah) that the heavens, the earth and the mountains declined (33:72). Humanity is placed on earth as successors (2:30).

The purpose is stated plainly: "I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me" (51:56), and life and death are created "to test which of you is best in deed" (67:2). "Did you think We created you without purpose?" (23:115).

The Qur'an is also candid about human weakness: created weak (4:28), hasty (17:11), anxious (70:19), ungrateful (100:6), argumentative (18:54), and forgetful, as Adam forgot (20:115). Life moves through stages, from weakness to strength and back to weakness and grey hair (30:54). Yet humans have an innate disposition (fitrah) that recognises God (30:30), and the guidance to rise above their weaknesses.
lessons: Your origin is humble, your dignity is from God.
You were created with a purpose: worship and doing good.
Know your weaknesses honestly; guidance is given to overcome them.
Life's stages are signs; prepare in strength for the weakness to come.

p.l: We created man out of clay from an altered black mud; I breathed into him of My spirit
He created man from clay like pottery
He began the creation of man from clay
He created him from dust
A sperm-drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump, then bones covered with flesh, then another creation
From dust, then a sperm-drop, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, formed and unformed
He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, within three darknesses
We created man from a sperm-drop mixture that We may try him
Created from a fluid ejected, emerging from between the backbone and the ribs
Created man from a clinging substance
We have certainly created man in the best of stature
We have honoured the children of Adam
We offered the Trust to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and man undertook it
I will make upon the earth a successive authority
It is He who has made you successors upon the earth
I did not create jinn and mankind except to worship Me
To test you as to which of you is best in deed
Did you think that We created you uselessly?
Does man think he will be left neglected?
The fitrah of God upon which He has created people
Am I not your Lord? They said: yes
Mankind was created weak
Man is ever hasty
Man has ever been, most of anything, prone to dispute
Man, to his Lord, is ungrateful
He forgot, and We found not in him determination
God created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then after strength weakness and white hair
He brings you out as a child, then you reach maturity, then become elders
Reversed to the most decrepit age, so that he knows nothing after having known

themes.title: Signs in nature
themes.hook: Sky, rain, wind, plants, animals, night and day: the Qur'an repeatedly asks us to look at creation as signs.
overview: The Qur'an uses the same word, ayah (sign), for its verses and for the phenomena of nature. Both are meant to be read. "In the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for those of understanding, who remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation" (3:190-191).

The signs are everyday things looked at with new eyes: rain that revives dead earth; winds that drive clouds and carry seeds; ships sailing on the sea; the alternation of night and day; the variety of colours in fruits, mountains, people and animals; the milk inside cattle; the bee and its honey; birds held aloft in the sky; the camel; the mountains set firm; the earth spread out (2:164; 16:10-18; 16:66-69; 35:27-28; 67:19; 88:17-20). Surah ar-Rum lists human signs too: our creation from dust, spouses and the love between them, our languages and colours, and our sleep (30:20-25).

These signs point beyond themselves: to the Creator's existence, power, wisdom and mercy, and to resurrection, since the God who revives the dead earth can revive the dead (30:19; 41:39). They ask for a response: reflection, gratitude and humility. The Qur'an criticises those who pass by the signs in the heavens and earth and turn away from them (12:105).
And it promises more signs to come: "We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth" (41:53).
lessons: Nature is a book of signs; read it with reflection and gratitude.
Ordinary things, rain, sleep, milk, are among the greatest signs.
The revival of the earth is a picture of resurrection.

p.l: In the creation of the heavens and earth are signs for those of understanding
The ships, the rain, the winds, the clouds: signs for a people who use reason
In the heavens and earth are signs for the believers
Created from dust; spouses; your languages and colours; your sleep
On the earth are signs for the certain, and in yourselves; do you not see?

subs.t: Rain and the revival of the earth

p.l: He sends down rain, from it drink and plants, crops, olives, palms and grapes
He brings the earth to life after its death, and thus will you be brought out
You see the earth stilled; when We send down rain it stirs and grows
He sends the winds as good tidings, and We send down from the sky pure water
God drives clouds, then brings them together, and you see rain emerge
He made the sun a shining light and the moon a derived light
The night: We remove from it the day; the sun runs to its stopping point
How He extends the shadow

subs.t: Plants and fruits of many colours

p.l: God is the cleaver of grain and date seeds; look at its fruit when it yields
Neighbouring plots, gardens of grapevines and palm trees, watered with one water
Fruits of varying colours, and in the mountains tracts white and red
Milk from between excretion and blood; the bee and its drink
Do they not see the birds above them with wings outspread? None holds them but the Most Merciful
Do they not see the birds controlled in the atmosphere of the sky?
The camels, the sky, the mountains, the earth
God created every creature from water: some move on their bellies, some on two legs, some on four
How many a sign within the heavens and earth do they pass over while turning away
We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves

themes.title: Cosmology
themes.hook: Six days of creation, seven heavens, the sun and moon in their orbits, the expanding sky, and the cosmos rolled up at the end.
overview: The Qur'an describes the cosmos to inspire awe and point to its Creator, not as a science textbook. Within that aim it gives a consistent picture.

The heavens and earth were created in six days (7:54), a period whose length the Qur'an leaves undefined, since a day with God can be like a thousand years (22:47). Surah Fussilat describes the earth formed and provisioned in stages, and the heaven, which was smoke, commanded with the earth to come "willingly or unwillingly" (41:9-12). The heavens and earth were once joined and then separated, and every living thing was made from water (21:30).

The sky is built and expanding: "We built the heaven with strength, and We are expanding it" (51:47). It is raised without visible pillars (13:2; 31:10) and is a protected roof (21:32). There are seven heavens in layers (67:3; 71:15), and the nearest is adorned with lamps, the stars (67:5; 37:6).

The sun, moon and stars move precisely: "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outpace the day; each is swimming in an orbit" (36:40). The sun runs to a resting place (36:38); the moon has phases (36:39); night is wrapped over day (39:5).

And the cosmos has an end: the sky will be rolled up like a scroll for books (21:104), the sun wrapped, the stars fallen (81:1-2), and the earth replaced by another earth (14:48). God swears by the positions of the stars, "and that is a great oath if you only knew" (56:75-76).
lessons: The order of the cosmos is a constant reminder of its Creator.
The universe had a beginning and will have an end.
Look up: the sky itself is a sign meant to humble us.

p.l: Your Lord created the heavens and earth in six days, then established Himself above the Throne
He turned to the heaven while it was smoke; come willingly or by compulsion
He directed Himself to the heaven and made them seven heavens
Are you more difficult to create or the heaven? He constructed it
The heavens and earth were a joined entity, and We separated them; We made from water every living thing
The heaven We constructed with strength, and We are its expander

subs.t: Raised without pillars, a protected roof

p.l: God is the one who erected the heavens without pillars that you see
He created the heavens without pillars that you see
We made the sky a protected ceiling
He restrains the sky from falling upon the earth, except by His permission
Seven heavens in layers; We adorned the nearest heaven with lamps
Seven heavens in layers; the moon a light and the sun a burning lamp
We have adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of stars
God created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them
Each, in an orbit, is swimming
The night and the day and the sun and the moon; all in an orbit are swimming
Blessed is He who has placed in the sky great stars and a burning lamp and a luminous moon
The sun and the moon calculated
He wraps the night over the day and wraps the day over the night
Have We not made the earth a resting place and the mountains as stakes?
After that He spread the earth
The Day We fold the heaven like the folding of a written sheet
When the sun is wrapped up and when the stars fall, dispersing
The Day the earth will be replaced by another earth

subs.t: Oaths by the sky and stars

p.l: I swear by the setting of the stars, and that is a great oath
By the sky and the night comer: the piercing star
By the sky which returns

themes.title: Scientific signs (contested approach)
themes.hook: Verses commonly cited as matching modern science, presented with the scholarly debate about reading the Qur'an this way.
overview: Since the late twentieth century, many writers have argued that certain verses anticipate modern scientific findings, an approach called i'jaz 'ilmi, the scientific miracle. This theme collects the verses most often cited so that users can study them, with an honest account of the debate.

The verses most cited include: the heavens and earth once joined then separated (21:30), often compared to the Big Bang; the sky "We are expanding" (51:47); the sun and moon each in an orbit (21:33; 36:40); mountains as pegs (78:7); the barrier between two seas (55:19-20; 25:53); layered darkness and waves in the deep sea (24:40); the water cycle (30:48; 39:21); the embryo's stages (23:12-14) within three darknesses (39:6); everything created in pairs (51:49); iron "sent down" (57:25); pain felt through the skin (4:56); and fingertips restored (75:4).

Scholars are divided. Supporters see these as signs fulfilling the promise "We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves" (41:53). Critics, including many classical-minded scholars, warn that the Qur'an is a book of guidance, not science; that interpretations are often stretched to fit current theories, which may later change; that the classical exegetes read the same verses differently; and that tying faith to scientific claims makes it vulnerable when the science shifts.

A balanced position, which this app follows, is to present the verses and their classical meaning first, note the modern reading as one interpretation, and never claim certainty where there is only resemblance.
lessons: Read the verse's classical meaning first; modern readings are secondary.
The Qur'an invites reflection on nature; that is its lasting scientific value.
Do not build faith on claims that may change with the next theory.

p.l: The heavens and earth were a joined entity, and We separated them
We are its expander
All in an orbit are swimming
The sun runs toward its stopping point; each in an orbit
We made the sky a protected ceiling
By the sky which returns
His breast tight and constricted as though he were climbing into the sky
The mountains as stakes
You see the mountains, thinking them rigid, while they pass as the passing of clouds
After that He spread the earth
He wraps the night over the day
We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits
We made from water every living thing
God sends the winds and they stir the clouds and spread them
He sends down rain and makes it flow as springs
We have sent the fertilising winds
He released the two seas meeting; between them is a barrier
He released the two seas, one fresh and sweet and one salty, with a barrier
Darknesses in a vast deep sea, covered by waves upon which are waves
