The stages of the embryo
Within three darknesses
He creates the two mates, the male and female, from a sperm-drop when emitted
Of all things We created two mates
Exalted is He who created all pairs
From between excretion and blood, pure milk
Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them, so they may taste the punishment
We are able to proportion his fingertips
A lying, sinning forelock
Today We will save you in body, that you may be a sign
The Byzantines have been defeated in the nearest land
We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves

themes.title: Animals
themes.hook: The dog of the Cave, Sulayman's ant and hoopoe, the spider's house, the elephant army, Salih's camel, Yunus's fish, and every creature as a community.
overview: Six surahs are named after animals: al-Baqarah (the Cow), al-An'am (Livestock), an-Nahl (the Bee), an-Naml (the Ant), al-'Ankabut (the Spider) and al-Fil (the Elephant). Animals appear throughout the Qur'an in four roles.

As signs: the camel, "how it was created" (88:17); the bee, inspired to build homes and produce honey of many colours with healing in it (16:68-69); birds held aloft by God alone (67:19); milk from between dung and blood (16:66). All animals are communities like humans and will be gathered (6:38).

In stories: the dog of the People of the Cave, stretching its paws at the entrance (18:18); the ant that warned its colony of Sulayman's army (27:18); the hoopoe that brought news of Saba' (27:20-28); the crow that showed Qabil how to bury his brother (5:31); Ibrahim's four birds (2:260); Salih's she-camel (7:73); the cow of Bani Israel (2:67-73); the wolf blamed for Yusuf (12:13-17); the fish that swallowed Yunus (37:142); the fish of Musa's journey (18:61-63); the serpent of Musa's staff (20:20); the donkey of the man who died for a hundred years (2:259); the elephant army (105); and the plagues of locusts, lice and frogs on Pharaoh (7:133).

In parables: the spider's frail house for false protectors (29:41); the donkey carrying books for those who do not act on knowledge (62:5); the panting dog for one who abandons God's signs (7:176); the fly that idols cannot create (22:73); the gnat (2:26); people scattered like moths and locusts (101:4; 54:7).
As provision: livestock for food, warmth, transport and beauty; horses, mules and donkeys to ride; trained hunting animals (16:5-8; 5:4).
lessons: Every animal is a sign and a community; look at them with wonder.
Even an ant can teach a king; even a hoopoe can carry great news.
Animal parables are mirrors: the donkey, the dog and the spider describe human failings.

p.l: No creature or bird but they are communities like you
God created every creature from water
No creature on earth but upon God is its provision
Their dog stretching its forelegs at the entrance
Three, the fourth of them their dog
His example is like that of the dog: if you chase him he pants
What you have taught your trained hunting animals
O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you
Your Lord inspired the bee: take for yourself among the mountains houses
The weakest of houses is the house of the spider

subs.t: The fly, the gnat, moths and locusts

p.l: They will never create a fly
God is not timid to present an example, a mosquito or what is smaller
The Day when people will be like moths dispersed
They will emerge from the graves as if they were locusts spreading
We sent upon them the flood, locusts, lice, frogs and blood
Nothing indicated his death except a creature of the earth eating his staff
The companions of the elephant
The hoopoe: I have encompassed that which you have not
God sent a crow searching in the ground to show him how to hide the body of his brother
Take four birds and commit them to yourself
I make for you from clay the form of a bird
We have been taught the language of birds
The mountains and the birds exalted with Dawud
Birds in flocks
The birds above them with wings outspread
We sent down to you manna and quails
God commands you to slaughter a cow
He brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound
Eight mates: of the sheep two and of the goats two; of the camels two and of the cattle two
The grazing livestock, horses, mules and donkeys
From what is in their bellies we give you pure milk
The camels and cattle We have appointed for you among the symbols of God
The she-camel of God
The she-camel of God and her drink
Do they not look at the camels, how they are created?
Until a camel enters into the eye of a needle
By the racers, panting
The poised standing horses
Like a donkey carrying volumes of books
The most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys
Look at your donkey
As if they were alarmed donkeys fleeing from a lion
I fear that a wolf would eat him
The fish swallowed him while he was blameworthy
They forgot their fish, and it took its course into the sea
Their fish came to them openly on their sabbath day
He threw it down, and it was a snake, moving swiftly
It was a serpent, manifest
Be apes, despised
Those whom God has cursed and made of them apes and pigs
This, my brother, has ninety-nine ewes, and I have one ewe
I bring down leaves for my sheep
When the sheep of a people strayed into the field at night

themes.title: Fruits
themes.hook: The fig and olive God swears by, the date palm that fed Maryam, grapes, pomegranates, the lote tree, and the fruits of Paradise and Hell.
overview: Fruits are among the Qur'an's favourite signs of God's generosity and creativity. "It is He who sends down water from the sky... and from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low, and gardens of grapes, olives and pomegranates, similar and dissimilar. Look at its fruit when it yields and at its ripening" (6:99).

The fig appears once, in a divine oath, alongside the olive: "By the fig and the olive" (95:1). The olive appears more often: the "blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor of the west" in the Light verse (24:35), and the tree from Mount Sinai that produces oil (23:20).

The date palm is the most frequently mentioned fruit tree. It fed Maryam in labour: "Shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates" (19:25). Its tall trunks and layered clusters are signs (50:10). The tiniest parts of the date stone, its thread, speck and skin, are used to describe the smallest possible thing (4:49; 4:53; 35:13).

Grapes are paired with palms in gardens (2:266; 18:32; 36:34). Pomegranates appear as signs and in Paradise (6:141; 55:68). The lote tree marks the farthest boundary of the heavens (53:14) and grows thornless in Paradise (56:28). Bani Israel asked for vegetables, cucumbers, garlic, lentils and onions instead of manna (2:61).

Paradise has fruits "of every kind", never cut off nor forbidden (56:32-33), clusters hanging low (69:23), that resemble the fruits of this world (2:25). Hell has the tree of Zaqqum, whose fruit is like the heads of devils (37:62-65).
lessons: Every fruit is a sign: one water, countless tastes and colours.
Remember the Giver when you eat; gratitude is the response.
The fruits of this world are a foretaste of Paradise.

p.l: By the fig and the olive, Mount Sinai and this secure city
Lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree, neither of the east nor the west
A tree issuing from Mount Sinai which produces oil
Shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripened, fresh dates
Lofty palm trees having fruit arranged in layers
People like trunks of palm trees uprooted
You would see the people therein fallen as if they were hollow trunks of palm trees
I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees

subs.t: The smallest things: the date stone

p.l: They will not be wronged even as much as the thread inside a date seed
They would not give the people even as much as the speck on a date seed
They do not possess even as much as the membrane of a date seed
God is the cleaver of grain and date seeds
Would one of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines?
Two gardens of grapevines, surrounded with palm trees
From the fruits of the palm trees and grapevines
Gardens of palm trees and grapevines
Gardens and grapevines
Olives and pomegranates, similar yet varied
Olives and pomegranates; eat of its fruit and give its due
In them are fruit, palm trees and pomegranates
At the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary
Among lote trees with thorns removed, and banana trees layered with fruit
We replaced their gardens with gardens of bitter fruit, tamarisks and something of sparse lote trees
Its green herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions
A seed of grain which grows seven spikes
The weight of a mustard seed
Grain, grapes and herbage, olives and palm trees, fruit and grass
From all of the fruits He made two mates; watered with one water, yet some exceed others in taste
Fruits of varying colours
Provide its people with fruits
To which are brought the fruits of all things
It produces its fruit all the time
His fruits were encompassed
The companions of the garden who swore to cut its fruit in the morning
Whenever they are provided with fruit therefrom, they say: this is what we were provided before
In both of them are of every fruit, two kinds
Abundant fruit, neither limited nor forbidden
Its fruit to be picked hanging near
Its fruit to be picked will be lowered in compliance
The tree of zaqqum; its emerging fruit is as if it was heads of the devils
The tree of zaqqum is food for the sinner

themes.title: Trees and plants
themes.hook: The good tree and the evil tree, the forbidden tree, the burning bush, the tree of the pledge, Yunus's gourd, and trees that prostrate.
overview: Trees in the Qur'an are both real and symbolic, and some of its most memorable images are built on them.

The good word is "like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and whose branches are in the sky, giving its fruit at all times by permission of its Lord"; the evil word is "like an evil tree, uprooted from the surface of the earth, having no stability" (14:24-26). The blessed olive tree in the Light verse (24:35) gives oil that almost glows without being touched by fire.

Trees mark turning points in sacred history. The forbidden tree tested Adam and Hawwa (2:35; 7:19), and Satan renamed it "the tree of eternity" to tempt them (20:120). Musa was called from a tree in the blessed spot at the valley's edge (28:30). The believers pledged allegiance to the Prophet ﷺ "under the tree" at Hudaybiyah, and God was pleased with them (48:18). Yunus, cast out ill, was shaded by a gourd plant (37:146). Maryam was fed by a palm tree (19:25). The Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary marks where the Prophet's ascension reached (53:14).

Trees also teach about God. They prostrate to Him with the stars (55:6). Fire comes from green trees (36:80). And if every tree on earth were pens and the sea ink, God's words would never be exhausted (31:27).
In Paradise there are lote trees without thorns and abundant shade (56:28-30); in Hell, the tree of Zaqqum (37:62).
lessons: A good word is like a good tree: rooted, rising and always fruitful.
Sacred moments in history happened beneath trees; nature witnesses faith.
Every tree glorifies its Creator.

subs.t: The good tree and the evil tree

p.l: A good word is like a good tree; a bad word like a bad tree uprooted
Lit from the oil of a blessed olive tree
Do not approach this tree
When they tasted of the tree
Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?

subs.t: The tree of the burning bush

p.l: He was called from the right side of the valley in the blessed spot, from the tree
When they pledged allegiance to you under the tree
We caused to grow over him a gourd vine
The pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree

subs.t: The Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary

p.l: At the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, near it the Garden of Refuge
The stars and trees prostrate
The trees and the moving creatures prostrate to God
He who made for you from the green tree fire
Have you seen the fire that you ignite? Is it you who produced its tree?

subs.t: If every tree were a pen

p.l: If whatever trees upon the earth were pens
We produce thereby the growth of all things
Every beautiful kind; gardens and grain from the harvest
Vegetation mingles with it and becomes dry remnants scattered by the winds
Among lote trees with thorns removed, and extended shade
The tree of zaqqum, a tree issuing from the bottom of the Hellfire
The accursed tree mentioned in the Qur'an

themes.title: The elements
themes.hook: Water as the source of life, fire from green trees, wind as messenger and punishment, clay as human origin, and iron sent down.
overview: The Qur'an returns repeatedly to the basic elements of the world, each carrying both blessing and warning.

Water: "We made from water every living thing" (21:30). Rain is sent down in measure and stored in the earth (23:18); it revives dead land (25:48-49); the sweet and salt seas are kept apart (25:53). It is a favour easily taken away: "If your water were to become sunken, who could bring you flowing water?" (67:30). Water also destroyed: the flood of Nuh, and the sea that closed over Pharaoh.

Fire: God brings fire out of green trees (36:80) and asks "Have you seen the fire you kindle?" (56:71-73). Musa saw a fire on the mountain and found revelation (20:10). For Ibrahim, fire became cool and safe (21:69). Jinn were made from smokeless fire (55:15), and Iblis boasted of his fiery origin (7:12). Fire is also the punishment of the Hereafter.
Wind: God sends winds as bearers of good news before His mercy (7:57), as fertilisers of clouds and plants (15:22), as servants to Sulayman (21:81), and as destruction to 'Ad (69:6-7).
Earth and clay: humanity was created from dust and clay (55:14; 30:20), "from it We created you, into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you out another time" (20:55).

Iron: "We sent down iron, in which is great strength and benefits for people" (57:25). It was made soft for Dawud (34:10), and Dhul-Qarnayn built his barrier from blocks of iron and molten copper (18:96). A whole surah is named after it.
lessons: Each element is both a blessing and a reminder of our dependence on God.
From the earth we came and to it we return.
Strength, like iron, is given for benefit and justice.

p.l: We made from water every living thing
We sent down rain from the sky in measure and settled it in the earth
We send down from the sky pure water, to bring to life a dead land
One fresh and sweet, one salty and bitter, with a barrier between
If your water were to become sunken
The water that you drink: if We willed, We could make it bitter
He made for you from the green tree fire
Have you seen the fire that you ignite?
When he saw a fire and said to his family: stay here; I have perceived a fire
O fire, be coolness and safety upon Ibrahim
He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire
You created me from fire and created him from clay
He sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy
We have sent the fertilising winds
Among His signs is that He sends the winds as bringers of good tidings
To Sulayman the wind, blowing forcefully
'Ad were destroyed by a screaming violent wind
We sent against them the barren wind
He created man from clay like pottery
He created you from dust
From the earth We created you, to it We return you, and from it We will extract you another time
God has caused you to grow from the earth a progressive growth
We sent down iron, wherein is great military might and benefits for people
We made pliable for him iron, and for Sulayman We made flow the spring of copper
Bring me sheets of iron; pour over it molten copper
Your hearts became like stones or even harder; among stones are those from which rivers burst
Striking them with stones of hard clay

themes.title: Light and darkness
themes.hook: "God is the Light of the heavens and the earth": guidance as light, misguidance as layers of darkness, and the light believers carry on the Day.
overview: Light and darkness are among the Qur'an's most powerful images. "God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp; the lamp is within glass, the glass as if it were a pearly star, lit from a blessed olive tree... Light upon light. God guides to His light whom He wills" (24:35).

Guidance is described as bringing people "out of the darknesses into the light" (2:257; 14:1; 57:9), and the Qur'an itself is called a light (4:174; 5:15; 64:8). Darkness is always plural in these verses, and light is singular: there are many ways to be lost and one way to be guided.

The deeds of those without faith are pictured as "darknesses in a deep sea, covered by waves upon waves, above them clouds: darknesses, some upon others; when one puts out his hand he can hardly see it. Whoever God has not granted light has no light" (24:40).

On the Day of Judgment, believers will have their light running before them and on their right (57:12; 66:8), while the hypocrites will plead: "Wait for us, that we may take some of your light" (57:13).

Physical light is a sign too: the sun as a radiant lamp and the moon as a light (10:5; 71:16), night and day as signs (17:12). Those who try to extinguish God's light with their mouths will fail; God will perfect His light (61:8).
lessons: Guidance is light; seek it in the Qur'an.
There are many darknesses but one light.
Your light on the Day is built by your faith and deeds now.

themes.title: Places
themes.hook: Makkah, Madinah, al-Aqsa, Egypt, Mount Sinai, the valley of Tuwa, al-Judi, Babylon, the dunes of 'Ad, the rock city of Thamud, Madyan and Saba'.
overview: The Qur'an names relatively few places, and each one carries meaning.

Makkah is named once as Makkah (48:24) and once as Bakkah, home of the first House established for mankind (3:96). God swears by "this secure city" (95:3; 90:1-2), and Ibrahim prayed for its security and provision (2:126; 14:35). Its rites are named: Safa and Marwa (2:158), Arafat (2:198), al-Mash'ar al-Haram (2:198). Madinah appears as Yathrib, where the hypocrites spread panic during the Trench (33:13), and as al-Madinah (63:8; 9:101).

The Night Journey connects al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, "whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1), and the Holy Land is the land God ordained for Bani Israel (5:21). Egypt (Misr) is the setting for Yusuf and Musa; Mount Sinai (Tur Sina') is sworn by alongside the fig and olive (95:2), and the sacred valley of Tuwa is where Musa was told to remove his sandals (20:12).

Other places mark the stories of earlier peoples: al-Judi, where the ark came to rest (11:44); Babylon, where Harut and Marut warned against sorcery (2:102); Iram of the pillars (89:7); al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes of 'Ad (46:21); al-Hijr, the rock dwellings of Thamud (15:80); Madyan, the town of Shu'ayb (7:85); and Saba', with its two gardens (34:15). The cave of the sleepers (18:9) and the cave of the Hijrah (9:40) are places of refuge.
The Qur'an's reason for naming these places is that people should "travel through the land and see" (3:137): places are witnesses to history.
lessons: Makkah is the centre of worship, made secure by God's command.
Al-Aqsa and its surroundings are blessed in the Qur'an.
Places of past nations are lessons to be visited with reflection.

themes.title: Architecture and structures
themes.hook: Thamud's carved mountains, Iram of the pillars, Pharaoh's tower, Dhul-Qarnayn's iron barrier, Sulayman's glass palace, and the Ka'bah.
overview: The Qur'an describes buildings as expressions of the people who built them, either of faith and justice or of pride.

Some are monuments of arrogance. 'Ad built "a sign on every elevation" for amusement and fortresses as if they would live forever (26:128-129); their city Iram "had lofty pillars, the like of which had never been created in the lands" (89:7-8). Thamud "carved out the rocks in the valley" and built palaces in the plains (89:9; 7:74). Pharaoh, "owner of the stakes" (89:10), ordered Haman to fire bricks and build a tower so he could "look at the God of Musa" (28:38; 40:36-37). None protected them.

Others are works of faith. Ibrahim and Ismail raised the foundations of the Ka'bah while praying "Our Lord, accept from us" (2:127). The mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is contrasted with the "mosque of harm" built to divide believers: "Is one who laid the foundation of his building on righteousness better, or one who laid it on the edge of a crumbling cliff?" (9:108-109).

Some show power used justly. Dhul-Qarnayn built a barrier of iron and molten copper against Gog and Magog, refusing payment and calling it "a mercy from my Lord" (18:94-98). Sulayman's jinn built prayer chambers, statues and great basins for him (34:13), and his palace floor of smooth glass led the Queen of Saba' to faith (27:44). Saba' had a great dam whose collapse destroyed their gardens (34:16).
The Qur'an also notes the believers in ranks "as if they were a solid structure" (61:4): the best building is a united community.
lessons: Buildings cannot protect a people from God; faith and justice can.
Build on taqwa, not on pride.
Use skill and power for the common good, as Dhul-Qarnayn did.

themes.title: Objects and symbols
themes.hook: Musa's staff, Yusuf's shirt, the king's cup, the Ark of the Covenant, Bilqis's throne, the Tablets, the pen, and the scales.
overview: Certain objects in the Qur'an carry whole stories, and following them is a memorable way to study the text.

Musa's staff is the most versatile: he leaned on it and herded sheep with it (20:18); it became a serpent before Pharaoh, swallowed the magicians' illusions, parted the sea, and struck water from a rock (20:20; 7:117; 26:63; 2:60). Its journey shows an ordinary thing transformed by God's command.

Yusuf's shirt appears three times: stained with false blood to deceive his father (12:18), torn from behind to prove his innocence (12:25-28), and finally cast over his father's face to restore his sight (12:93-96). The king's drinking cup, placed in Binyamin's bag, kept the brother with Yusuf (12:70-76).

The Ark of the Covenant (tabut) carried tranquillity and relics of the families of Musa and Harun, borne by angels as a sign of Talut's kingship (2:248). The Tablets given to Musa contained guidance and mercy (7:145; 7:154). Bilqis's throne was brought to Sulayman before the blink of an eye (27:38-40), and his glass palace floor led her to faith (27:44). Nuh's ark became a sign for all (29:15). The table spread from heaven was requested by Isa's disciples (5:112-115). Sulayman's staff, eaten by a creature of the earth, revealed his death (34:14).
Some objects are symbols of God's order: the pen by which He taught (68:1; 96:4), the Preserved Tablet (85:22), the Throne and Footstool (2:255), and the scales of justice on the Day (21:47).
lessons: God can make ordinary objects carry extraordinary meaning.
Evidence matters: a torn shirt proved innocence.
The pen and the scales stand for knowledge and justice, the pillars of a just life.
